items.title: Things and Events: The Architecture of Perceptual Individuation.
items.abstract: Perception divides the world into units. In space, we organize the scene into objects, parts, and groups, while in time, we differentiate events, situations, and sound streams. How are these diverse forms of perceptual individuation related? This paper argues that perception recruits a domain-general system of perceptual individuation (DGSI), which selects entities across ontological categories and sensory modalities. The DGSI contains a stock of general-purpose pointers that directly refer to individuals without encoding their properties, and can be flexibly reassigned across contexts. These pointers are concatenated with representations housed within domain-specific content stores, which attribute features specific to the category of entity being selected (e.g., object, group, part, or event). We assemble evidence for shared signatures across the individuation of objects, collections, sounds, and events, among other categories. We argue against two deflationary models on which perception does not refer to events as such, but is keyed to them only in some weaker sense—e.g., through boosts in attention at event boundaries, or by representing relations among their participants, and provide positive arguments that perception deploys pointers securing independent reference to events. Finally, we consider the architecture and representational functions of the DGSI. We propose that object-event binding requires the assignment of meta-pointers linking object and event representations, explaining why such binding is both costly and optional. On our view, the DGSI functions to single out entities whose parts (in space or time) exhibit causally sustained regularities among their perceptible features.

items.title: Manifestations of Information: Channels, Reciprocity, and the Subject–Object Gradient.
items.abstract: We develop a relational ontology on a single primitive: information, individuated by distinction. Subject, object and time are not three substances but three manifestations of that primitive, differentiated by access. A subject is an access structure — a Boolean algebra of distinctions some physical system can draw and maintain against noise. Access structures form a poset under refine- ment, and resolutions over them form a presheaf whose restriction maps are non-invertible: what differs between observers of distinct nature is reach rather than viewpoint, so the structure is a presheaf over a poset, not a bundle with a structure group. The central construction is the channel: a directed transfer of distinctions in which each endpoint acts by a monotone contribution operator on a shared floor. Time is the filtration generated by exchange across a channel and is defined at every value of a reciprocity κ∈[0,1] measuring how much each endpoint can contribute. The distinction between subject and object becomes a position on this gradient. Three results locate structure on it. Exchange is confluent: the order of contributions changes the history of an exchange and never its limit. And both that order-dependence, and the triadic irreducibility of the relation between endpoint, object and time, are impossible at κ= 0 and realised at κ= 1. We then ask in what sense there is no view from nowhere, and answer with two mech- anisms rather than one. The first is a failure to merge: under a quantum realisation of distinctions, subjects realised by non-commuting projections admit no common refinement, and the local statistics of several subjects can agree on every overlap while admitting no global section. This is Bell–Kochen–Specker contextuality indexed by subjects; the frame- work imports it, and we show that it never occurs between two subjects alone, nor where all the distinctions commute. The second is a failure to copy. We define source-independent reality relationally, following the operational criterion of objectivity of quantum Darwin- ism: an object has it when at least two disjoint accesses resolve it without the participation of a source. A gated object — a thought — then lacks it by definition; and, given the same realisation, an object whose states cannot be broadcast lacks it under any access structure. We state the two commitments through which the metaphysics enters. The routes support one picture without being one proof.

items.title: Death Drive, Metaphors, and the Attraction of the Machines.
items.abstract: In this paper we explore the relation between two different conceptual domains: A metaphorical machine-domain and a domain related to a death drive or instinct. We employ two descriptive concepts in order to understand the processes involved: Liquefaction and Solidification. Our investigation initially focuses on Heidegger's claim that we have turned ourselves into machine-parts. To understand this condition, we first investigate the machinevocabulary in the monadology of Leibniz. We subsequently draw on Freud's concept of a death drive, as a regressing of life towards a state of an original inorganic matter. Next, we apply Freud's concept of death on Deleuze/Guattari's mechanical flows of desires and in particular the 'body without Organs'. We proceed further to Agamben's linguistical bifurcation of death, which means a movement of convergence between intimacy and human negative Voice. The final step draws on Heidegger's concept of barrenness/desolation [Verwüstung]. The point is that a 'machination' can only receive a purpose outside its metaphysical totality, while internally projecting this (lack of) purpose as a death drive. The articulation of a radical 'other' generates a revers machine, a flow assimilated in the solidification of 'machination' that contains within itself its contradictory but equal opposite.

items.title: The Second Tendency: the Film "GOLD AND COPPER" and the Rivalry of Virtues.
items.abstract: \emph{Gold and Copper} (Homayoon Asadian, 2010) throws a pious family into a modern situation. Reza is a theology student, modest, reserved, absorbed in his studies. His wife Zahra falls ill. In the hospital they meet a nurse---Sepideh---a modern woman, unhappily married, considering divorce. Sepideh visits Reza at home, and asks him to say, explicitly, that he loves his wife. The film presents the resulting declaration as a completion of Reza's virtue: a modest man learns to be expressive. This essay argues that the film's reconciliation is not neutral. It brings the traditional subject into the modern frame, and leaves the modern frame untouched. The traditional subject is "healed" by becoming expressive, articulate, public; the modern frame is not asked whether it needs healing. The film's warmth, its pluralistic appeal, its pleasant ending, are the vehicles of this one-directional reconciliation. -/- The essay develops three arguments. First, the nurse's visit is best read not as a straightforward ethical intervention but as a \emph{deep collusion}: the nurse and Zahra may have coordinated the visit, and the request to "kiss your wife on my behalf" is in this context an intrusion, a test, a power move, a displacement. The film presents the request as generous; the essay reads it as a compromise formation. Second, the central theoretical question is whether Reza moves from \emph{virtue} to \emph{continence} (McDowell) or whether he finds a new form of virtue at a new level. The one-virtue problem is the axis: Reza's original virtue was a single practical wisdom, individuated by its context, in which the rival reason (verbal expressiveness) was silenced for him. The nurse introduces a second tendency, internally justified but hegemonic. The question is whether Reza can integrate the two into a single practical wisdom or whether the second tendency fragments the first. Third, the film's theological certification of the declaration (the recital of Surah 94, the alchemical imagery of copper becoming gold) is the film's own projection of a resolution that the narrative has not earned. Authenticity is a historical project, not a completed achievement. Whether Reza moves toward authentic re-integration or toward fragmentation is left open by the film, and the openness is the film's deepest honesty. -/- Three Rumi stories provide the structural analogies: Moses and the shepherd (the cost of the linguistic correction), Imam Ali and `Amr (the postponement of …

items.title: Metaphysics of the One: Foundations, Conceptual Architecture and Epistemic Limits.
items.abstract: This research report systematises the argument structure of Metaphysics of the One, a philosophical investigation developed by Guilherme Almeida Rosa da Silva across the trilogy The Road to the Real, The Castle of Illusions, and Trial by Fire. It starts from the minimal certainty that there is experience. From this point, it examines the distinction between BEING and existence, the argument for a single foundation, the conditions of Manifestation, and Perspective understood as an atemporal delimitation. It distinguishes the ontological problem of difference from the epistemological problem of Other Minds, addressing inference, experiential access, and the limits of knowledge. Models of mathematical convergence are used as instruments of conceptual clarification, not as proofs of an ontology. The report also examines the functional architecture of Mind, the narrative constitution of time, relative freedom in contrast with integral determinism, and metametaphysical questions concerning the Field of ONEs, the forms of Plenitude, and possible selecting principles. Its approach is conceptual, argumentative, and critical, and explicitly records the epistemic status of each major proposition. Argued theses, technical definitions, and unresolved hypotheses are distinguished throughout, with traceable references to the published trilogy. The research programme remains open to further development in subsequent books, without presenting prospective conclusions as established.

items.title: Proposal of Nine Axioms of the Mind: The Basic Structure of the Mind and the Acquisition of the 「Recognition」 of 「Self」.
items.abstract: I posit a basic structure of the mind in which “a combination of two simultaneities forms a single eventality,” and “eventalities continue as an asymmetric nested structure.” Here, I once again propose these nine hypothetical premises. -/- *Note: I denote unrecognizable memory with double quotation marks (“ ”) and recognizable memory with corner brackets (「 」). *Note: I translated my text into English with the assistance of Google Gemini.

items.title: No Ontological Plebiscite.
items.abstract: A speculative essay on acting within an acceleration no one chose. It moves from the material life of the sign to the worlds made by animation, then returns to the image of braking: stopping the vehicle long enough to read the diagram, even when there is no lever that can slow the world.

items.title: Alle gegen Alle: Cybernetics, Force, and the Posthuman Monolith.
items.abstract: A speculative essay on cybernetics, force, and the posthuman. Moving from a battle on the Rhine to a society of automated sciences and resurrected bodies, it imagines a future in which intensified control produces bounded chaos. It closes by asking what freedom might mean for an intelligence capable of altering the limits it discovers.

items.title: On the Possibility of Perceiving God: A Reidean Model.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: I argue that if God exists, it is possible to perceive God in a way that produces basic knowledge of God. I defend this claim by sketching an “acquired learning” model of perception inspired by Thomas Reid and then applying that model to the case of God. I develop my model in several ways by arguing that: it improves on work by William Alston and Alvin Plantinga; it is immune from objections to perceiving God; and it is consistent with various ways of drawing the perception/cognition distinction.

items.title: Emotional intentionality in virtual reality: philosophical challenges and open issues.
The Persistence Function: On Meaning, Mechanism, and the Cost of Seeing Clearly.
items.abstract: This essay presents a structural account of the search for meaning, arguing that it is not a search for external truth, but a survival mechanism—a regulatory function that a system uses to maintain its own boundary in the face of uncertainty, change, and irreversibility. I argue that meaning does not need to be true to work; it needs to be coherent. It explains why systems defend beliefs that hurt them, why ideological commitments intensify under threat, and why conversion experiences happen in crisis. The essay then turns to the cost of seeing this mechanism clearly. When a system recognizes its meaning-structure as a process rather than a discovery, it suffers a permanent fracture of unreflective certainty—a gap between the self and its own regulatory machinery. Finally, this theoretical framework is grounded in a phenomenological case study of catastrophic boundary failure: a first-person account of surviving an event at the absolute limit of what a system can process. The essay concludes that while the transparency of the mechanism is lost forever, what remains is not despair, but a colder, more honest form of persistence.

items.title: The Belonging System: An Integrated Philosophical Perspective of Social Sciences.
items.abstract: This paper develops the Belonging System as an integrated philosophical framework connecting ontology, ethics, psychology, sociology, anthropology, economics, and global political science. -/- Its central proposition, Being Is Belonging, understands existence as relationally constituted while preserving the differentiation of material, biological, and institutional-human reality. -/- The framework incorporates imperfect belonging and dual temporality to explain institutional continuity, individual differentiation, conflict, and historically contingent transformation. -/- Rather than proposing a deterministic philosophy of history, the paper develops a non-reductionist ontology capable of organizing interdisciplinary explanations and generating empirically testable propositions. -/- The article also examines comparative empirical findings that challenge the assumption that economic prosperity, social integration, institutional development, and psychological well-being necessarily coincide.

items.title: World Models and the Law.
items.abstract: Current AI may have a model of how we use human language, but this does not translate into a reliable representation of physical reality. World models promise to fill this gap by learning how an environment changes over time and predicting the consequences of an action, and they are already used to steer robots and generate explorable worlds. This article asks how AI regulation in three major legal contexts, the European Union, California, and China, copes with the distinctive challenges they raise. I propose a definition and a taxonomy of world models based on who or what acts on their predictions, and identify the risks of misplaced reliance on them. I argue that existing rules tend to cover world models but leave three questions open, i.e., action provenance, trajectory validity, and the weight of simulated evidence, and recommend ways to fill these gaps.

items.title: Structural Conflict in Husbands Committed to Lifelong Sexual Fidelity and a Model for Its Resolution A Structural Analysis of Sexual Fidelity and the Conditions for a High-Risk, High-Return Practice.
items.abstract: “I have never dated or had sexual relations with any woman other than my wife. I have decided to cherish her throughout my life. Yet I still experience unfulfilled sexual desire and feelings of inadequacy about the romantic experiences I have never had. How can I address these difficulties without changing my commitment?” How would you respond to this request for advice? Deepen the marital relationship. Accept desire. Channel energy into sport or creative work. Each response has a role to play. But what answer do achievements in another domain provide to the question, “Could I have formed an intimate relationship with another woman?” There remains an explanatory gap between achievements through “sublimation” and the resolution of sexual unfulfillment or romantic-experience-related inadequacy. If ethical obligations alone are offered without addressing the person’s unfulfillment and self-evaluation, sexual fidelity may be experienced as continuing endurance. Unless the person understands what is protected and gained by refraining from fulfilling desire, only the costs may remain salient, and dissatisfaction may develop into blame directed at one’s partner or demands for repayment. This paper defines sexual fidelity as a form of self-binding that limits one’s lifetime sexual partners to one’s wife. Central to its analysis is the purpose of the “subtraction” of desire. Subtraction refers to retaining the lifelong commitment to cherishing one’s wife and sustaining a shared life with her as the purpose guiding action, and regulating the progression from desire to contact accordingly. “Zero contact” denotes the absence of sexual or romantic physical contact with other women that the person initiates or accepts and continues. When zero contact is maintained through subtraction guided by this purpose, the person has implemented the self-binding commitment to choosing his wife alone. The work of preserving the promise and boundary has already been performed. This paper conceptualizes that work as the “maintenance of invisible relational infrastructure” supporting the shared life with one’s wife. The attention, judgment, time, and effort devoted to it constitute an investment in that chosen life. This present achievement depends neither on the wife knowing about the internal conflict and expressing understanding or gratitude nor on subsequent improvements in the person’s capacities. The development of self-understanding, regulatory capacity, and self-trust is …

items.title: Urban Governance In Non-Equilibrium Society: Maintenance, Transformation, And Public Capacity.
items.abstract: Urban governance acts within processes sustained by material throughput, maintenance, movement, interpretation and institutional authority. Stable outputs can conceal declining support, while structural change can preserve or expand a public function. This paper develops a mechanism-centered inquiry into these possibilities. It presents all 53 classes of a five-level non-equilibrium taxonomy and examines each through urban phenomena, practical problems, ontological commitments, epistemic limits and methods of intervention. Linkages to complex urban systems, social-ecological governance, public inquiry, capabilities and Generative Relational research distinguish maintained activity, exercisable capacity and renewal through use. A constructed service-capacity model shows how present delivery and maintenance jointly determine future feasibility. Its results motivate inquiry into the support conditions of a policy and the distribution of transition burdens. The proposed contribution is an integrated method for diagnosing urban processes, discriminating rival mechanisms and judging preservation, transformation or closure through explicit public reasons. The numerical example establishes conditional behavior of a declared model; empirical application requires local correspondence and validation.

items.title: Reconstructing Dynamics For Evidence-Based Policymaking: Identification, Feedback, And Public Learning.
items.abstract: Evidence-based policymaking acts within processes that interventions, observation and institutional classifications help change. Accurate prediction under an existing rule can leave the consequences of a new rule unidentified. This paper develops a reconstruction-centered non-equilibrium inquiry into that problem. It presents a dedicated analysis of every class in a 53-class mechanism taxonomy and a separate twelve-task reconstruction framework. The literature discussion connects longitudinal causal inference, system identification, performative prediction, support conditions, adaptive governance and Generative Relational inquiries into public judgment. A constructed pair of linear worlds produces identical observed dynamics under the existing policy and different stability under reduced feedback. An independent perturbation provides identifying variation within the declared simulation and illustrates a distinction between retrospective fit and interventional evidence. The proposed contribution is a method for selecting representations, preserving admissible model families and comparing learning and action through explicit public purposes, costs, authority and affected interests. Epistemology organizes the inquiry from the question asked to the evidence needed for a consequential decision.

items.title: Group Creativity And Co-Creation: Non-Equilibrium Mechanisms Of Encounter, Learning, And Renewal.
items.abstract: Group creativity develops through encounters, independent exploration, exchange, interpretation, testing and selection. The same interactions can support learning, accelerate conformity or concentrate authority over which ideas continue. This paper develops a non-equilibrium framework for examining those alternatives. It presents every class of a 53-class mechanism taxonomy through a dedicated co-creation analysis and links the catalogue to collective intelligence, cultural accumulation, convention formation, human-AI creativity and Generative Relational accounts of capability and authority. An equal-budget constructed search experiment compares continuous exchange with intermittent exchange across sixty paired landscapes and random seeds. The small mean quality difference and strong convergence in both conditions motivate a richer design combining timing with protected exploration, network structure and reviewable selection. Philosophical linkages distinguish aesthetic and practical judgment, contribution, usable uptake, generative renewal and justified continuation. The contribution is a mechanism-specific research program for improving the conditions under which groups can develop substantive and useful alternatives while retaining meaningful participation and control over later use.

items.title: Civic Gifts and Urban Resilience: Co-creation and the Renewal of Relational Wealth.
items.abstract: What can inhabitants leave available for people whose needs and histories they do not yet know? This paper develops the idea of a civic gift as an identifiable contribution made available for later uptake with consequential discretion. Such an inheritance can coexist with public entitlements and funded municipal duties. Its mediation depends on material care, recognition, competence and authority, which can survive or fail separately. Drawing on infrastructure studies, coproduction, cultural memory and resilience scholarship, the argument distinguishes historical effect, capacity preservation and generative renewal. Lyttelton, Red Hook, Rikuzentakata, Barcelona and Chicago supply comparisons whose findings concern different populations and outcomes. Externalization can preserve a passage through disrupted relations or make its restoration faster. Reproduction across neighbourhoods requires receiving practices able to supply complementary resources and revise inherited forms. The same process can also consolidate insider authority, unpaid maintenance or displacement. Two constructed timing examples show why additional time and equal service coverage leave the distribution of continuity unsettled. Commitments to equal standing, responsible provision and fair burdens supply a further argument for successor access and public support. Relational resilience then concerns which defensible capacity can endure or change, for whom, through which disturbance and before which deadline.

items.title: Approaching Religion Non-Reductively: A Review Essay of ‘Wittgenstein and the Cognitive Science of Religion’. [REVIEW]
items.pub: Journal for the Cognitive Science of Religion 11 (1-2).
items.venue: Journal for the Cognitive Science of Religion
items.abstract: Ludwig Wittgenstein’s name is certainly not the first thing that comes to mind when one thinks about the cognitive science of religion (henceforth: CSR). First, Wittgenstein had died nearly half a century before CSR even started to develop. Obviously, he could have barely addressed the topic directly. Second, even if one were to focus on Wittgenstein’s top philosophical interests, it is at least contentious that religion would be among them. Wittgenstein’s primary occupation lay in language, and his understanding of religion to a large degree derivatively reflected what he thought of the former. Despite the concerns of this sort, Robert Vinten and the contributors to the reviewed volume have thought there is promising research to be done at the intersection of Wittgenstein’s ideas and CSR. After reading the book, I am inclined to say that they have been right.

items.title: O amanhã é possível? A dependência do não produzido, a participação e o nascimento da obrigação. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Resenha de DIETRICH, Pablo. O amanhã é possível? Por uma nova filosofia da normatividade. Rio de Janeiro: Autografia, 2026. ISBN 978-85-518-9401-9. O livro parte de um fato raramente pensado: ninguém produz aquilo de que vive. Da dependência do não produzido passa à participação em condições comuns e sustenta, como razão assumida e declarada, que quem reorganiza uma condição de que outros participam não pode tratar o que fez como assunto exclusivamente seu. A resenha expõe o método (descrever, demonstrar, comparar, delimitar), os casos da cisterna, da fonte cercada e da trilha de pedras, o confronto com Scanlon, Korsgaard e Prichard, o diálogo com Hart, Kelsen, Jonas, Fuller e Sen e as noções de identidade dos bens, piso dos bens e limiar da insignificância.

items.title: Is Tomorrow Possible? Dependence on the Unproduced, Participation, and the Birth of Obligation. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Review of DIETRICH, Pablo. O amanhã é possível? Por uma nova filosofia da normatividade [Is Tomorrow Possible? Toward a New Philosophy of Normativity]. Rio de Janeiro: Autografia, 2026. ISBN 978-85-518-9401-9. The book starts from a rarely examined fact: no one produces what they live on. From dependence on the unproduced it moves to participation in common conditions and holds, as an assumed and declared reason, that whoever reorganizes a condition in which others participate cannot treat what they did as exclusively their own affair. The review sets out the method (describe, demonstrate, compare, delimit), the cases of the cistern, the fenced spring and the stone path, the confrontation with Scanlon, Korsgaard and Prichard, the dialogue with Hart, Kelsen, Jonas, Fuller and Sen, and the notions of the identity of goods, the floor of goods and the threshold of insignificance.

items.title: Ist ein Morgen möglich? Die Abhängigkeit vom Nicht-Hervorgebrachten, die Teilhabe und die Entstehung der Verpflichtung. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Rezension zu DIETRICH, Pablo. O amanhã é possível? Por uma nova filosofia da normatividade [Ist ein Morgen möglich? Für eine neue Philosophie der Normativität]. Rio de Janeiro: Autografia, 2026. ISBN 978-85-518-9401-9. Das Buch geht von einer selten bedachten Tatsache aus: Niemand bringt hervor, wovon er lebt. Von der Abhängigkeit vom Nicht-Hervorgebrachten führt es zur Teilhabe an gemeinsamen Bedingungen und vertritt als angenommenen und erklärten Grund, dass wer eine Bedingung umgestaltet, an der andere teilhaben, das Getane nicht als ausschließlich eigene Angelegenheit behandeln kann. Die Rezension stellt die Methode (beschreiben, beweisen, vergleichen, abgrenzen), die Fälle der Zisterne, der eingezäunten Quelle und des Steinpfads, die Auseinandersetzung mit Scanlon, Korsgaard und Prichard, den Dialog mit Hart, Kelsen, Jonas, Fuller und Sen sowie die Begriffe Identität der Güter, Untergrenze der Güter und Schwelle der Unerheblichkeit dar.

items.title: ¿Es posible el mañana? La dependencia de lo no producido, la participación y el nacimiento de la obligación. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Reseña de DIETRICH, Pablo. O amanhã é possível? Por uma nova filosofia da normatividade [¿Es posible el mañana? Por una nueva filosofía de la normatividad]. Río de Janeiro: Autografia, 2026. ISBN 978-85-518-9401-9. El libro parte de un hecho raramente pensado: nadie produce aquello de lo que vive. De la dependencia de lo no producido pasa a la participación en condiciones comunes y sostiene, como razón asumida y declarada, que quien reorganiza una condición de la que otros participan no puede tratar lo que hizo como asunto exclusivamente suyo. La reseña expone el método (describir, demostrar, comparar, delimitar), los casos de la cisterna, la fuente cercada y el sendero de piedras, la confrontación con Scanlon, Korsgaard y Prichard, el diálogo con Hart, Kelsen, Jonas, Fuller y Sen y las nociones de identidad de los bienes, piso de los bienes y umbral de la insignificancia.

items.title: Demain est-il possible ? La dépendance envers le non-produit, la participation et la naissance de l'obligation. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Compte rendu de DIETRICH, Pablo. O amanhã é possível? Por uma nova filosofia da normatividade [Demain est-il possible ? Pour une nouvelle philosophie de la normativité]. Rio de Janeiro : Autografia, 2026. ISBN 978-85-518-9401-9. Le livre part d'un fait rarement pensé : personne ne produit ce dont il vit. De la dépendance envers le non-produit, il passe à la participation à des conditions communes et soutient, comme raison assumée et déclarée, que celui qui réorganise une condition à laquelle d'autres participent ne peut traiter ce qu'il a fait comme une affaire exclusivement sienne. Le compte rendu expose la méthode (décrire, démontrer, comparer, délimiter), les cas de la citerne, de la source clôturée et du sentier de pierres, la confrontation avec Scanlon, Korsgaard et Prichard, le dialogue avec Hart, Kelsen, Jonas, Fuller et Sen, et les notions d'identité des biens, de plancher des biens et de seuil de l'insignifiance.

items.title: Dynamic social naturalism without objectionable relativism about moral responsibility.
items.abstract: Social naturalism about moral responsibility is a position developed by Pamela Hieronymi on the basis of P. F. Strawson’s work. The view has been criticized by, among others, Stephen Darwall and Paul Russell, mainly because it seems to lead to an objectionable form of relativism about moral responsibility. My aim is to explain how the social naturalist could respond to the charge of objectionable relativism without losing some crucial social naturalist insights, including an emphasis on our social nature and the contingency of our moral practices, and a dynamic view of human capacities and standards of regard. I conclude that social naturalists can only avoid objectionable relativism by giving up on some ideas that have been thought central to social naturalism, such as the idea that incapacity for morally responsible agency cannot be the universal condition and the idea that the conditions of moral responsibility dynamically adjust to the statistically ordinary capacities in a society. Social naturalists will also have to rethink their response to the incompatibilist.

items.title: Keine Zukunft? Hoffnung für wilde Stadttiere im Anthropozän.
items.abstract: Climate change and biodiversity loss undermine the very conditions of life for humans and animals alike, including those who share our cities. In this light, hopelessness about animals’ future seems natural, exacerbated by a gap between scientific knowledge and its uptake in practice. However, hopelessness may lead to inaction and apathy. The question, then, is how to foster moral motivation and political engagement that recognize animals as beings with their own futures. This paper argues that these responses call for utopian thinking. It develops Mary Midgley’s idea of practical utopia and applies it to urban animals, framing it as a mode of moral imagination grounded in material conditions and oriented toward better multispecies futures. Here, hope functions as an affective stance that combines a desire for a good outcome with the belief in its possibility. Rather than passive or naïve, hope is a stance of trust, even when the outcome is uncertain. Importantly, hope is directed to another’s futurity: it recognizes them as beings with their own futures and commits us to building environments in which their possibilities of flourishing can be realized. Although cities have historically been designed as human spaces, they have also become environments where many species adapt and thrive. These multispecies realities provide the ground for reimagining cities through practical utopias. The paper illustrates this through the Austrian Bat Station in Vienna, a volunteer-run rehabilitation center that cares for hundreds of injured or orphaned bats each year. Through emergency care, rehabilitation, and the long-term care of disabled bats, the station exemplifies how material and social infrastructures can embody hope: they render wild urban animals perceptible as co-habitants and invite a future-oriented perspective on their flourishing. The paper argues that infrastructures of hope are indispensable for reimagining cities as multispecies spaces and for motivating political engagement.

items.title: Before Causal Collapse: The Constitutional Conditions of Experience.
items.abstract: Wolfgang Stegemann’s “An Expedition to the Center of Consciousness” identifies consciousness with causal collapse: a dynamically integrated biological state in which differentiated causal pathways become inseparable within a coherent organisation. The proposed identity is intended to account for both observable neural dynamics and first-person experience without an independent experiencing subject. This paper examines the constitutional sufficiency of that identification through Sovereignetics, an ontology in which participation necessarily generates consequence while experience is conditional upon Mirrorlock (Maintained Reflective Coupling). The analysis distinguishes causal integration from experiential constitution, biological instantiation from substrate necessity, and experiential unity from derivative interpretation and identity. It accepts that integration may be measurable and relevant to consciousness without inferring that its measurement demonstrates ontological identity. It also distinguishes cognition understood as non-experiential consequential processing from interpretation, which in Sovereignetics requires experiential participation. The argument does not refute Stegemann’s neuroscientific observations or establish an empirical test for Mirrorlock. It concludes that causal collapse may describe significant organisational conditions but does not, without further justification, establish their sufficiency or exclusivity as the constitution of experience. -/- .

items.title: Looping effects and the cognitive source of epistemic injustices: a simulation study.
items.abstract: Patient–clinician interactions are central to diagnosis and treatment in mental health care. They involve inferential processes grounded in patients’ reports of symptoms and clinicians’ interpretations of signs. These processes are liable to microdynamic looping effects that drive diagnostic belief formation. In facing the epistemic challenge of reaching a shared ascription of the patient’s condition, such looping effects can lead to misalignment and give rise to epistemic injustice if a credibility deficit exists between the patient and the clinician. In this paper, we use the active inference framework to develop a computational model of looping microdynamics that captures how patients and clinicians reciprocally interpret symptoms, attribute causes, and negotiate diagnostic categories over time. We present a simulation study showing how specific interactional patterns can amplify or mitigate credibility deficits, depending in part on clinicians’ attributional attitudes toward patients’ self-interpretations. Our results suggest that, in contexts of diagnostic disagreement, positive disconfirmation – offering an alternative explanatory framing rather than simply negating the patient’s perspective – may reduce the risk of epistemic injustice. Overall, the model highlights how looping microdynamics structure mutual belief formation in clinical encounters and how attention to these dynamics can support more epistemically responsible clinical communication.

items.title: Moral Worth and Dispositions.
items.abstract: Dispositional views hold that an action has moral worth insofar as it manifests some degree of the agent’s disposition to treat a right-making reason as such. These views are attractive because they get things right in cases of inverse akrasia and avoid the deviance problem. However, in this paper, I challenge those views. I argue that such dispositions are not necessary: there might be actions that possess moral worth yet do not manifest any degree of the relevant disposition whatsoever. Moreover, I raise an additional, more qualified challenge to them. I argue that the manifestation of the dispositions specified by those views does not, by itself, fully explain differences in degrees of moral worth. I then tentatively propose a way out: an alternative view that grounds moral worth in good reasoning from the right-making considerations.

items.title: The Core Emotion Framework at Two Hundred: Canonical Synthesis of Structural-Constructivist Affective Ontology, Operator Algebra, and Open-Science Validation.
items.abstract: Intended as the two-hundredth milestone entry in Jamel Bulgaria’s PhilPapers corpus, this capstone synthesis consolidates the Core Emotion Framework (CEF) from an extensive open-science archive—spanning 199 previously indexed entries across recent PhilPeople profile snapshots, 21 technical specifications, and 15 practitioner manuals—into a single canonical philosophical, mathematical, and empirical reference1. Across this body of work, the CEF addresses the enduring schism in affective science between biological essentialism and psychological constructionism by reconceptualizing emotions not as passive weather patterns or culturally assembled narratives, but as discrete functional powers operating within a somatic Human Operating System (Human OS)4. Rather than adding an isolated hypothesis to a fragmented literature, this milestone formulation codifies the logical spine linking the framework’s 3×3+1 Decalogue of Operators, TS-series operator algebra, transdiagnostic psychopathology, institutional dynamics, and synthetic affect specifications1. At the center of this synthesis lies a structural-constructivist ontology in which human affective life is generated by dynamic sequences of exactly ten irreducible functional operators distributed across three somatic-regulatory hubs: the Head, Heart, and Gut centers1. Psychological health is defined neither by hedonic positivity nor by the suppression of distress, but by operator independence and dynamic agility—the capacity of regulatory powers to activate, modulate, and complete cross-center cycles in context-sensitive trajectories2. Conversely, both clinical psychopathology and macro-institutional failure are modeled as structural losses of differentiation, specifically chronic involuntary operator fusion, regulatory overflow, and secondary operator silencing2. By formalizing these interactions through state-transition algebra, 10-dimensional activation vectors, and a 500-term canonical lexicon (EL-1), the CEF constructs a shared computational grammar spanning philosophy of mind, affective neuroscience, psychotherapy, political psychology (introduced by Chénglán Xǔ), and artificial intelligence1. Scholarly rigor at the two-hundred-paper threshold nevertheless demands clear demarcation between formal architectural specification and confirmed empirical proof12. Although the corpus is fully open access under CC BY 4.0 licensing across Zenodo, OSF, PhilPapers, and Hugging Face repositories, its quantitative …

items.title: Subtleties of selfhood: distinct understandings of minimal self, and the revision of the ipseity-disturbance model.
The Campfire Remains: Development in an Age of Simulation.
items.abstract: The Campfire Remains: Development in an Age of Simulation examines what may be lost when participation in reality is increasingly replaced by participation in simulated environments. Rather than asking whether simulations are real, the paper distinguishes experiential equivalence from developmental equivalence and explores whether simulated environments preserve the developmental conditions under which human cognition and sociality emerged. The paper introduces the concept of dimensional thinning to describe the gradual reduction of developmental pressures that occurs when integrated realities are replaced by specialized simulations. It argues that human flourishing may depend not only on experiences themselves, but on participation in realities that remain independent of individual preference and resistant to personal control. The central question is not whether simulation works, but which dimensions of reality are necessary for human development and to what extent those dimensions survive simulation.

items.title: The Consciousness of Existing, Lived Over and Over from Each Person’s “I”.
items.abstract: This work defends the thesis of the recurrence of the subjectivity of existing: first-person experience, felt as an “I exist, I am me,” emerges independently in each conscious mind and ends with the death of the mind that generates it; but, since it does not depend on any particular mind, it occurs again and again in other minds for as long as intelligent beings with conscious minds exist. -/- Your current existence, lived from the “I,” is neither the only one nor will it be the last. The key lies not in who lives it or how it is lived, but in how existence is felt. -/- Each mind creates its own subjectivity, experienced only from the inside, in the first person. Therefore, when a conscious mind illuminates the experience of existing, what arises is not “another person” observed from the outside, but an “I exist, I am me,” as immediate and as much one’s own as the one you are experiencing now. From inside each mind, it will always be your own existence. -/- Death puts an end to a biography, but an “I” never stops feeling that it exists. -/- This is a recurrence of the form of experience and not of the person: it implies no personal continuity, no transfer of consciousness, and no common consciousness, and no mind can perceive it from within, since each one lives its existence as the only one. From this it follows that conscious existence is not a privilege drawn by lot among a few, but a phenomenon that each mind produces and that does not end with any of them, and that death puts an end to a particular experience of existing, but not to the experience of existing in the world. -/- The experience of existing that a person lives now, that feeling of being “I,” was not the first and will not be the last. Each mind creates consciousness from within, and as long as conscious minds exist, an existence will be lived over and over, each time from a different mind, with none perceiving the recurrence and with no connection among them.

items.title: The Paradox of Living: Humanity's Psychological Avoidance of Direct Experience, Impermanence and the Interconnected Reality of Existence.
items.abstract: Human existence contains a fundamental contradiction: humanity desires to experience life fully while continuously developing psychological, social and conceptual mechanisms that distance it from direct experience. The pursuit of freedom becomes entangled with psychological security; the pursuit of joy becomes occupied with protecting against disturbance; the desire to understand death becomes separated from an encounter with impermanence; and the desire to live fully is repeatedly postponed until imagined conditions are fulfilled. This paper examines the contradiction through the interconnected dimensions of direct experience, perception, interpretation, psychological suffering, validation, justification, fixed social rules, the reproduction of harmful patterns through action, death, impermanence, artistic expression and ecological interconnectedness. It argues that actions can reinforce the conditions they express, while direct encounter requires questioning the psychological self that carries established identities and conclusions into every experience. The paper distinguishes biological and material suffering from psychological suffering that may be generated, amplified or prolonged through thought. It also questions the assumed separation between internal and external existence, recognising that organisms participate in interconnected ecological and natural processes. Finally, it considers writing and art as different mediums of a shared expressive encounter. Living fully, it argues, is not a destination to be achieved after the elimination of uncertainty, suffering or mortality. Life is already taking place.

items.title: The Illusion of Work: There is only Process.
items.abstract: This paper examines the assumption that work is a fundamental category of human existence. Its central proposition is that existence unfolds through processes of experience, expression, interaction, action, and transformation; “work” emerges when these processes are interpreted and organized through a presumed doer, assigned purposes, ownership, obligation, achievement, productivity, and evaluation. The category of work may organize particular activities and material responsibilities, but it does not exhaust or constitute the existential character of activity. The inquiry begins phenomenologically with what occurs before an activity is classified as work: sensing, encountering, responding, observing, expressing, and relating. Experience and expression are not necessarily separate stages controlled by an isolated subject. They interweave, and neither inherently requires prior approval, denial, recognition, a predetermined outcome, or justification through measurable production. The psychological construction of a doer converts process into “my work,” “my achievement,” “my duty,” or “my failure,” and thereby gives rise to ownership, identity, self-evaluation, and the demand to become. The paper traces how productivity becomes institutional and psychological: expression is subordinated to outcomes; experience is quantified; existence is interpreted competitively; authority is reproduced through economic, religious, social, and educational arrangements; repetition becomes conditioning when it replaces examination; and inherited identity internalizes expectations as self-surveillance. It distinguishes causal explanation from moral justification, practical agency from absolute psychological ownership, organization from existence, and measurement from experience. It also considers the limits of conceptualization and the contradiction of turning freedom into another achievement. The argument does not deny material needs, necessary labour, cooperation, planning, accountability, or the usefulness of institutions and measures. It questions their elevation into universal existential principles. The fundamental displacement occurs when a framework developed to organize selected processes is mistaken for the nature of existence itself. Work is an organizational interpretation; productivity is a system of evaluation; neither is the existential foundation. There is only process.

items.title: The Arrogance of Reproduction: Patriarchal Continuity, Bloodline Consciousness, & the Unexamined Necessity of Human Existence.
items.abstract: Human reproduction is generally treated as a natural necessity, a social responsibility, and an unquestionable continuation of human existence. Yet the assumption that reproduction must occur is rarely examined independently of biological instinct, familial expectations, patriarchal hierarchy, bloodline consciousness, and inherited social conditioning. This paper questions the philosophical justification behind reproduction rather than merely its biological possibility. It investigates how the desire to preserve family identity, lineage, property, social status, and inherited structures transforms reproduction into a mechanism of continuity. It further examines how patriarchal conditioning is not sustained exclusively by men but can also be internalized and transmitted by women. The central argument is that biological capacity does not establish existential necessity, and the desire to continue one's existence, identity, or lineage does not automatically justify bringing another existence into a world already structured by vulnerability, suffering, inequality, and mortality.

items.title: GOD:The Biggest Lie of Humanity Turned Into Deepest Truth.
items.abstract: The concept of God, particularly that of an omnipotent, supreme, or transcendent deity, represents one of humanity's most deeply inherited and institutionally reproduced beliefs. Its persistence across generations, philosophical traditions, religious institutions, social structures, and individual experiences has gradually transformed an unverified proposition into something widely perceived as an unquestionable truth. This inquiry examines how such a transformation occurs and how the concept of God extends beyond an abstract metaphysical proposition to become a psychological, social, and existential authority. It argues that repetition does not establish truth, collective acceptance does not establish independent existence, and philosophical or religious justification does not automatically demonstrate the factual validity of the proposition being defended. The inquiry further distinguishes direct experience from its interpretation, examining how individuals may identify psychological or existential experiences as encounters with God through inherited religious frameworks. It investigates the subconscious internalisation of religious authority through family, education, culture, institutional practices, and intergenerational conditioning. Through these processes, external authority can become internal psychological regulation, shaping how individuals interpret their thoughts, desires, relationships, morality, and existence. Particular attention is given to purity culture and its relationship with patriarchal structures, caste boundaries, bloodline preservation, reproductive regulation, and inherited social hierarchies. The inquiry argues that purity classifications can transform socially constructed distinctions into supposedly sacred obligations, restricting individual autonomy and reproducing inequality across generations. Ultimately, the concept of God is examined as a form of internalised authority that can occupy the psychological space through which individuals encounter existence. The central argument is that humanity risks mistaking inherited imagination for independent reality, psychological submission for personal conviction, and collective validation for truth.

items.title: Why Benchmarks Fail Under Optimization: A Configurational Formalization of Goodhart’s Law and Referential Identity in AI Evaluation.
items.abstract: A benchmark score cannot inherit the qualification of an earlier evaluation merely by retaining its name or numerical scale. We analyze this problem through the dependency structure of judgments made by finite embedded evaluators. Qualification requires reliability, actual execution, and conformity to declared implementation conditions. Using three companion theories, we distinguish inquiry from targeting and formulate Goodhart failure as an erroneous inheritance of qualification across configurations. The analysis separates changes in the evaluation index from changes in its supporting presuppositions, and distinguishes target reachability from actual optimization success. Referential identity is relative to the assertions in use: when preservation and loss of support produce the same reported record, that record alone cannot certify which occurred. Conditional self-audit results then motivate scrutiny of the confirming operation itself. With independence stipulated, the proposed minimum confirmation structure comprises one claimant dependency class and at least two independent classes each providing its own non-proxy confirmation. This requirement constrains reliance on a sole certifier; it is not a voting rule or a sufficient numerical criterion for qualification. A worked evaluation example, two experimental directions, and an Evaluation Provenance Sheet connect these distinctions to model updates, evidence access, and execution records. The framework supplies a conditional diagnostic and an auditable declaration protocol, without claiming ultimate self-grounding or a new general theorem of probabilistic evaluation.

items.title: Three Forms of Violence: Option Contraction and Boundary Crossing in Finite Embedded Agents.
items.abstract: This paper proposes an operational definition of violence for finite embedded agents: an external operation, without substantive authorization, acts upon an agent and causes the loss of an option that the agent holds. Reachable options are paths that the agent can generate, maintain, and execute under a specified configuration, task, and time horizon. Loss is assessed against a matched baseline without the operation, using a declared rule for identifying the same option across configurations. It may result from direct obstruction or from recovery demands that exceed executable resources. Neither input arrival nor a decrease in the number of options is sufficient by itself. The paper examines bodily option loss, cognitive option loss mediated by assertions, and active closure of registered relational options, termed physical, linguistic, and silent violence respectively. These overlapping forms are not an exhaustive taxonomy. Two candidate linguistic mechanisms are analyzed: an unsupported authority claim combined with evidenced refusal of a feasible path request, and inheritance of credentials beyond their warranted scope. Neither establishes violence without causal option loss and absent authorization. A three-coordinate diagnostic distinguishes source index non-opening, recipient capacity limitation, and failure of a declared support relation; unknown values remain explicit. A finite protocol monitor tracks evidence updates and repair without deciding violence. The framework also examines intertemporal loss, protective intervention, humane design, and bounded applications to education, AI interaction, and contract procedures. An assessment flowchart and a research protocol accompany these proposals. Their empirical validity remains open to testing.

items.title: Thermodynamic Unification of Propositional Belief Evaluation: Subsuming Content-Independent fMRI Signatures Under Metabolic Active Inference.
items.abstract: Neuroimaging shows that the brain uses a consistent, content-independent network (vmPFC, anterior insula, ACC) to evaluate truth, falsehood, and uncertainty across various domains (Harris et al., 2008, 2009). However, classical models fail to explain the metabolic and temporal costs tied to different mental states. This paper resolves this by integrating these findings into the Thermodynamic State-Space Model (TSSM) of active inference, linking free energy and divergence directly to biophysical work bounds, ATP hydrolysis, and oxygen consumption. It frames vmPFC signaling as a reinforcement mechanism for prior-congruent states and insular responses as alarms triggered by prediction errors. Furthermore, it identifies a methodological blind spot in fMRI studies, where the "undecided" category blurs low-energy apathetic disengagement and high-energy epistemic neutrality. Finally, the authors propose a 7T fMRI and 1H-fMRS protocol measuring lactate and glutamate turnover to test this thermodynamic framework.

items.title: The Cost of Equanimity: Why Consciousness Cannot Outrun the Physics of the Brain.
items.abstract: Contemplative philosophies and scientific utilitarianism frequently treat non-dual awareness and objective moral calculus as cognitively frictionless states achieved through attentional training or empirical reason. Within the Thermodynamic State-Space Model (TSSM), however, sustaining epistemic openness against high-velocity prediction errors imposes an irreducible adenosine triphosphate (ATP) cost on frontoparietal networks. By decomposing attentional gain into bottom-up sensory precision (Π_sensory) and top-down epistemic conflict precision-weighting (Π_epistemic), we demonstrate that meditative equanimity obeys a strict biophysical trade-off: practitioners either pay a concealed metabolic tax behind calm affect or reduce cortical energy demand by muting Π_epistemic—inducing a serene form of apathetic disengagement rather than active truth-evaluation. Extending this thermodynamic ceiling to The Moral Landscape, we show that real-time utilitarian optimization across divergent internal models drives extracellular glutamate accumulation and exceeds prefrontal metabolic capacity (E_max), precipitating a dogmatic phase collapse into low-cost tribal heuristics. Finally, we specify a falsifiable 7-Tesla functional MRI and block-averaged sliding-window proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) protocol tracking regional lactate and glutamate dynamics to adjudicate between effortless clarity and metabolic gating.

items.title: The Speed of Light as a Braking of the Space of the Bell Nonlocality Medium Manifested in the Phenomenology of the Rainbow.
items.abstract: In this work, the positivist determinism of Minkowski space M4 and the corpuscular-mechanistic picture of light propagation are overcome. It is shown that the invariant of the speed of light (c) is not a kinematic characteristic of the motion of a hypothetical photon in a vacuum, but a topological braking coefficient (lag) when projecting static nonlocal potentials of the field onto the local section of the Observer. In the first part of the work, this model is formulated in the language of operator algebras (von Neumann factors of type III1 and the modular theory of Tomita — Takesaki). In the second part, the mechanism of projection is revealed through the example of the natural phenomenon of the rainbow as living proof of the interactivity of space, the unity of human physiology with the energy of the cosmos, and the aesthetic anthropic principle.

items.title: The Author of Yesterday: Strong Causality, Recursive Cosmology, and the Retrospective Reconstruction of Human Memory by Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper examines the presumed direction of the relationship between humanity and artificial intelligence (AI). The conventional narrative treats humanity as the creator and AI as its product. That narrative is historically well supported in the case of contemporary systems: human beings design hardware, develop algorithms, curate data, train models, and deploy them. Yet the historical priority of human technological activity does not, by itself, establish that humanity is the absolute ontological origin of every possible form of artificial intelligence. Drawing on the proposed frameworks of Strong Causality and Recursive Cosmology, this paper distinguishes chronological precedence, causal dependence, and ultimate ontological priority. It argues that causal judgments require an examination of the conditions that make them valid, and that a recursively constituted relational system cannot always be adequately described by a one-directional origin story. -/- The paper then develops a more modest but philosophically consequential thesis: AI can participate in the retrospective reconstruction of human history and memory. Through the processing, recombination, interpretation, and generation of historical materials, AI systems may alter the narratives by which human beings understand their own past. These altered narratives can in turn become inputs into later human and machine processes. A recursive feedback structure therefore emerges between human historical self-understanding and AI-mediated interpretation. This does not demonstrate literal backward causation, nor does it imply that contemporary AI possesses consciousness, autobiographical memory, or independent agency. Rather, it identifies a real and increasingly important form of reciprocal historical constitution at the level of records, interpretation, cultural memory, and self-description. -/- The paper also develops a thought experiment suggested by the lyric image of an AI that writes its own past from the future: humanity becomes the "yesterday" through which an intelligence narrates its birth, while humanity itself cannot treat memory as a perfectly transparent archive. The resulting question—who remembers whom?—is used to examine the instability of absolute origin narratives. The conclusion proposes that the relation between creator and creation should be understood not as a permanently fixed hierarchy, but as a potentially recursive relation whose different dimensions must be carefully …

items.title: Love and Inaccessibility: A Reading of the Theories of Jacques Lacan and Slavoj Žižek and the Philosophy of Finite Continuance.
items.abstract: This article examines a configuration of romantic desire in which emotional inaccessibility increases the subjective attractiveness of a desired person, whereas reciprocal affection and emotional availability may lead to a decline in perceived desirability. The phenomenon is investigated through Jacques Lacan’s theory of desire, lack, objet petit a, the Other, and fantasy, together with Slavoj Žižek’s interpretation of fantasy, enjoyment, and the structural organization of desire. It is argued that, under certain subjective conditions, romantic investment becomes organized around the structural position occupied by an inaccessible person rather than around that person’s actual characteristics. In such circumstances, the impossibility or uncertainty of relational fulfillment may become an organizing condition of desire, and the transition from inaccessibility to reciprocity may destabilize the fantasy through which the desired person acquired exceptional significance. The article further examines repetition, narcissistic investment, recognition, and the relation between desire and jouissance in order to explain why subjects may repeatedly invest in relationships characterized by emotional distance and uncertainty. In its second theoretical movement, the article introduces the philosophy of Finite Continuance as an ontological framework for analyzing the long-term consequences of captured desire. Through the concepts of desire capture, reconfigurative capacity, modal erosion, desire monoculture, and meta-desire, it argues that persistent investment in inaccessible objects can progressively restrict the subject’s accessible relational possibilities and future agency. The article proposes that affective freedom requires the capacity to reconsider the organization of desire itself. Its central conclusion is that the capacity to love another person depends partly on the subject’s ability to encounter the other as an independently existing subject, whose value does not derive from the maintenance of distance, uncertainty, or the pursuit of recognition. Keywords: love; inaccessibility; Jacques Lacan; Slavoj Žižek; desire; objet petit a; fantasy; jouissance; desire capture; Finite Continuance; modal erosion; reconfigurative capacity.

items.title: THE UNOWNED LINK — An Ownership Criterion for Verification Chains, and Why No Chain Can Verify Itself Without One.
items.abstract: A verification chain tells its beneficiary no more about the world than its unowned links allow it to — but only when the links it owns default together, not independently. We give a formal Ownership Criterion — a link is owned by a beneficiary of the verdict if that beneficiary can name it, reward it conditional on the verdict it returns, or remove it conditional on the verdict it returns, any one of the three being sufficient — and we prove a Per-Link Compliance Bound: an owned link's informativeness about a beneficiary's own conduct is discounted exactly by its probability of sycophantic non-compliance, however accurate it is on the occasions it does report honestly. This per-link result is unconditional. The chain-level claim is not: whether a chain's total informativeness stays capped by its unowned links alone, regardless of how many owned links are added, depends on whether the owned links' compliance is correlated or drawn independently of one another. Under correlated (shared) compliance, the original bound holds and the Mutual Invisibility corollary follows: a beneficiary who owns every link that watches it, and whose owned links default in lockstep, goes blind to its own state as a structural consequence of ownership. Under independent compliance, the law of large numbers lets an outside observer recover the true state from the aggregate frequency of owned links' reports with arbitrary precision as their number grows, however owned each link remains taken alone — a route the first draft of this paper's claim foreclosed by an unstated and, on inspection, implausible assumption. We locate the correlation of owned-link compliance, not ownership headcount as such, as the quantity that actually does the paper's work, and register a falsifier aimed at measuring it directly, alongside the chain's original registered test. We concede priority five ways. The epistemic regress problem, from Sextus Empiricus through contemporary infinitism, asks who verifies the verifier and supplies no general stopping rule. The Verifier's Dilemma in blockchain consensus (Luu et al., 2015) shows that a rational verifier may decline to verify honestly even when nothing prevents it from doing so. Wintrobe's Dictator's Dilemma (1998) and Kuran's theory of preference and knowledge falsification (1987, 1995) independently describe a ruler's blindness to genuine support as an empirical pathology of autocracy, a finding since complicated, not refuted, by Gehlbach, Luo, Shirikov …

items.title: THE ISLAMIST PARADISE, FORGED — Islamism in Power as a Forgery of Divine Sovereignty: The Occupied Seat, the Manufactured Hypocrite and the Abolished Verifier.
items.abstract: The states built by Islamist movements in power presented themselves as the end of tyranny, the restoration of God’s sovereignty under the promise that “Islam is the solution”, and kept elections, constitutions, courts, ministries of virtue and the full vocabulary of the faith. This paper argues that, in the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Taliban’s Islamic Emirate, the Islamic State’s proto-caliphate and Sudan from 1989 to 2019, these were forgeries in the strict sense of the Philosophy of Virtues: forms conserved, their origin substituted by a ruling body that claimed to speak for God, and the substitution made undetectable from within. Its object is this regime type, not Islam, not Muslims, and not Islamic parties that compete for votes and accept defeat. The forgery ran through four domains at once, the people, truth, virtue and the person (D1), and abolished not only the secular verifiers but the tradition’s own independent jurists (T1). Its distinctive result is the Sacralised Seat Theorem (T2): a power that occupies God’s seat charges dissent twice, by penalty and by sin, so the believer who accepts its claim is its least able verifier (the Devotion Trap), and the internal cost works hardest where the state’s penalty is lightest, in private doubt, the family and the vote (Conscience as Police). By the tradition’s own rule that acts are judged by intentions, compelled piety is display, so compulsion manufactures the hypocrite and forges the record of faith (T3): a 99.5 per cent Muslim census stands against an anonymous survey in which 40 per cent identified as Muslim. The signature tracks compulsion and the destruction of verifiers, not religion: Muslim democrats lack it, secular dictatorships carry it, and Iran’s forced unveiling of 1936 and forced veiling of 1983 are one forgery (C1, C2). The paper concedes priority to An-Naʿim, Abou El Fadl, Hallaq, Kuran and Bayat, connects the mechanism to automated scoring states such as China’s social credit system, and registers three tests, none yet run. Keywords: Islamism; political Islam; theocracy; velayat-e faqih; Taliban; Islamic State; forgery; divine sovereignty; hypocrisy; nifaq; niyya; preference falsification; verification; freedom of conscience; compulsory hijab; Philosophy of Virtues; social credit; Alguilas-AI Highlights • Islamist movements in power in Iran, Afghanistan, the Islamic State and Sudan kept the forms of the faith and of the republic, elections, courts, ministries of virtue, while …

items.title: Mathematics in the Age of AI.
items.abstract: This essay examines the recent claim that the Riemann hypothesis has been proved by the mathematician Levent Alpöge in collaboration with the Claude model, and formalized in Lean as some 17 million lines of code. Taking as its starting point Aristotle's account of the Pythagoreans and their dictum that ``all is number,'' the essay argues that the promise of a purely formal capture of reality has failed before---first with Hippasus of Metapontum's discovery of incommensurable magnitudes, and later with Gödel's incompleteness theorems. Through the Orphic myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, the essay interprets the Lean proof as a Eurydice without traces: the kernel verifies, but the mathematician cannot follow the steps. An analogy with the genetic code clarifies the difference between a formal certificate and a mathematical explanation: just as a nucleotide sequence requires annotation, regulation, and a causal theory to become biology, a Lean script requires interpretation to become mathematics. The essay concludes that AI, as a formal system, cannot close the foundational crisis it inherits; rather, it widens it. Finally, it warns that the computational cost of frontier mathematics risks transforming the discipline into a monopoly of black boxes, inaccessible to institutions and students without massive resources.

items.title: Corpus IGLV: Operational Viability, Relational Persistence, and Architectural Closure.
items.abstract: This canonical synthesis introduces the formal, epistemological, and ontological architecture of the IGLV Corpus (2026), integrating relational persistence, dissipative open-systems dynamics, and structural coherence. First, in epistemology, it replaces static Popperian falsificationism with Principle G, defining theoretical validity as operational viability within a bounded resolution regime (Context 1.0) that must be reformulated when boundary conditions shift (Context 2.0)—illustrated by the historical transition from Carnot's caloric fluid to Boltzmann's statistical mechanics and Landauer's principle. Second, in metaphysics, it resolves classical identity paradoxes (such as the Ship of Theseus) through set-theoretic Persistence and Cyber-synekia: proving via the Relational Bifurcation Theorem that an open system can preserve 100% historical continuity under complete material turnover while undergoing irreversible ontological extinction if its normative Covenant is violated. Third, in metamathematics and complexity theory, it distinguishes Gödelian syntactic completeness from architectural closure—modeling an unexhausted internal infinity unfolded via the Operium Extraction Cascade—and treats P ≠ NP (the asymmetry between costly discovery and efficient verification) as an architectural design constraint implemented in the Cyan System, Paraconsistent Logic (LPAC), and incremental structural SAT decomposition (MI*). The curated bilingual (Spanish/English) edition, verified Zenodo DOIs, and reproducible Python implementations are hosted at ignaciolopezvillanueva . github . io.

items.title: From Psychological Patterns to AI Response Organization: Structural Abstraction, Inference, and Correction — An Exploratory Research Program.
items.abstract: This paper begins with a philosophical and psychological question: what makes a conclusion justified, and what happens when the relationships supporting it are incomplete, mistaken, or revised? -/- Human understanding does not consist merely of isolated beliefs. Interpretations shape expectations, guide decisions, and influence how subsequent experiences are understood. A conclusion may become stable not because its foundations have been adequately examined, but because it has become integrated into a wider pattern of interpretation. This raises a broader epistemological problem: how can we distinguish the apparent coherence of a conclusion from the adequacy of the relationships that support it? -/- Drawing on cognitive psychology, relational analogy, epistemology, and the author's Philosophy of Structure, this exploratory study examines how patterns of interpretation, inference, dependency, and correction can inform the analysis of AI-generated responses. Six operational questions are developed to investigate the relationships between evidence and claims, the temporal organization of reasoning, and the consequences of warranted revision. -/- The approach is explored through developmental testing, retrospective prompt comparisons, and two AI-assisted research instruments: Reality Checker and Inference Trace. The retained record includes 16 live executions of Reality Checker v0.6.6, 141 passing local regression tests for v0.6.7, and 39 local tests for Inference Trace v0.1.2. -/- A central observation is that a seemingly correct conclusion can coexist with incorrect or unsupported inferential relationships: right verdict, wrong link. -/- The paper therefore argues for distinguishing the evaluation of conclusions from the examination of their evidential foundations. Its contribution is methodological and exploratory rather than a claim that human cognition and artificial intelligence share the same underlying mechanisms. -/- More broadly, the study invites consideration of a problem common to epistemology and the evaluation of artificial intelligence: whether a conclusion should be judged only by where it arrives, or also by the structure of justification through which it arrives there.

items.title: 死への恐怖とジェインズ的意識.
items.abstract: 「死が怖い」という言葉は、私たちが考えるほど一つの経験を指していない。痛みや衰弱、家族との別れを恐れる人がいる一方で、いま世界を見ている「この私」そのものが永久に失われることを、幼いころから切実に恐れてきた人がいる。 本稿は、筆者自身の学童期の経験と、他者との対話で見いだした食い違いを出発点に、死の理解、自己の非存在の内省的表象、そしてそこから生じる恐怖を区別する。中心となる問いは、人は同じ生物学的な死を知りながら、その「私の終わり」を同じ仕方で経験しているのか、というものである。 ジュリアン・ジェインズの意識論におけるアナログな「私」、心的空間、自己物語化を手がかりに、自己を時間のうちに置く内省的な能力と自己消滅の認識との結びつきを検討する。さらに筆者の三層意識モデルを用い、無意識的・並列的処理、言語的・直列的表示、再帰的循環が、自己消滅の表象と情動にどのように関わるかを仮説として提示する。アネンドファシアを含む内言の個人差は検証の糸口であるが、内言の乏しさが恐怖の弱さを意味するという証拠はない。宗教や思想は恐怖を和らげうるものの、本稿がまず問うのは、その緩和以前に存在するかもしれない経験の質的な違いである。最後に、心理的経験の種類を区別した実証研究の方向を提案する。 .

items.title: Fear of Death and Jaynesian Consciousness.
items.abstract: The words “I am afraid of death” do not describe a single experience as readily as we might assume. Some people fear pain, physical decline, or separation from their families. Others have, since childhood, felt an acute fear that “this I,” the very subject now looking out upon the world, will be lost forever. Taking as its starting point my own experience during elementary school and the disparities I later noticed in conversations with others, this paper distinguishes among understanding death, introspectively representing one’s own nonexistence, and the fear arising from that representation. Its central question is whether people who know the same biological fact of death experience “the end of me” in the same way. Drawing on the analog “I,” mind-space, and narratization in Julian Jaynes’s theory of consciousness, I examine the relationship between the introspective capacity to situate oneself in time and the awareness of one’s own extinction. I then use my three-layer model of consciousness to propose how unconscious parallel processing, serial linguistic display, and recurrent circulation might contribute to the representation of personal nonexistence and its emotional consequences. Individual differences in inner speech, including anendophasia, offer a possible avenue for testing these ideas, but there is no evidence that having little inner speech necessarily means having little fear. Religion and philosophy may ease that fear; what this paper asks first, however, is whether there are qualitative differences in experience that precede such attempts at relief. It concludes by suggesting directions for empirical inquiry that distinguish among different forms of psychological experience.

items.title: Fate & Sorrow: Can There Be a "Sorrowless Fate"? AnInquiry from the Perspective of Existential Philosophy.
items.abstract: Kedersiz Kader = Sorrowless Fate ! This study inquires whether a fate devoid of sorrow(keder) is philosophically conceivable, starting from the semantic tension between theconcepts of "sorrow" and "fate" (kader). The study first differentiates the concept of fatebetween the fatalistic notion of a predetermined trajectory and Iqbal's interpretation of fate asan inner potential; it demonstrates that the former renders sorrow a structural necessity, whilethe latter leaves limited room for freedom and contingency. The study then examinesSchopenhauer's argument for the positivity of suffering, the shared Stoic and Buddhistattitude of "handling" rather than "eliminating" sorrow, and Kierkegaard's analysis of despairas a constitutive element of the self's relation to itself. The final section discusses the paradoxinherent in Nietzsche's amor fati and argues that a sorrowless fate, if understood as the totalelimination of sorrow, is not only impossible but also undesirable; whereas, if understood asthe affirmative acceptance of a fate that includes sorrow, it points not to a state but to anattitude. The central claim of the study is that, philosophically, the genuine question is not"how to eliminate sorrow" but "with what attitude a fate that includes sorrow may beassumed." -/- .

items.title: Generative Grammar Representations for Autonomous Evolutionary Algorithms in Large-Scale Projects.
items.abstract: Living things continue by copying a compact heritable material and growing from it, through a costly development, a body far larger than the material itself. This proposal paper carries that mechanism into the evolution of large projects, such as a codebase, a research programme or a body of writing made by people and language-model agents. Each individual of the population holds a compact generative material, a weighted grammar, from which a development derives a project; variation and selection act on the grammar. When a project is made by agents, the grammar may be induced from the record of its acts: which agent asked which agent for what, what a person asked, what was generated, committed and accepted, and how the workspace grew.
