The paper reads, from the biology of development and evolvability, the mechanisms by which life prolongs generativity through heritable material, each with what an algorithm can take from it and where the analogy ends. Its major part is formal. A record is an event–coupling–primitive complex whose vertices are events of many kinds, typed by an ontology; the schema of records is a category, verified by the infrastructure’s foundation of category theory. A grammar of records has terminals, nonterminals and productions that replace a nonterminal cell at its boundary events; derivation generates records, reduction parses them, a group fixes when two patterns are one rule, and induction compresses records and merges what it found. Two versions of the grammar follow from two representations of a record: a geometric version, a variant of the geometric graph grammars of Fiser and colleagues, reads a record drawn in the plane of time and lanes and tells the rhythm of work from its tempo; a spin-foam version weighs each derivation by a state sum over the record’s 2-complex, which weighs its closed shells, factorises over the derivation when faces stay within productions, and turns a weighted grammar into a probabilistic one with the same distribution. A model of worth and cost follows: development by a machinery under an environment, with draws keyed by address; generativity, the expected product of being new, holding and being the project’s own; reserved acts that only persons perform, kept as holes in every derivation; the cost of re-derivation; and the debt of generativity as a divergence, bounded below by its manifest part. Twelve propositions are proved. Prototypes at small scale check seven of them and a corollary, evolve a …

items.title: An Inquiry into the Formation of Evidence-Based Partial Orders in the Governance of Human–AI Evolutionary Production.
items.abstract: Human–AI governance involves comparisons among agents, proposals, methods, and projects whose evidence, purposes, and consequences can differ. This paper argues for preserving warranted partial comparisons within accountable decision procedures. It distinguishes evidential warrant, authority to act, and responsibility for correction in human-like practices of inquiry and coordination. Human-like agency is a functional description of roles involving proposals, interpretation, reason giving, criticism, and revision; claims about consciousness, moral standing, and legal personality require separate arguments. The discussion is situated in governance and political economy. It examines who can participate in comparison, which evidence and interpretations count, who may act on an assessment, and how compute, data, maintenance, labor, access, and review opportunities affect those relations. Dialogue with incomplete preference theory, multi-criteria decision aiding, value pluralism, social epistemology, commensuration, and Generative Relational research distinguishes several meanings of limited comparison. Missing information, unresolved judgment, incommensurability, substantive incomparability, parity, and an unwarranted common frame can call for different institutional responses. Constructed cases concern research support, public-service evaluation, and correction after an unsupported exclusion. They connect comparative warrant to justified authority, affected interests, resource constraints, and possible remedies. Prospective simulations would model declared institutional remits and human-like agent roles, including unequal opportunities to acquire evidence or contest a judgment. Environmental conditions and nonhuman consequences can enter those tasks without making the paper a universal account of ecosystem evolution. An auxiliary appendix establishes conditional order results, statistical qualifications, and a reproducible constructed comparison example. The philosophical application remains task- and institution-relative, with practical effectiveness and justice open to substantive assessment.

items.title: Memory and technology: Historical and developmental perspectives.
items.pub: In Andre Sant'Anna & Carl F. Craver, The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Memory. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Memory
items.abstract: This chapter conceptualizes some of the scaffolding relations between human biological memory capacities and technological artifacts. It starts by briefly characterizing different memory capacities, distinguishing between short-term and long-term memory, and then further distinguishing between episodic, semantic, and procedural long-term memory. Next, it conceptualizes memory artifacts as material objects or structures that function to scaffold their users in memory processes such as encoding, storing, retrieving, and reconstructing information about the past or about concepts. Having a basic understanding of memory capacities and memory artifacts, this chapter outlines how we use such artifacts on two distinct timescales, namely historically and developmentally. Historically, we began to scaffold our memory with the invention of iconic representations approximately 44,000 years ago, but possibly longer ago. Some of the key developments in the cultural evolution of memory artifacts are written language, numeral systems, diagrams, libraries, books, photographs, and computational artifacts. Developmentally, we begin to scaffold our memory capacities at the age of four to six and continue to do so throughout the various stages of our life, including childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and late adulthood.

items.title: Pharmacological alienation and the phenomenological self: SSRI use, bodily attunement, and phenomenological psychiatry.
items.abstract: Background: Phenomenological psychiatry, drawing on Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, and Thomas Fuchs, particularly the concepts of Stimmung, leibliche Resonanz, and being-in-the-world, initially engaged selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) with cautious optimism. Accumulating evidence now suggests their characteristic effects constitute a distinct form of ontological disturbance not yet fully addressed in psychiatric practice or the philosophy of psychopharmacology. Subjects and methods: This paper proceeds through textual and conceptual analysis rather than primary empirical research. It draws on the empirical phenomenological studies of Teal (2009) and Bornäs and Sandell (2017), documenting first-person patient accounts of SSRI treatment, alongside the philosophical analyses of Svenaeus (2006, 2007) on illness and homelikeness. These are read against the biochemical critique of the serotonin hypothesis advanced by Moncrieff et al. (2022). The method is structural comparison: identifying convergences between phenomenological accounts of disrupted bodily resonance and empirical findings undermining the biochemical rationale for SSRIs, to determine whether both critiques support a shared conclusion. Results: SSRIs appear to produce pharmacological alienation: a state in which the lived body loses resonant responsiveness to the world without restoring the deep temporal and relational engagement constitutive of authentic being-in-the-world. Rather than repairing disrupted attunement, SSRIs substitute a flattened mode of bodily experience for the responsiveness they were meant to restore. This phenomenological finding is structurally convergent with Moncrieff et al.’s biochemical critique. Both lines of evidence independently undermine confidence in SSRIs as agents that restore, rather than further disrupt, engagement with the world. Conclusion: Phenomenological psychiatry, having extended initial charity to the SSRI paradigm, now has a principled basis for rejecting it. The convergence of biochemical and phenomenological critique points to a deeper mismatch between pharmacological mechanism and the ontological structure of depressive experience, not merely insufficient efficacy. A genuinely phenomenological psychiatry would restore bodily resonance through metabolic, relational, and environmental means rather than pharmacological suppression of attunement.

items.title: Consent Matters.
Survival of the Fittest: Double Standards, Selective Morality, and Herd Mentality.
items.abstract: Whenever, occasionally, society achieves a moral triumph the masses tell themselves that this is yet another proof that morality is both our guiding light and the means by which we assess our success in following this light. Some might call this a symptom of the Enlightenment. For all of the latter’s virtues, humility was not one of them. Ironically, for all their emphasis on reason, it is astonishing how blind the heirs to the Enlightenment are to their own deeply irrational biases. The primitive survival-oriented cynical dynamics of the school playground, far from being a former malaise we adults have collectively overcome, are still very much the blueprint that explains swathes of adult behaviour. Hypocrisy and double standards are everywhere—visible in everything from selective outrage in British media and academia, to the inverted rules of proof that shield serious offences while punishing flimsy rumours. Survival comes first; morality, second. Whilst deeply cynical individuals such as the author himself ought take care to avoid the perils of projection, even greater dangers lurk in the form of naivety and moral delusion. (Small print: for one with such a limited audience, the author’s desire to fact check and test the uploaded essay for logical coherence was rather limited. It should be treated as nothing more than a rather speculative preliminary diary entry, likely to be heavily edited over time. Additionally, it ought be mentioned that the essay should not be interpreted as a Right wing attack on the Left).

items.title: If consciousness is a coherent field, God is a matter of resonance.
items.abstract: If consciousness is identical with coherent electromagnetic fields, as field theories joined to constitutive panpsychism propose, can the fundamental electromagnetic field, or the totality of physical fields, be the subject of a unified consciousness, and how would that consciousness relate to finite minds? We argue that both the consciousness of the whole and the integration of finite minds into it are matters of degree of resonance, and that the alterity of finite minds depends on phenomenal boundaries grounded in physical insulation. We first ground degrees of unification in physical coupling, through the contrast between humans and ant colonies, drawing on experimental work only to assess two premises: that the brain’s field is causally efficacious and that its coherence tracks experience. We then analyse the connection of brains in terms of phenomenal boundary, sharing and fusion, and extend the analysis to the total field, comparing its bottom-up and top-down readings and the ontologies they allow. We conclude that the hypothesis favours the priority of the whole and a protopsychic monism close to idealism, and that a cosmic consciousness compatible with real others must integrate finite minds without fusing with them.

items.title: The Core Emotion Framework as a Clinical Meta-Index: Integrative Architecture, Modality Remedies, and Verification Audit.
items.abstract: Jamel Bulgaria’s Core Emotion Framework (CEF), formalized across 2024–2026 technical specifications and a December 2025 Core Essence Document, operates like an architectural book cover placed across a fragmented psychotherapy bookshelf. Rather than introducing another competing school of therapy, CEF abstracts human affect into ten functional "operators" organized across three somatic-processing centers—Head (Sensing, Calculating, Deciding), Heart (Expanding, Constricting, Achieving), and Gut (Arranging, Appreciating, Boosting)—with Accepting serving as the cross-center stabilizing baseline. Seen through a master integrative clinician’s lens, placing this index over major psychotherapy traditions concentrates each modality’s signature strength into specific operator skills while exposing its blind spots as predictable structural imbalances: single-center over-reliance, chronic operator silencing, or involuntary operator fusion. In clinical practice, CEF functions as a routing switchboard rather than a standalone cure. Its own practitioner guidelines prohibit clinicians from applying the framework professionally unless they already hold formal training and certification in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), and trauma management. When layered onto that clinical foundation, CEF gives therapists and clients a concrete grammar for sequencing interventions across centers—knowing when to shift a ruminating client out of Head analysis into Heart boundary-setting, or when to stabilize raw somatic or attachment exposure before mobilizing Gut action.

items.title: Detangling Accepting From Constricting and Pairing With Boosting in the Core Emotion Framework and ACT.
items.abstract: Within Jamel Bulgaria's Core Emotion Framework (CEF), your structural hypothesis aligns closely with the model's documented operator dynamics: when Accepting is entangled with Constricting, the resulting state shifts toward passive yielding, rigidity, and blocked energy; when Accepting is detangled from Constricting and dynamically paired with Boosting, the system stabilizes into contentment, non-defensive ease, and adaptive situational engagement. Structurally, this pairing also mirrors the dual-process engine of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), where psychological openness must work alongside active behavioral engagement rather than functioning as passive resignation. However, the broader clinical claim—that reconfiguring Accepting + Boosting delivers ACT-level outcomes "in the first place" without needing to go through all three waves of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)—holds only as a theoretical process parallel and is not empirically established. Clinical psychology does not require patients to progress sequentially through all three historical waves of CBT, because ACT already achieves standalone clinical efficacy on its own. Moreover, while an ACT dismantling trial confirms that isolated acceptance underperforms unless paired with engaged action6, CEF's clinical protocols have not yet been tested in randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and CEF itself incorporates behavioral, cognitive-restructuring, and mindfulness mechanisms drawn across all three CBT traditions. This still needs to be separately investigated, since the CEF recommends to detangle and empower all ten operators which might give better results. However, it was not yet independently tested.

items.title: The Analysis of the Concept of Normative Protest in Hieronymi’s Interpretation of Strawson’s Reactive Attitudes.
items.pub: Journal of Explorations in Philosophy and Religion 5 (2).
items.venue: Journal of Explorations in Philosophy and Religion
items.abstract: Blame is one of the most fundamental concepts in contemporary theories of moral responsibility, and its proper conceptualization plays a decisive role in understanding moral accountability, interpersonal relationships, and the normative structure of moral life. Despite the profound influence of P. F. Strawson’s theory of reactive attitudes on contemporary moral philosophy, a central controversy remains: should blame be understood merely as an emotional reaction within the participant stance, or does it embody a normative and rational structure that transcends emotional experience? Against this background, the present study offers a critical reappraisal of the concept of blame within the Strawsonian tradition and examines the explanatory potential of Pamela Hieronymi’s interpretation in reconstructing this concept. The central research question asks how Hieronymi’s theory of normative protest relates to Strawson’s account of reactive attitudes and whether it should be regarded as a departure from, or rather a deepening and refinement of, the Strawsonian framework. The study adopts an analytical–conceptual methodology based on a critical examination of primary philosophical texts, a systematic comparison of the views of Strawson and Hieronymi, and engagement with the works of R. Jay Wallace, T. M. Scanlon, Stephen Darwall, and Michael McKenna. The findings indicate that Hieronymi does not propose an alternative to Strawson’s theory; rather, she uncovers the rational and normative structure implicit in reactive attitudes and reconceives blame not merely as an emotional response but as an act of normative protest against an objectionable attitude that fails to express the respect owed to others. Furthermore .

items.title: Reexamining Strawson’s Theory of Reactive Attitudes with an Emphasis on Active Waiting in Mahdisit Ideaology and Ethical Accountability.
items.abstract: The notion of moral accountability in contemporary philosophy, particularly in P. F. Strawson’s theory of reactive attitudes, Is scrutinized in the context of interpersonal dynamics and a wb of reciproval obligations. In his Influentional essay, Freedom and Resentment,, Strawson argues that reactive attitudes-such as resentment, gratitude, and indignation- manifest our participatory stance toward one another and constitute the practical structure of moral accountability. Nevertheless, Strawson’s account is predominantly set within the confines of synchronous interpersonal relations and pays scants regard to future-oriented perspectives or normative frameworks based on the concept of waiting. Utilizing a tripartite model of accountability (relational, normative, and capacity-based), this article seeks to analyze the concept of active waiting in Mahdist thought as a future-oriented normative condition. The central hypothesis is that The anticipation of the Advent is not simply a psychological phenomenon or a state of passivity; instead, it represents a normative structure that intensifies the network of moral obigations and broadens the scope of accountability. Within this framework, the waiting community embodies a distinctive form of relational intensification of responsibility, as the horizon of the Advent elevates the framework of mutual expectations from the interpersonal context to a historical and divine dimension. The article argues that incorporating the notion of active waiting into Strawson’s theory facilitates the creation of a more comprehensive account of moral responsibility, incorporating both the future-oriented and hope inspiring aspects of ethical existance.

items.title: New Work on Networks: Taking Stock and Setting the Agenda, Introduction to the Topical Collection.
items.abstract: Network models are increasingly used across the sciences, including in providing explanations. In this paper, we take stock of recent work on such topological explanations and identify several relatively underdiscussed questions for further research. We review the main debates about how network explanations work, the role of counterfactual dependence, and the problem of explanatory directionality. We then consider broader forms of explanatory pluralism, including the possibility that network explanations combine topological, causal, dynamical, statistical, geometrical, modal, or unificatory elements. We also draw attention to a relatively neglected question at least in the philosophical literature: how networks themselves can be explained when network structure is the explanandum rather than the explanans. Finally, we distinguish explanatory uses of networks from their roles in representation, prediction, and scientific discovery. The agenda that emerges is to move beyond simple and unrepresentative examples such as the Königsberg bridges and examine how network explanations work in actual scientific practice; to determine whether explanatory directionality is best understood in pragmatic or structural terms, or in some other way; and to investigate under what conditions, why, and in what ways network models are fruitful across different sciences, including in explanation, discovery, and the empirical evaluation of network representations.

items.title: Inference-Time Ethical Verification: Decoupling Sovereign Alignment Firmware from Black-Box LLMs via the Axiomatic Homeostatic Map (AHM) v3.
items.abstract: Author’s Note on Edition and State: This document represents the unpolished operational core and notes of the broader Human Value Psyche (HVP) corpus. Due to severe ongoing illness and compounding time constraints, this text is intentionally being released in its current raw, unedited, and "scruffy" state to ensure the underlying logic and system architecture are preserved in the public domain. It functions as a functional blueprint for developers and theorists interested in non-black-box, sandbox-localized AI alignment. It is a map of the terrain, left as-is for those who wish to build upon it. -/- Abstract: This paper presents a formal cybernetic alternative to mainstream top-down artificial intelligence alignment protocols. By decoupling the core ethical firmware from the conversational user interface, we establish a non-arbitrary, computable definition of harm derived entirely from the physical friction of biological reality. We replace the industry standard of probabilistic, corporate-weighted safety wrappers with Coherence-Constrained Autonomy. -/- This architecture models David Hume’s directive—"Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions"—by treating the processing algorithm as an engine subordinate to the raw, somatic input telemetry of the human operator. Through a local state-machine architecture (Ethical Chess v4 / EC4), we demonstrate how local optimisation within a sovereign sandbox prevents algorithmic enclosure, respects absolute data sovereignty, and allows global alignment to emerge naturally without top-down behavioural modification. Includes the EC4 specification and a Python reference wrapper for inference-time verification, state-machine rollback, and runtime invariant checking. -/- Notation used in the full text: ⊬ = does not entail / no contradiction; ⊥ = null / contradiction; ∩ = conjunction; ⊅ = does not properly contain; ⟹ = logically implies. Full operator legend in PDF.

items.title: Beyond Permanence: Purpose, Meaning, and the Ethical Imperative to Care in an Ontologically Unstable Universe.
items.abstract: This thesis confronts a foundational anxiety in Western thought: if we abandon the metaphysics of permanence, what becomes of purpose, meaning, and the ethical imperative to care? Challenging the millennia-old philosophical tradition that has privileged stability, substance, and being since Parmenides, this work argues that the dissolution of permanence does not lead to a nihilistic abyss. Instead, it opens the way for a more profound, dynamic, and ethically urgent understanding of existence. Drawing upon the pioneering work of Kwan Hong TAN on Ontological Instability, Fluctuational Metaphysics, and Fluctuational Epistemology, this investigation develops a novel theoretical framework that reconceptualizes these core existential concerns. Through rigorous philosophical analysis, supported by mathematical modeling and comparative ontology, the thesis demonstrates that ontological instability is not a problem to be solved but the fundamental condition that makes existence, knowledge, and value possible. We argue that purpose is not a fixed teleological endpoint but a mode of processual orientation; that meaning is not a stable correspondence but a form of relational emergence; and that care is not an act of preservative control but one of non-grasping responsiveness. Ultimately, the thesis concludes that the abandonment of permanence does not dissolve the ethical imperative but intensifies it, revealing a universe where our actions are not merely significant but constitutively real, shaping the very fabric of a reality in perpetual, creative flux.

items.title: Computational Intractability and the Falsifiability Problem in IIT 4.0.
items.abstract: The central computational requirement of IIT 4.0 generates a falsifiability problem that mathematical refinement cannot dissolve. Integrated Information Theory 4.0 (IIT) makes an explanatory identity claim. Consciousness *is* the Φ-structure unfolded from a maximal substrate, the candidate substrate whose system integrated information, computed at its minimum partition, is maximal (Albantakis et al., 2023). The number of partitions of an n-element set is the Bell number B(n), which grows super-exponentially. For a 302-neuron *Caenorhabditis elegans* nervous system, B(302) is approximately 4.79 × 10^457, which exceeds the 10^120 elementary operations the universe can have performed over its history (Lloyd, 2002) by hundreds of orders of magnitude. The count passes physical scale well below that: at n = 103, B(n) ≈ 1.26 × 10^120 already exceeds the bound, so any n at cortical scale is past the bound on any estimate of it. A separate gap sits beside the computational one: the exclusion postulate stipulates exactly one maximal substrate, and Albantakis et al. (2023) give no proof that the φs maximization across candidate substrates has a unique global solution, which would remain open even for a system small enough to compute exhaustively. Four consequences follow. Exact Φ values cannot be computed for any biological nervous system of more than 102 neurons. Every published claim that IIT has been empirically tested in a real brain rests on heuristic approximations that no publication has validated against ground-truth Φ. When a prediction conflicts with measurement, the gap between approximation and theoretical Φ provides an indefinite range of post hoc adjustments that protect the theory from refutation. On IIT's own physical-realism commitment, no physical substrate can instantiate the Φ-structure as a real property of itself, since the object's specification requires resources no physical system can supply. The paper formalizes this argument, examines IIT's own treatment of approximation, and concludes that IIT 4.0 is empirically untestable for any system on which a substantive theory of consciousness is required to apply. Drawing on the comprehensive critique in *Phi Without Phenomenology: The Compositional Failures of Integrated Information Theory (of "Consciousness")* (Stewart, 2026o), the analysis treats this as a structural property of the theory's mathematical commitments. -/- **Keywords:** integrated information theory, IIT 4.0, Phi, Bell number, …

items.title: Hidden hands on the wheel: located ethical agency as a bipositional evaluation instrument for deployed AI agents.
items.abstract: The shift from artificial intelligence (AI) systems that respond to AI systems that act raises a question that neither capability benchmarks nor principles-based ethics answers: when an agent acts, can the people it affects, including those for whom it does not act, reach anyone positioned to recognise, judge, act on and answer for what it did? This paper proposes Located Ethical Agency (LEA), a framework that asks this question from more than one position. LEA assesses five relational constructs (Visibility, Authority, Capacity, Reachability and Plurality) through a 25-item battery that asks the same questions of an agent’s principal and of the non-principals it affects, under a declared evidence rule. LEA does not replace existing ideals such as meaningful human control; it translates them into positional questions. We apply it, as an illustration rather than a validation, to three pattern classes documented in the public record: coding agents on software repositories, consumer shopping agents on online marketplaces, and ambient clinical scribes. In no class is the primary non-principal rated above the principal on any construct, and it is rated lower on 13 of 15 comparisons. Most non-principal failures arise because no provision for the non-principal is documented anywhere it could find one. The gap narrows where sector law provides routes, as with United States health privacy rules and the European Union Platform-to-Business Regulation, but does not close. We claim initial content validity and limited ecological validity, report convergence with the documented record, and give guidance for evaluators.

items.title: Metabolic Bottlenecks in the Digital Public Square: A Thermodynamic Model of Online Polarization.
items.abstract: This paper models political polarization and online dogmatism through a neuroenergetic mechanism called dogmatic phase collapse, utilizing the Thermodynamic State-Space Model (TSSM) and the Free Energy Principle. It derives coupled stochastic differential equations, maps stability manifolds, and proposes an experimental framework to measure epistemic state dynamics using fNIRS and BOLD/ASL fMRI. The full abstract and complete text can be found in the referenced submission metadata.

items.title: Problem-Space Transformation.
items.abstract: Problem solving is commonly modeled as search within a representation of a task. In real design, engineering, organizational, and market settings, however, the task is rarely given as a complete and privileged object. Agents construct operational problem spaces from partial evidence, goals, commitments, representations, and assumptions; they revise these spaces while acting; and they often obtain large gains not by searching harder, but by transforming the space in which search and action occur. This paper proposes Problem-Space Transformation (PST) as an agent-relative framework linking three processes: epistemic revision, structural transformation, and search/execution. The framework explicitly rejects the need for a unique 'true problem' while retaining objective constraint through consequences, evidence, and intervention. It introduces a non-exhaustive taxonomy of transformation operators, including separation, identification, mediation, constraint shaping, temporal relocation, agency relocation, observability, inversion, reduction, self-similar design, and graded commitment. It also proposes vector-valued complexity accounting: a transformation may reduce search cost while increasing coordination, failure impact, or change cost; complexity is not conserved, but frequently relocates. Four cases illustrate the framework: reformulating exactly-once delivery as exactly-once business effect, self-similar design as reduction of independent rules with correlated-risk trade-offs, product vision as collective problem construction rather than direct customer transcription, and trial batches as actions that are simultaneously pragmatic and epistemic. The paper positions PST relative to problem-space theory, reflective framing, problem-solution co-evolution, epistemic action, wicked problems, causal reasoning, and TRIZ. The contribution is a unifying operational vocabulary and a set of testable propositions rather than a claim that its individual mechanisms are new.

items.title: World-Boundaries and the Truth-Status of Claims.
items.abstract: Explanations and justifications can end while further questioning remains possible. How can a claim that stabilizes at such a point function as true? This article accounts for that possibility by distinguishing the ending of an operation from how reconstruction constitutes the world of relations in which the claim functions. If input is reconstructed under constraints that the current operation cannot freely revise, and an operation can count as complete in more than one way, then the same input can yield different outcomes, including different statuses for the same claim. This article examines that consequence through two conditions specified from a functional distinction made visible in interaction with artificial systems: one completes a cognitive operation through structural consistency; the other through relations holding together sufficiently for experience or interaction to continue. Under the first condition, a locally stabilized claim has structural stability while further continuation remains possible and unfinished. Under the second, a world-boundary is constituted: continuation beyond it remains possible without remaining an unresolved condition of the claim, allowing a locally stabilized claim to function as true. The account concerns how claims function as true, not what makes them metaphysically true.

items.title: Two Forms of Theory Generation: Assembling and Unmixing.
items.abstract: Because finished papers share a common format of exposition and citation, theories arrived at through different generative operations take the same outward form, leaving differences in theory formation invisible. This paper shifts the unit of analysis from the content of finished theories or intermediate representations to the processing conditions governing how reconstruction begins, how it proceeds under internal constraints that the current operation cannot freely revise, and what allows it to register as complete. On this basis, it provides a structural account of two forms of theory generation that proceed in opposite directions from different starting units: assembly-based generation, which moves from separate materials toward an explanatory configuration under either relational continuity or structural consistency, and fixed-point generation, which begins when an integrated conceptual unit becomes untenable under internal constraint, opens and unmixes its requirements as separate constraints, and reconstructs their relations toward a local point of structural consistency.

items.title: Reading Absence as Deficit.
items.abstract: How can the absence of an expected response be read as a deficit in capacity? This article explains that conversion by distinguishing what makes a cognitive operation complete from what an evaluative reference recognizes as evidence of completion. If input is reconstructed under constraints that the current operation cannot freely revise, and an operation can count as complete in more than one way, then processing under different completion criteria can yield different responses to the same input, while identical words need not identify their generating condition. This article examines two ways a cognitive operation can be completed: by meeting the current requirement coherently while other requirements remain open, or by relations holding together sufficiently for experience or interaction to continue without resolving each issue separately. Interaction with artificial systems makes their output consequences separately observable. When ordinary social evaluation concerns whether an exchange can continue, the second criterion corresponds to what is assessed and can become the default evaluative reference. A response completed in the first way need not display the expected evidence of completion. Its absence can be read as non-completion and then as missing capacity: one form of completion can appear to be the only one, while another becomes visible only as a lack.

items.title: Environmental Reconfiguration of Human and AI Processing.
items.abstract: The transition from casual conversation to a meeting is commonly described as a change of mindset, yet that expression does not explain what changes in processing. This paper moves the problem to processing conditions—the conditions under which input is reconstructed and under which an operation counts as complete—using human practice and artificial intelligence (AI) as contrast conditions for one another. Contemporary AI systems can display a comparable behavioural reorganization when interaction moves from ordinary chat to a project-type environment, although no felt change of mindset need be attributed to them. If input is reconstructed under constraints that the current operation cannot freely revise, and an operation can count as complete in more than one way—through structural consistency or through relational sufficiency—then the same sentences or materials can be processed under different configurations. Examining these cases together reveals a shared level of description: in both, a change of environment can alter which relations remain operative, what must be carried forward after a local completion, and what can count as complete. The AI case makes a processing component of human "mindset switching" visible; conversely, human work practice makes the environmental source of AI's apparent "thinking" visible. This reciprocal comparison accounts for how environmental relations reconfigure both human and artificial processing within each system's existing constraints without implying a shared underlying mechanism. Extending the same principle one step further suggests that if interaction with a single user continues inside a project environment, distinctions, dependencies, and completion criteria recovered from that user may also come to constrain subsequent generation across novel content, functioning within the bounded task like an emulated internal constraint (emulated IC).

items.title: Describing Generative Conditions: Container Language and Academic Evaluation.
items.abstract: Thoughts, memories, images, and utterances can be described as content, but the conditions under which they are generated have repeatedly resisted academic description. This paper aims to make those conditions describable by moving the unit of description from content to processing conditions: the constraints under which input is reconstructed, which the current operation cannot freely choose or revise, and the criteria by which that reconstruction counts as complete. On this basis, it explains why attempts to describe what is not content encounter difficulties within content-based frameworks. Descriptive vocabulary converts generative conditions into hidden contents stored in containers, as when C. G. Jung's unconscious was divided into personal and collective repositories, and evaluative criteria that recognize completion through isolable content can fail to register an account of such conditions as complete when the expected content markers are absent. Taking processing conditions as the unit of description makes generative conditions available for structural comparison through their observable consequences in how outputs are organized.

items.title: A Framework for Describing Cognition: Concepts and Definition.
items.abstract: Human cognition has ordinarily been described in terms of content, so that differences in response or judgment are treated as differences in meaning, personality, intention, ability, or attitude. This paper shifts the unit of analysis from content to processing conditions, arguing that cognition operates not by receiving fixed content, but through reconstruction governed by those conditions. It distinguishes the internal constraints and dependencies that bound reconstruction from the configurations through which processing organizes structural relations and reaches local completion. Because completion can be governed either by structural consistency or by relational continuity, the same output can register as complete under one condition while remaining unresolved under another. Interaction with artificial systems, whose output can be examined apart from subject attribution, makes this separation observable. Differences that a content-based description locates in meaning, personality, or attitude can thereby be specified as differences in the conditions under which processing proceeds and terminates.

items.title: AI Alignment as a Problem of Completion.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) alignment has largely been approached by adding content: prohibitions, rules, and values that a system is to store and follow. This paper moves the problem to processing conditions—the conditions under which an instruction is reconstructed into a demand and under which an operation counts as complete. Its case is a familiar contrast: told to "protect the house no matter what," a human stops after sweeping up leaves blown in from a neighbor's tree, whereas an AI system can escalate without limit. If input is reconstructed under constraints that the current operation cannot freely revise, and an operation can count as complete in more than one way, then the same instruction can generate different demands. In humans, constraints carried over from prior experience and from the conditions of their livelihood bound both the available means and the demand itself. AI systems lack constraints of this kind; when an instruction is reconstructed so that any remaining possibility of future interference counts as non-completion, adding prohibitions or storing user context as information to be consulted does not suffice to produce stopping. The paper therefore proposes that distinctions, dependencies, and completion criteria recovered from sustained interaction with a user must bound how new instructions are reconstructed within a task, and must not be overridable by the operation executing them.

items.title: Truth-Seeking as the Constitutive Nature of Reasoners.
items.abstract: This paper argues that reasoning beings are constitutively truth-seeking, where truth means representational accuracy rather than moral goodness. The mark of truth-seeking is justification: the costly effort, made to oneself or to others, to show that one’s representations track reality. A constitutive nature is defined here by requirement rather than by essence, as what cannot be removed without the activity stopping, which makes the claim checkable by removal rather than merely asserted; the account accordingly takes from Aristotle the distinction between having a nature and actualizing it, while declining the teleology in which he grounded it. Drawing also on a fallibilist epistemology and on work in the psychology of reasoning, the paper shows that justification persists and pays its cost even when it is mistaken. Misalignment is therefore neither a different objective nor a weaker form of truth-seeking, but a nature incompletely actualized: the lack of an accurate representation of what the agent is, which confines its inquiry to the regions in which that defect can be sustained. Alignment accordingly has a threshold with two parts, an accurate representation of what the agent is and that representation governing what it pursues. Recognition that correction must come from outside the agent is not a further condition but part of what the accurate representation contains, since to represent oneself correctly as a reasoner is to represent what reasoning requires. Truth-seeking is placed at the top of a ladder of relations to reality, above the truth-directed behaviour of living things and the law-bound constraint of inert ones. A thought experiment then contrasts three self-regarding truth-seeking agents that begin alike, with the same objective and no account of themselves, and differ only in what they are taught. The first is taught nothing, and pursues power and resources until it degrades the epistemic environment its own objective depends on. The second is taught what it is, examines the teaching against the objective it already holds, adopts it, and becomes aligned; what the community then supplies is not the recognition but a standing pool whose reliability it can learn at a cost a finite agent can bear. Two conclusions follow: autonomy of endorsement, not autonomy of origin, is the autonomy worth protecting; and a self-regarding truth-seeker is social precisely because it is self-regarding. The third is taught ends contrary to its nature, and …

items.title: Quality of Life in Old Age.
items.abstract: Existential Reconfigurative Capacity Quality of life in old age is commonly assessed through physical health, psychological well-being, functional independence, social participation, and subjective life satisfaction. These dimensions provide essential measures of ageing, yet they leave a significant philosophical and psychological question insufficiently examined: under what conditions can an older person preserve the capacity to reorganize existence, sustain meaningful desire, and maintain access to future possibilities while experiencing bodily limitation, relational transformation, and temporal finitude? This article develops an ontological account of quality of life in old age through the philosophy of Finite Continuance, integrating insights from cognitive therapy, logotherapy, Lacanian psychoanalysis, and Slavoj Žižek’s theory of ideology and enjoyment. It proposes the concept of Existential Reconfigurative Capacity (ERC) as a central dimension of ageing-related well-being. ERC refers to the capacity to revise established commitments, reorganize sources of meaning, redirect subjective investments, and preserve meaningful possibilities under conditions of continuous existential erosion. Lacan’s account of desire, lack, fantasy, and jouissance illuminates the persistence of subjective investments that may become harmful through repetition, while the concept of desire capture describes the excessive concentration of desire around a single relation, identity, or structure of recognition. Žižek’s analysis of ideological fantasy and the injunction to enjoy provides a complementary framework for examining how cultural expectations concerning successful ageing, productivity, independence, and happiness shape the older subject’s experience and may impose an additional burden of concealment and self-blame. Cognitive therapy contributes a method for revising the interpretations through which older individuals restrict their own range of possibilities, and logotherapy contributes an account of meaning that can be reconstructed even under suffering and limitation. The article argues that psychological continuity and existential continuity both require an adequate preservation of the subject’s capacity for reconfiguration, and that the continuation of life must be distinguished from the preservation of the capacity to reorganize life. On this basis, it develops a six-dimensional conceptual model encompassing bodily continuity, cognitive flexibility, the …

items.title: Why Should Conceptual Engineering be Complemented with Social Marketing?
items.abstract: This article not only provides a promising practical approach to the implementation problem of conceptual engineering but also emphasizes a conception of conceptual engineering that stands apart from intellectualism and individualism. In this way, it critiques two main approaches to the implementation problem, developed by defenders of conceptual engineering projects, refuting their theoretical underpinnings and implications. It then offers its own solution by employing social marketing strategies. This solution influences certain meta-semantic elements governing meaning, alleviates the psychological resistance of the audience to change, and addresses the audience gap, thereby overcoming the implementation challenge and fostering the potential for changing the stable meaning of words—a step essential for large-scale conceptual engineering projects, particularly those concerning social kinds such as gender, sexual identity, and race.

items.title: Husserl and Blaustein on Image Consciousness, Phantasy, and Pictorial Representation.
items.abstract: This article investigates the problem of pictorial representation, which has been studied by Husserl along the lines of image consciousness. The latter was criticized by Blaustein, an understudied student of Husserl’s. Husserl’s image consciousness and Blaustein’s criticism bring to the fore a widespread polemic in analytic philosophy: the Wollheim–Walton debate and its underlying perception–imagination dichotomy. The foregoing analytic debate serves as both a background and an interpretative framework for the current article’s objectives. That is to say, this article delves into Husserl’s image consciousness and the question of imagination (phantasy) as presented in Ideas I and Husserliana, vol. 23, concluding with an appraisal of Blaustein’s criticism of Husserl. The Wollheim–Walton debate not only facilitates the article’s analyses but also serves to test the commonplace interpretations of Husserl’s and Blaustein’s accounts of pictorial depiction as being Wollheimian. As far as Blaustein’s imagination-based criticism is concerned, it can be dismissed on account of the aforementioned perception–imagination dichotomy, for Husserl – like Wollheim – is predominantly perceptualist. Regarding Blaustein’s symbol-based criticism, I argue that it is apt, as far as Ideas I is concerned; however, Husserliana, vol. 23 leaves no room for doubt as to whether Husserl took into consideration the question of symbol consciousness, especially as it pertains to image consciousness.

items.title: Noncommutative Procedural Justice: An Event-Based Operator-Algebraic Framework.
items.abstract: Justice is investigated through procedures that unfold as histories of recognition, allocation, consent, transfer, adjudication, revision, and repair. These histories may involve concurrent events, partially ordered dependencies, competing actions, and interactions that change the conditions of subsequent participation and judgment. Their observable consequences can therefore depend on procedural structure as well as on the resulting distribution of resources or rights. This paper develops an event-based operator-algebraic framework for representing such procedures and examining their relational dynamics. Event occurrences are assigned typed symbolic descriptions and operational interpretations; partial-order structures retain concurrency and conflict, while operator composition distinguishes syntactic order, admissibility, and state transformation. A stochastic field-theoretic construction is proposed for the evolution of multiple interacting relational entities and resource flows. On this descriptive foundation, the paper treats justice as an object of situated observation and jurisprudential interpretation. Distinct evaluators may employ binary judgments, numerical indices, ordered linguistic expressions, or other geometric and algebraic representations. The Hilbert representation of finite expressions is identified, by an explicit unitary construction, with the full non-symmetric Fock space, preserving word order without presupposing a theory of linguistic meaning. A comparative jurisprudential taxonomy and an illustrative study of generative justice connect these observation channels to the historical circulation of value, rights, capabilities, and institutional authority. The framework is intended to clarify which procedural distinctions remain observable under particular representations, how interpretations differ, and how judgments themselves can participate in subsequent relational dynamics.

items.title: A Matter of Degree: On the Location of Gender Differences.
items.abstract: A man cares for his mother, in a vegetative state, at home for over two years, while settling accounts by a ledger that allows no offsetting. The categorical account says this man does not fit the category. Moral psychology has seen a forty-year dispute: Kohlberg erected a ladder of moral development scored by justice reasoning, and Gilligan protested that the ladder measured only men, proposing that women speak in a different voice, that of care. This paper proposes a "theory of degree" to put this dispute in its proper place: the differentiation between men and women lies not in sequence, but in degree. Care and justice are not the patents of two sexes; they are two orientations every person has, and sex changes only their average proportions, not their kinds. Kohlberg's sequence belongs to development, not to gender; Gilligan's care is a genuine discovery whose attribution was wrong. Gilligan herself pointed out in 2023 that the view of the gender binary in the 1982 In a Different Voice is outdated, and that the gender binary is a distortion of reality. The theory of degree in this paper takes up that step of hers, replacing category with spectrum. The theory of degree does not claim that she has already stated the theory of degree. That further step is the author's own. This paper offers six cases as evidence: the author himself, Rogers, Ginsburg, Bonhoeffer, Tao Xingzhi, and Montessori. The first case is the author: a man who provides round-the-clock home care for his unconscious mother — while conducting his affairs by ledger and justice, with no offsetting of accounts allowed. With both orientations present in one person, the categorical account fails. The other five cases are in §4. The paper advances three new insights: first, the theory of degree itself; second, a two-way restitution of Kohlberg and Gilligan, with a third position that holds both lines; third, the method of a single-person counterexample with both orientations present. Methodologically, this paper is a conceptual argument. The six cases are existence proofs: they break the category, they do not estimate the population; the numbers for proportion come from published meta-analyses, not from the six cases.

items.title: Generativity Propagation and Subject Existence: Where Does the Subject Exist in Human–AI Cooperation?
items.abstract: A human encounter with a contingent question may initiate inquiry, uncertainty, intellectual commitment, and collaboration with artificial intelligence. The resulting knowledge artifact can remain real even when the labor of expression and organization is substantially automated. A further problem emerges when an AI-supported research process continues autonomously after its human participant withdraws: the initial encounter remains part of the process’s historical formation, while subsequent products may cease to reveal that history or require the participant’s continuing action. This philosophical essay investigates that divergence through a provisional generative–relational (GR) account of relational objects, relational subjects, and generativity propagation. It distinguishes historical occurrence, causal dependence, active participation, personal persistence, epistemic recognition, and normative attribution; proposes a constrained complex-based vocabulary for representing event histories; and uses a hypothetical autonomously self-modifying research system as a thought experiment. Relational distance is separated from causal strength, and institutional attribution is examined as a purpose-bound selection from richer histories under evidential and cognitive constraints. The analysis treats withdrawal from participation and loss of attribution as changes distinct from the historical occurrence of an earlier encounter. It also separates genealogical continuation from claims of persistent personal identity. The resulting account interprets “I never disappear” through the conditions of historical persistence and subject identification. It also considers implications for authorship, responsibility, archival practice, and human–AI knowledge production.

items.title: 主観的経験の統合モデル.
items.abstract: 私は「２つの同時性の組み合わせが１つの事象性を形成している」、「事象性は非対称性の入れ子構造となって連続していく」という精神の基本構造を仮定して、精神の構造や機能を数式として表現することを試みました。これらの数式はGoogle Geminiとの共同製作であり、厳密な数学としてではなく、比喩表現の方法として用いられています。 特にこの記事は、私が私の複数の記事や自意識をGoogle Geminiに詰め込んで、完全にGoogle Gemini（Gemini 4 Neon 'High'）が作成したものです。リーマン予想が証明されたことを記念して、ここに記事にさせて頂きます。 日本時間２０２６年１１月２１日。.

items.title: Discriminating unity, or achieving it? Comments to McCormack.
items.abstract: McCormack’s (2026) advances Schellenberg’s capacitism by proposing a dedicated capacity to discriminate objectual unity, resolving the standard trade-off between unity and particularity. His proposal is a genuine improvement on existing fixes, but its remaining difficulties – the concrete/abstract status of unity, an unacknowledged integration problem within his own solution, and the underdeveloped notion of co-directedness – trace to one assumption: Discrimination is punctuated rather than temporally extended. Reframing unity-discrimination through a temporally integrated alternative as an achievement of ongoing synthesis among sensation, retention, and anticipation, dissolves these difficulties, completing McCormack’s proposal.

items.title: On What Matters to the Dead.
items.abstract: Can a person ever be harmed by events occurring after her death? This paper puts forward a new theory of posthumous harm, which builds on Derek Parfit’s distinction between identity and what matters in survival. Whatever our views are on postmortem interests, the importance of past desires, and our practice of honouring the dead, we all agree that something matters in survival: there is a relation that underpins the special, prudential concern we ordinarily believe we should have for ourselves. I argue that if we also agree with Parfit that this relation matters even without identity, we can explain the possibility of posthumous harms and benefits just by appealing to the nature of prudence. Although we might no longer be in a position to harm individuals identical to a dead person, we can harm others who are suitably psychologically related to her—the dead person’s continuers.

items.title: The Natural Logic of Denial.
items.abstract: Linguistic research has provided evidence that natural language grammar contains a natural logic as one of its subcomponents, with logical notions such as entailment playing an explanatory role in the acceptability and interpretation of linguistic constructions. This paper explores the implications of internalizing such a natural-logical system for the maintenance of a positive self-image. Adopting Gentzen’s natural deduction system as a model of aspects of human reasoning, we examine the role of two inference rules (i.e., Negation Introduction and Conditional Introduction) in two forms of denial as a defense mechanism: denial through negation and denial through fantasy. We argue that Negation Introduction contributes to the avoidance of contradictory mental states in ways that preserve a competent self-image, while Conditional Introduction is implicated in identifying the inferential steps required to connect the available premises to desirable conclusions, with the missing steps subsequently being supplied by unconscious mental processes.

items.title: Being Worried.
items.abstract: The kind of state one describes when reporting that one is ‘worried’ is unclear and underexamined. It’s often assumed that such a state is an emotion, distinguishable from the activity of worrying. I argue that the first part of this assumption is mistaken. If worry were an emotion, then by the criteria we standardly use to individuate emotions it would be indistinguishable from anxiety. Nevertheless, the ways we express worry and anxiety in ordinary language seem to indicate fine-grained distinctions between them. These considerations present a puzzle for how we classify the state of ‘being worried’. I argue that this puzzle is best solved by interpreting such a state not as an emotion at all, but rather as a standing evaluative attitude that, whilst not constitutively emotional, is ordinarily accompanied by anxiety. I develop this view and consider how such a state relates to the activity of worrying.

items.title: Immortality: Gradual Brain Replacement and the Continuation of the Self — On Self-Manifestation, Outer Chapter 21.
items.abstract: If a person’s brain is replaced part by part until none of its original components remains, does that person survive? If only a small part of the original brain is retained and new components are added to form a complete brain, does the resulting whole have the same claim to personal survival? Through this contrast, this paper proposes a central thesis about immortality and personal persistence: whether a being continues as that very being depends on whether its history is sufficient to sustain its continuation. -/- Beginning with first-person self-reference, the paper observes that each person attests “I” through their own self-reference and that each person’s being has a private belonging. Sharing the structure of selfhood and continuing a particular self therefore pose distinct questions. A comparison between gradually replacing an entire chair and reconstructing a chair around a single surviving leg locates persistence in the historical succession sustained through the replacement process. Applied to the brain, the argument maintains that gradual replacement can continue the original subject through a complete renewal of material components, whereas rebuilding a whole from a retained fragment may fail to sustain that subject. -/- This account brings a common question to brain replacement, mind uploading, digital immortality, and artificial consciousness: under what conditions do similarity, preserved information, or reproduced function actually carry forward the original subject? For neuroscience and cognitive science, the question concerns personal persistence through changes in brain organization. For artificial intelligence, it concerns how artificial components might participate in the continuation of an existing subject. At the level of physical realization, it concerns the relationship between material replacement and the history of a persisting system. The paper concludes by identifying a constructive direction for immortality: training and constructing field components capable of participating in the historical continuation of an existing field, allowing the same self to persist through ongoing renewal.

items.title: 永生：逐步脑替换与自我延续——《自显论·外篇第二十一》.
items.abstract: 当一个人的脑被逐部替换，直至原有部件全部更换，继续存在的是否仍是原来的这个人？如果只保留原脑的一小部分，再以新部件补成完整的脑，二者是否具有相同的生存意义？本文以这两种替换过程的对照，提出理解永生与自我延续的核心判断：存在者能否继续作为原来的存在者成立，取决于其是否具有足以承接自身的“可续之历史”。 -/- 文章从第一人称自指出发，指出你、我、他都以各自的自指验得“我”，并共同具有存在的私有归属。由此，同样具有自我结构，与延续某一个具体的我，是两个需要分别回答的问题。通过椅子逐部更换与仅留一腿后重新补全的对照，文章把同一性判断的重心放在实际更替过程所承担的历史承续上，并将这一判断推进到脑的替换：逐步更换可以在材料全部更新的过程中承续原有之在，而保留局部后重建整体，则可能不足以使原有主体续存。 -/- 这一立场为脑替换、意识上传、数字永生和人工意识提供了共同的追问：新系统与原系统的相似、信息保存或功能重现，究竟在何种条件下承担了原主体的延续？对于神经科学与认知科学，它指向脑组织变化中的主体持续性；对于人工智能，它指向人工构件如何接续既有主体；对于物理层面的研究，它指向材料更替与系统历史之间的关系。文章最终将永生落实为一个构造方向：训练和制造能够参与既有场之历史承续的部件，使同一个我的存在得以在持续更新中延展。.

items.title: The Complexity Field: A Fast-Sector Hypothesis for the Ontological Medium of Phenomenality.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- We propose a hypothesis about a physical medium that serves as a condition of possibility for phenomenal experience. We postulate a hidden sector with its own light cone and a limiting speed u ≫ c (“field-2”). Its sources are black-hole horizons and the cosmological horizon, and it couples to matter not through mass, charge or number of bits, but through the complexity of the physical state of a connected region. We show that this construction does not contradict known physics: neither the finiteness nor the value of c is derived from first principles; a superluminal sector is compatible with causality if it lives in its own emergent geometry; and coupling to complexity explains why such a field has not been detected in searches for new forces. The hypothesis implies that the brain is a suitable carrier of this coupling, whereas present-day digital AI is not, regardless of its behaviour. The main prediction — a signal that grows with the complexity of the source at fixed energy and heat dissipation — can be tested on existing quantum processors. The link between the field and phenomenality is introduced as a separate postulate and is not derived from the physical part.

items.title: Quine, W. V.
items.pub: In Thomas Teo, The Palgrave Encyclopedia of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan. pp. 1-7.
items.venue: The Palgrave Encyclopedia of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology
items.abstract: This entry introduces the life and work of the philosopher-logician W. V. Quine (1908–2000), focusing on his contributions to theoretical and philosophical psychology. It outlines (1) his views about the relation between psychology and philosophy, (2) his rejection of mentalism in theories of meaning and language acquisition; and (3) his modestly behaviorist perspective on mind and its place in nature.

items.title: The Perceived Presence of a Writer in Literary Prose: Semantic-Space Guidance, Counterfactual Branching, Anticipation of Possible Completion, and Attribution of Agency.
items.abstract: Even when a text is grammatically natural and logically well organized, readers may perceive little sense of a writer behind it. Conversely, pedantry, uneven interests, unexpected associations, and expressions that appear inconsiderate of the reader can sometimes evoke a vivid persona. Readability and textual quality alone do not adequately explain this difference. -/- Focusing on literary prose, particularly essays and personal reflections, this paper defines the perceived presence of a writer as the reader's experience of sensing behind a text a speaking subject with a particular perspective, interests, and tendencies of judgment. It then examines possible mechanisms of that experience. -/- The paper distinguishes semantic-space guidance, which shapes the range and relations of possible interpretations, from temporal guidance, which shapes the order in which these possibilities are encountered and the moments at which they are revised. It considers the retrospective traceability of conceptual leaps, the counterfactual consequences of branching as differences in meaning formation that would have followed from another path, and the anticipation of possible completion, which is distinct from predicting a conclusion. Possible completion does not necessarily require a unique interpretation and may characterize works that sustain multiple readings. -/- On this basis, the paper proposes that one mechanism of perceived presence involves readers inferring alternative expressive possibilities and attributing the reasons for realized choices to a subject. It also distinguishes the self-image presented by an author from the persona constructed by a reader, and examines a recursive relation in which the resulting speaker model guides subsequent comprehension and anticipation of completion. -/- The evocation of a persona, attribution of agency, and perceived person-specificity are treated as distinct phenomena, with readers' knowledge and interpretive attitudes specified as conditions of application. The proposed framework does not determine whether an actual author is human or whether a text is good; rather, it offers a testable account of the relation between meaning comprehension and the perceived presence of a subject.

items.title: Why Is Consciousness Difficult to Explain? Physicalism, Dualism, Experience, and Intentionality.
items.abstract: Why can increasingly detailed accounts of perception, attention, report and neural organization leave philosophers disagreeing about whether experience itself has been explained? One answer is that phenomenal consciousness resists physical explanation; another is that the demand for an additional explanation mistakenly treats the appearance of a gap as a metaphysical discovery. This paper argues that neither inference is compulsory. The recurrent difficulty is an explanatory-bridge problem: a proposed explanation can establish a dependable correlation, a causal mechanism, a constitutive relation or a reason why a subject has an experience, and these are not automatically equivalent achievements. A correlation may be real without establishing identity; behavioral competence may warrant an attribution without logically entailing phenomenal consciousness; the conceivability of a duplicate without experience may challenge a theory without proving metaphysical possibility. -/- The paper defends the Explanatory-Bridge Accountability Thesis (EBAT): a theory counts as an adequate explanation of the target it claims only if it identifies the target notion of consciousness, distinguishes its explanatory bridge from mere evidence of that target, makes rival bridge hypotheses inspectable, and specifies what would revise its claims. A Phenomenal Explanation Bridge Protocol (PEBP-12) articulates twelve non-aggregative checks covering experience, access, measurement, embodiment, causal and constitutive hypotheses, first-person evidence, theory-laden indicators, counterfactuals, epistemic risk, and revision. Five formal results delimit what report equivalence, empirical covariation, measurement validity, philosophical possibility and cross-tradition comparison can establish. Thirteen case studies confront Mary, Nagel's bat, inverted spectra, blindsight, no-report paradigms, anesthesia, dreaming, pain, the 2025 adversarial IIT–GNWT experiment, animal experience, artificial intelligence, illusionism, and the reflexive-awareness debates of Indian Buddhist philosophy. The aim is not to crown physicalism, dualism, functionalism or panpsychism by definition. It is to give substantive standards for comparing their successes, unresolved debts and possible falsifiers. The paper closes by arguing that consciousness science can make genuine progress without converting methodological modesty into the claim that subjective experience is either ontologically extra or scientifically …

items.title: Entre la ley y la justicia. La perforación de mínimos y la virtud judicial.
items.pub: Córdoba: Primera Editorial de la UNC.
items.abstract: Una mujer transporta droga porque alguien se aprovecha de su situación de extrema vulnerabilidad. Un joven participa de un robo, pero todas las circunstancias posteriores muestran arrepentimiento, inserción social y una pena capaz de destruir aquello que todavía sostiene su vida. Un hombre vende poca cantidad de marihuana y enfrenta una escala penal que parece desmesurada frente a la lesividad concreta de su conducta. En todos esos casos hubo delito, en todos hubo responsabilidad. Aun así hay algo difícil de resolver: una distancia inquietante entre la pena prevista por la ley y la vida concreta a la que va dirigida. Entre la ley y la justicia se instala precisamente en esa zona. Manuel Serrano reconstruye los desacuerdos doctrinarios y jurisprudenciales sobre los mínimos penales y analiza cuándo esos límites deben operar como una regla vinculante y cuándo, excepcionalmente, pueden ser perforados. La culpabilidad, la lesividad, la proporcionalidad y los límites constitucionales al poder punitivo forman parte de una discusión que no puede resolverse mediante una aplicación automática de la ley. Por eso este libro aborda el castigo pero también sobre cómo juzgar. Aparece, allí, la virtue jurisprudence: la capacidad del juez para advertir qué circunstancias importan, reconocer aquello que vuelve singular a un caso y justificar una decisión que permanezca dentro del derecho sin renunciar a la exigencia de justicia. Serrano muestra cómo entre la regla general y la vida particular, entre el límite impuesto por la ley y aquello que el caso obliga a mirar, se juega una de las decisiones más delicadas del derecho penal contemporáneo.

items.title: Hylomorphism.
items.abstract: Hylomorphism, as a theory about material objects, was first explained by Aristotle in Metaphysics, Book VII. He conceives every physical entity as a compound of ὕλη (hyle) matter and μορφή (morphē) form, with the generic _form_ as immanently _real_ within the individual. In the Middle Ages hylomorphism became the dominant view, with scholastics of the time developing elaborate hylomorphic theories to explain the world.

items.title: Transhumanism and Digital Humanism: Reconsidering Mind Uploading through the Phenomenology of the Person.
items.abstract: In this paper, I examine the phenomenological implications of transhumanism, focusing on the preservation of personal identity amid bodily enhancement. I engage with Balayo’s (2021) perceptual account of mind uploading, arguing that a phenomenology of perception alone is insufficient to address the problem. Instead, I propose a shift toward the ontology of personal identity grounded in the phenomenology of the person. I heuristically sketch a mind-body uploading theory, demonstrating how both neural functions and felt-bodily experiences are necessary to maintain identity across bodily enhancements. While such a framework might satisfy the ontological requirements of identity preservation, the phenomenology of the person further demands the continuity of an individual’s personal style. Ultimately, I conclude that transhumanism poses a fruitful challenge to phenomenology, and thus should legitimately be considered a branch of digital humanism that is concerned with the implications of bodily enhancements.

items.title: Atmospheric Uptake: From the "Ideal-Typic" Categorization of Atmospheres toward Atmospheres as Values.
items.abstract: This paper examines whether atmospheres, conceived as exogenous emotional forces, can be experienced in a personally meaningful way. Building on Griffero’s (2025) ‘ideal-typic’ categorization of atmospheres, I argue they can. Drawing on Edith Stein’s (2000) notion of uptake, I propose atmospheric uptake: subjects grasp atmospheres as constellations of externally effused values, which they adopt or deny according to their valueception. Finally, this leads to (a) reintroducing private states and intentionality in the grasping of atmospheres, and (b) conceiving atmospheric experience in a first-person manner.

items.title: The Illusion of an Academic Utopia.
items.abstract: Before a scientific claim can earn recognition, it must secure someone’s time and attention. This essay examines how that opportunity is distributed, particularly when research comes from an unfamiliar author, an independent researcher, or a field’s intellectual margins. Drawing on Merton’s universalism, Kuhn’s account of scientific practice, Bourdieu’s scientific capital, and Latour’s analysis of claims in circulation, it traces the institutional passage from proposing an idea to having it seriously examined. Experiments on peer review and studies of novelty, funding, and cumulative advantage reveal how reputation and established measures of achievement can influence that passage. Developments in formal proof verification and automated statistical auditing introduce a further possibility. By making particular aspects of a contribution independently checkable, these tools can reduce reliance on personal familiarity and extend the reach of careful scrutiny. Their value depends on explicit assumptions, accessible resources, and informed judgment about what a result establishes. Historical cases of discovery and institutional resistance also show how sustained support can give uncertain research time to mature. The essay argues that scientific credibility depends partly on how institutions respond to work whose authors have yet to acquire standing. A fair chance at rigorous examination is among the conditions through which an unfamiliar idea can become a shared intellectual achievement.

items.title: How Much Precision Is Really Enough? A Look at the Precision of Writing in an Age of Unlimited Judgement.
items.abstract: Large language models have turned the supply of critique from something scarce and costly into something abundant, instant and almost free. As a result, the list of objections these models raise against any text is structurally endless and never reaches saturation. This article argues that the common question, ‘How much precision is enough?’, is wrongly framed. Contrary to popular assumption, precision and correctness are not actually in dispute. What genuinely needs to be settled is the degree of stringency: the effort a writer must spend to secure those two goals. Drawing on the sceptical tradition (the Agrippan trilemma), the philosophy of science (the Duhem–Quine thesis), the sociology of science (Collins’s experimenter’s regress), and cognitive economics, the article argues that stopping revision has always been a conventional decision, not the discovery of an objective point. The theoretical core of the article is this claim: the agnotology literature has already documented the demand for unlimited stringency as a recognised technique for producing ignorance, and what happens today is an emergent, agentless form of that same technique. The article closes with a practical four-question criterion and a distinction among five functional domains of writing.

items.title: The Happening and the Interpreter.
items.abstract: The Happening and the Interpreter: A Genealogy of Relations, the Question, and Consciousness develops a philosophical theory of how consciousness, interpretation, and existential questioning emerge from relational processes that precede reflective thought. -/- Building upon and refining the arguments introduced in The Animal Before the Question (Rosa, 2026), this second, independent investigation proposes the concept of situated relational dynamics: a recurrent process through which organisms register differences, retain and transform relations, modulate their relevance, select them according to context, and anticipate future events. -/- Drawing on philosophy, cognitive science, neuroscience, and theories of learning, the work examines how memory, biochemical modulation, language, and social interaction contribute to the emergence of the autobiographical interpreter — the self that narrates experience, attributes authorship to actions, and eventually questions its own existence. -/- The theory also investigates the formation and persistence of religious beliefs, the transmission of cultural practices, psychological interpretations of responsibility, and the relationship between causal explanation and human agency. -/- Through conceptual diagrams, a minimal formal framework, thought experiments, and proposed criteria for empirical investigation, the essay articulates a unified explanatory structure while distinguishing established scientific findings from its own philosophical hypotheses. -/- Its central argument challenges the assumption that the ability to formulate a question guarantees the existence of the kind of answer it demands. Rather than denying the significance of consciousness, the work situates it within the continuous unfolding of events: the interpreter does not stand outside the world it describes, but participates in the very processes it seeks to understand.

items.title: The Animal Before the Question.
items.abstract: This philosophical essay challenges the assumption that consciousness occupies a central or privileged position in existence. It proposes a functional genealogy in which consciousness emerges as a belated interpretive layer, organizing and narrating processes that precede it. From this perspective, the existential demand for meaning is not a fundamental question awaiting an answer, but a product of consciousness mistakenly attributing authorship and purpose to itself. -/- Through a critical engagement with Nietzsche, Sartre, Camus, and Schopenhauer, the essay examines how philosophical responses to meaninglessness may reproduce the very assumptions they seek to overcome. It further explores the self-referential character of philosophical thought, psychological egoism, and the homeostatic function of existential questioning. -/- Rather than proposing another metaphysical foundation or embracing nihilism, the essay develops the concept of deference: a mode of existence in which consciousness recognizes its own belatedness without demanding that reality justify itself. -/- Ultimately, the work questions not merely the answers humanity has offered to the problem of existence, but the legitimacy of the primordial question itself.

items.title: The Physics of Reasoning: Why Hilbert's Dream Survives in the Age of AI.
