Rather than trying to settle this debate or explore new avenues of conceptualizing trust, it asks what the persistent appeal to the language of trust reveals about the moral and social concerns that are at stake in contemporary human–AI relations. Consequently, the long-standing discussion on trust and technology itself becomes the focal point of analysis. Rather than a contested concept, trust then becomes a moral lens through which the shared concerns and interests underpinning the debate become visible. The paper first situates the current trustworthy AI debate within a longer tradition of philosophical discussions concerning the (im)possibility of meaningfully attributing trust and trustworthiness to technology. Next, it analyses three prominent positions in the trustworthy AI debate, ranging from sceptical rejection of trust language, through attempts to reconceptualise trust to account for AI applications, to a more relational understanding of AI as part of a socio-technical system. Taking a reverse-engineering approach, the paper argues that, despite their differences, these positions are driven by shared underlying concerns about vulnerability under increasing technological dependency, the entanglement of humans and technologies, the uncertainty and opacity inherent in AI applications impacting moral orientation and meaningful human agency, the distribution of responsibility, and the maintenance of institutional legitimacy. Looking under the conceptual hood of the trust and technology discussion uncovers their shared moral drivers and helps to move the debate beyond conceptual impasses towards a richer understanding of the ethical impact of AI.

items.title: Dilemmas in Lingual Philosophy: A Formal Survey from Whorf to the Liar.
items.abstract: This paper surveys six persistent dilemmas in the philosophy of language: the Whorfian-Wittgensteinian tension over whether language bounds or merely clarifies thought; Quine's indeterminacy of translation; Wittgenstein's private language argument; Frege's sense-reference distinction; the analytic-synthetic distinction and Quine's attack on it; and the Liar paradox. For each, we state the dilemma, formalize its core claims where possible, and identify the cost exacted by each horn. The unifying structure is a collision between a compelling intuition and an equally compelling counter-intuition, neither of which can be abandoned without loss.

items.title: People Trust Medicine Too Much.
Public Support for Science Might Worsen Policy.
items.pub: Journal of the National Science Foundation of Sri Lanka 53 (4):309-310.
items.venue: Journal of the National Science Foundation of Sri Lanka
items.abstract: Evidence-based policy has become the gold standard for trustworthy governance, yet the relationship between trust and trustworthiness in science-policy interactions is more complex than commonly assumed. This letter argues that increased public trust in science may undermine policy quality because of policy-based evidence-making–the selective use of scientific evidence to justify predetermined political decisions. Drawing on political science literature and Britain’s experience with evidence-based policy, it is argued that high trust allows policymakers to obscure necessary value judgements behind scientific authority. Efforts to increase trust in science, such as the National Academy of Sciences Sri Lanka’s recent initiative to restore trust in science, must therefore consider these perverse incentives to avoid inadvertently compromising evidence-informed policymaking.

items.title: Political Polarization of Trust in Science.
items.abstract: Contrary to widespread claims of a crisis in public trust in science, this article argues that recent pandemic-era trends reflect a long-term pattern of bilateral political polarization rather than a universal decline in scientific confidence. Recent empirical data show that trust and distrust in science have both increased – producing an apparent “pandemic paradox” – driven by ideological bias operating within gaps in public understanding. The study identifies a misunderstanding of how science works as the fundamental cause of politicized trust, where misconceptions create space for ideological bias to shape which claims individuals find credible. Critically, the article argues that existing interventions – improved science communication and increased science education – are insufficient. The core problem is not the quantity of science education but its type. Only by teaching the methodological and institutional limitations of science can the field depolarize public trust and build politically stable confidence in scientific institutions.

items.title: Patients Might Distrust Honest Doctors.
items.abstract: Evidence-based medicine revolutionized clinical practice, bringing expectations that physician–patient communication should be similarly transparent about scientific evidence and uncertainty. However, the replication crisis has revealed significant weaknesses in biomedical research. This creates something of a paradox: honest disclosure of uncertainty is ethically obligatory but often breeds patient distrust rather than confidence. This commentary argues that trust in medicine requires systemic educational reform to improve public scientific literacy, and offers some practical communicative strategies physicians can employ immediately, including deliberate language hedging and setting realistic expectations. Critically, such approaches only succeed when grounded in compassionate physician–patient relationships. In an era of increasing commercialization and artificial intelligence in medicine, preserving this fundamental relationship is essential for maintaining public trust in healthcare.

items.title: Conceptually Engineering the Notion of Time Travel.
items.abstract: The field of philosophy of time is lacking a clear definition of time travel. The novel approach in this essay is to conceptually engineer a coherent definition of time travel that avoids (i.e. incorporates) the problematics associated with current vague conceptions. This reveals that all current arguments – assuming they all obtain – only entail the impossibility of a certain conception of time travel, not the impossibility of time travel outright. This study in conceptual engineering reveals that there are other coherent conceptions of time travel, the possibility of which that might yet obtain.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence is (Only) a Useful Tool to Assist with Peer Review.
items.abstract: A recent survey of more than 1600 researchers spanning 111 countries found that over half of respondents reported using artificial intelligence (AI) in peer review. A majority of these stated they used AI to assist with drafting peer review reports, while significant minorities reported using AI to summarise findings, detect plagiarism or assess methodology or statistical soundness of manuscript. -/- What should journal editors do when they receive an AI-generated review? There is little guidance. I argue that editors should not assume that it is a bad review (because AI can be a valuable tool), but they should remain vigilant that AI may be misused as a proxy for human expertise.

items.title: Socratic Ignorance and Me.
items.abstract: A settled popular reading takes Socratic ignorance to be an awareness that one does not know, or a form of humility. This essay offers a personal reading on a different axis: Socratic ignorance is not an awareness of the quantity of one's knowledge but an understanding of the causal structure of unknowability, that is, of why something is unknowable for the human being as an observing apparatus. On this reading, Socrates' questioning in the streets gauged where each interlocutor's cognitive reach stopped and why, and his restriction, at the close of the Apology, to the binary of nothingness or transition reflects logical precision rather than modesty. The essay then argues that death admits two descriptions, death never reached from within the subjective frame and death that arrives for an external observer, which describe the same event from reference frames that cannot be translated into each other. The same asymmetry is traced along the time axis: drawing on chronostasis, flash-lag, and postdiction, the essay holds that subjective time is assembled after the fact rather than sampled from objective time, and it reads the gamma surge reported in the dying brain only as a bounded hypothesis about what may happen just before the wall. Since access to the meaning of intelligence passes through the meaning of existence, and that through the meaning of death, death appears not as a wall to be crossed but as one that always lies across the path of inquiry. The essay closes with a private settlement with Socratic ignorance: understanding why the unknowable is unknowable, and continuing to inquire nonetheless. A closing sentence is given in the original Japanese with a note on its translation.

items.title: Decolonising Autistic Phenomenology: Towards a Critical-Enactive Account of Cognitive Diversity.
items.abstract: Recent years have seen a turn toward phenomenological, ecological, and enactive approaches to autism and neurodiversity, within the philosophy of psychiatry and cognitive science. These approaches challenge dominant neuro-reductionist and computational biomedical paradigms, centring embodiment, relationality, affectivity, and the constitutive role of sociomaterial environments in cognition. However, both phenomenological and ecological-enactive approaches are heterogeneous; not all escape the Eurocentric neuronormative assumptions underlying colonial modernity. This paper argues that, where classical phenomenology positions autism as a deviation from implicitly Western standards of ‘neurotypical’ embodiment and intersubjectivity, critical phenomenology and enactivism supply promising resources to reconceive autistic traits as intrinsically meaningful forms of sense-making – whilst interrogating the universality of categories such as ‘autism’ and ‘neurotypicality.’ Critical phenomenology draws attention to how power shapes embodiment, stretching the phenomenological method to confront its own complicity in Eurocentric neuronormativity. Enactivism goes further, providing an inclusive relational ontology of cognitive diversity that can facilitate dialogue with non-Western and Indigenous ways of knowing. Yet it risks becoming politically neutralised when inattentive to coloniality and intersectional oppression. Drawing insight from South Asian autistic experiences, I sketch out a critical-enactive framework oriented toward dismantling both neuronormative and Eurocentric (including logocentric and anthropocentric) assumptions in phenomenology and cognitive science. This decolonial approach paves the way for a pluralistic, intercultural understanding of autism – and embodied cognitive diversity, more broadly – doing justice to culturally and ecologically situated styles of sense-making, without essentialising neurological or cognitive differences.

items.title: Can habits account for ecological agency? The habit trilemma.
items.abstract: Many ecological psychologists understand agency in terms of selecting among affordances or possibilities for action. This gives rise to the selection problem: given the abundance of affordances available in any situation, what explains the organism’s selecting some of them? In this paper, I examine one of the most promising responses, which I call the Habit View: the claim that habits, understood as information-seeking tendencies, explain selection in normative and non-representational terms. I argue that the Habit View faces a trilemma. If habits are guided by prior intentions, the view collapses into a form of representationalism. If, instead, habits are constitutive of intentions, the organism must perceive solicitations rather than (mere) possibilities for action, contrary to the framing of the selection problem. I suggest that this trilemma does not depend on any distinctive feature of habits but derives from what I call Independence: the assumption that the relation of information is determined independently of the organism’s activity. As long as this assumption is in place, no normative and non-representational explanation of selection seems available. I conclude that we should question the theory of information from which the problem arises and suggest that the usage-based account of ecological information offers a promising alternative.

items.title: Aquinas on Moral Responsibility.
items.pub: Notre Dame, IN: Notre Dame Press.
items.abstract: Aquinas on Moral Responsibility explores how Aquinas understands what it means to be morally responsible. Rather than focusing narrowly on freedom of the will alone, Furlong reconstructs Aquinas’s view by examining the practices through which we hold each other responsible, such as praise and blame or reward and punishment. These practices, he argues, are central to understanding what it means to be morally responsible in light of one’s actions. -/- The book opens by clarifying Aquinas’s conception of moral responsibility itself before asking what sort of control must someone possess over their actions in order to be responsible for them. Furlong argues that Aquinas adopts a version of the Principle of Alternative Possibilities, in which agents are responsible for their actions only if they could have done otherwise. He also defends an incompatibilist interpretation of Aquinas, arguing that moral responsibility is incompatible with determinism. -/- Furlong considers, through Aquinas, the ways in which a theory of moral responsibility must take into account ignorance, our settled character, luck, and passions. The result is a unified and carefully argued interpretation of Aquinas’s enduring contributions to debates about freedom and moral responsibility.

items.title: Natural Law and the New Aristotelianism.
items.pub: In William M. R. Simpson & Justin Buckley Dyer, A History of Natural Law: From the Ancient World to the New Aristotelianism. Cambridge University Press. pp. 295-317.
items.venue: A History of Natural Law: From the Ancient World to the New Aristotelianism
items.abstract: The aim of this chapter is to show how the New Aristotelianism can inform “natural law theory” (NLT). While many neo-Aristotelian ethical naturalists—following Philippa Foot and Michael Thompson—are uncommitted to NLT, we believe there is a neo-Aristotelian approach to NLT, distinct from both “classical natural law theory” (CNLT) and “new natural law theory” (NNLT) (Shea; Moschella, this volume), which draws upon the insights of the New Aristotelians and is worth developing. Alasdair MacIntyre characterizes his own approach to NLT as a form of Thomistic-Aristotelianism, because it emphasizes the ways the Thomistic tradition is an elaboration and development of Aristotelian principles. Following MacIntyre’s lead, this chapter draws on a range of neo-Aristotelian insights to elaborate an Aristotelian approach to NLT which we might call “phronetic natural law theory” (PNLT) due to the central role that Aristotelian phronesis (i.e., practical wisdom) and the virtues play in its account of how humans discover the basic goods and norms of the natural law. We offer a sketch of that theory here. In the first section, we discuss various ways PNLT differs from CNLT and NNLT, drawing attention to its neo-Aristotelian features. In the second section, we show how the neo-Aristotelian metaphysics of powers adopted by PNLT supports a normative anthropology which challenges the accounts of basic goods and the virtues we find in CNLT and NNLT.

items.title: Children as deliberators in the present. A book review of Children, Democracy, and Education: A Deliberative Reconstruction. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Kei Nishiyama’s book Children, Democracy, and Education: A Deliberative Reconsideration makes a significant contribution to the fields of deliberative education, civics and citizenship education, and Philosophy for/with Children. I highly recommend this book to anyone whose research intersects education, democracy, and deliberative communication. It is a must for practitioners, educators, philosophers of education, and academics from related disciplines in the humanities and social sciences. The book would be suitable for courses on social and political philosophy and theory, philosophy of education, issues in education, pedagogy, and civics and citizenship education.

items.title: The Right to Share in the AI Era: Economic Equality Beyond Employment.
items.abstract: Distributive institutions that make market employment the gateway to a share of social output are losing their justification. Whether or not automation shrinks aggregate labor demand, the claim that a person must work for pay in order to share in what society produces was never a principle of justice; it was an arrangement fitted to scarcity. This paper argues that the basic right to share in the fruits of social production rests on equal membership in an economic community, and is therefore prior to, and independent of, employment status. The argument runs through four steps. Production is the joint yield of natural wealth, inherited knowledge and ongoing cooperation, so no current employer, owner or worker holds exclusive title to it. Market compensation and the right to share answer different questions and must be kept apart. Non-employment is a normal position within the social division of labor, not a deficiency. A dual-tier distributive structure—an equal foundational share, bounded by a principle against structural hierarchy, and a differentiated tier of labor and innovation returns—gives these claims institutional content. The paper meets the reciprocity objection directly, specifies how the two tiers are fixed relative to each other, and shows that institutionalized exclusion from common yields is a form of exploitation when it enriches some at the expense of others’ standing. Public distribution is then an enforceable obligation of justice owed to every member, not charity.

items.title: Why the Observer is Immaterial: A Relativistic and Epistemological Proof on Reference Frames, Geometric Invariance, and Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper presents a formal physical and epistemological argument for the thesis that the observer—both as an operational reference frame and as conscious awareness—is fundamentally non-material. First, we analyze the kinematic asymmetry between observed matter and the observing center under relativistic motion. When an observer watches an external material body travel at velocity v parallel to a photon, the separation speed within the observational field is c − v. However, when the observer accelerates to co-move with that object, the local measurement does not yield c − v; the measured speed of light remains strictly invariant at c. To enforce this invariance, spacetime dynamically recalibrates via Lorentz transformations: external space contracts (Δx) and external time dilates (Δt) relative to the newly established frame. Because the metric structure of space and time reorganizes around the observer rather than allowing the observer to register an altered velocity relative to light, the observer does not behave as an internal material component of the physical flow, but as the non-material reference center around which spacetime geometry is structured. Second, we demonstrate the category error inherent in equating reference frames with physical instrumentation. While physical measuring devices are material bodies characterized by non-zero spatial dimensions, mass, and static 4D worldlines in the block universe, a relativistic coordinate system requires a dimensionless geometric origin (0, 0, 0, 0) and an abstract metric grid. Physical matter undergoes localized interactions—analogous to a mechanical collision producing a local dent in a pole—yet these blind impacts contain no inherent speed, duration, or spatial metric. Physical properties such as velocity, length contraction, and time dilation do not reside within isolated matter, as proven by the frame-dependent lifetimes and atmospheric distances of relativistic muons; they emerge strictly in relation to a coordinate system. Finally, we argue that this geometric framework is inherently mental: a material detector cannot intrinsically single out a preferential hypersurface of simultaneity or an active "now" along its worldline. It requires a conscious observer to project an origin, maintain temporal synthesis across discrete events, and experience the unfolding present. We conclude that both the coordinate reference frame and the conscious subject performing the metrical synthesis belong to an …

items.title: Waarom de Waarnemer Niet-Materieel Is: Een relativistisch en epistemologisch bewijs over referentiestelsels, meetkundige invariantie en bewustzijn.
items.abstract: Dit artikel formuleert een formele natuurkundige en kennistheoretische onderbouwing voor de stelling dat de waarnemer — zowel opgevat als operationeel referentiestelsel als in de hoedanigheid van bewust gewaarzijn — fundamenteel niet-materieel van aard is. Ten eerste analyseren we de kinematische asymmetrie tussen waargenomen materie en het waarnemende nulpunt onder relativistische beweging. Wanneer een waarnemer ziet hoe een extern materieel voorwerp met snelheid v parallel meebeweegt met een lichtpuls, bedraagt de scheidingssnelheid binnen het waarnemingsveld klassiek c − v. Echter, zodra de waarnemende instantie accelereert om dezelfde snelheid v aan te nemen, meet deze lokaal géén verminderde snelheid c − v: de lichtsnelheid blijft strikt en onvoorwaardelijk invariant op c. Om deze invariantie af te dwingen, herkalibreert de ruimtetijd zich dynamisch via de Lorentztransformaties: de externe ruimte ondergaat lengtecontractie (Δx) en de externe tijd ondergaat tijdsdilatatie (Δt) ten opzichte van het nieuw gevestigde ruststelsel. Omdat de meetkundige structuur van ruimte en tijd zich actief rond de waarnemer reorganiseert in plaats van toe te staan dat de waarnemer een gewijzigde snelheid ten opzichte van het licht registreert, gedraagt de waarnemer zich niet als een intern materieel deeltje binnen de materiële stroom, maar als het niet-materiële referentiecentrum waaromheen de ruimtetijdgeometrie wordt geordend. Ten tweede leggen we de categoriefout bloot die optreedt wanneer referentiestelsels worden gelijkgesteld aan materiële meetinstrumenten. Waar fysische instrumenten (detectoren, netvliezen of fotografische emulsies) materiële lichamen zijn met eindige ruimtelijke afmetingen, massa en statische vierdimensionale wereldlijnen in het blokuniversum, vereist een relativistisch coördinatenstelsel een dimensieloze meetkundige oorsprong (0, 0, 0, 0) en een abstract coördinatenrooster. Fysische materie ondergaat uitsluitend lokale interacties — vergelijkbaar met een mechanische botsing die een deuk in een paal achterlaat — maar deze blinde inslagen bevatten uit zichzelf noch snelheid, noch tijdsduur, noch een ruimtelijke metriek. Fysische eigenschappen zoals snelheid, lengtekrimp en tijdrek liggen niet opgesloten in geïsoleerde materie, zoals onweerlegbaar blijkt uit de stelselafhankelijke levensduren en atmosferische afstanden van relativistische muonen; ze ontstaan uitsluitend in relatie tot een gekozen referentiekader. Ten slotte betogen we dat dit …

items.title: Abstraction, Analogy, and Analogical Reasoning.
items.abstract: Analogy is the bedrock of communication. Even that sentence makes use of analogy: as bedrock underlies and supports structures, so too does analogy underlie and support communication, allowing us to coordinate activity and manipulate our environment. Analogy allows a reasoner to transfer previously learned structure to a new situation, generating hypotheses and thereby facilitating new understanding. So fundamental is analogy to language that it proves challenging to articulate the abstract structure of analogy and to codify analogical reasoning. Nonetheless, it remains a fundamental endeavor for any interested in understanding mentation. In the foregoing, I introduce and augment one popular model of analogy, and I utilize the formalism thus achieved to offer a definition of analogical reasoning, specifying how an analogical reasoning step generates hypotheses about a target domain from facts in a source domain. Whether a hypothesis comes to be believed is a matter of empirical testing and environmental feedback, which lies outside the present formalism.

items.title: The Right to Be More Than a Record: Narrative Non-Exhaustion, Human Dignity, and the Ethics of Institutional Judgment.
items.pub: International Journal of Law Management and Humanities 9 (6):796-815.
items.venue: International Journal of Law Management and Humanities
items.abstract: Institutional records can be accurate yet insufficient to justify consequential judgments about a person’s character, credibility, or future capacity. This article asks when that gap amounts to wrongful institutional misrecognition rather than ordinary evidential uncertainty. Using a purposive critical-interpretive synthesis of narrative identity, recognition theory, epistemic injustice, classification studies, privacy, and reasoned administration, it develops the Principle of Narrative Non-Exhaustion (PNE). The principle holds that an institution must justify the inferential distance between a purpose-bounded record and the wider conclusion on which it acts. Its distinctive concern is inferential overreach, including implicit generalizations through repeated decisions, not mere record inaccuracy or the duration of an algorithmic label. A refined Narrative Non-Exhaustion Review differentiates consequentiality and generalization gateways and evaluates scope, warrant, voice, revisability, and proportionality. A hypothetical professional-safeguarding case involving proven misconduct, subsequent remediation, uncertain risk, and third-party safety demonstrates how a restrictive decision may remain justified without treating a historical finding as an immutable identity. The paper situates this proposal alongside administrative reasonableness, contextual integrity, procedural fairness, and temporal authorship, acknowledging substantial overlap rather than asserting a new positive-law right. Its contribution is an operationally precise specification of what reasoned, non-exhaustive institutional judgment demands, together with decision standards and limitations requiring future empirical testing.

items.title: Valence as a universal principle of binding and weighting.
items.abstract: This work develops a unified theory of valence as a scale-spanning organizational principle from quantum chemistry to political ideology. Valence is defined as preferential stabilization - a mechanism that begins with energetic preferences in chemical bonds and continues through biochemical affinities and neuromodulatory signaling to cognitive evaluation processes. The central thesis states that ideological beliefs emerge and are stabilized through the same valence-based weighting mechanisms that modulate synaptic plasticity. This perspective explains the persistence and rigidity of political worldviews as natural consequences of neurochemical reinforcement systems, not as cognitive defects. The theory generates testable predictions for pharmacological, psychophysiological, and neuroimaging studies and has implications for therapeutic interventions in ideological rigidity as well as for the design of democratic institutions. In contrast to rationalistic approaches, valence theory emphasizes the fundamental role of emotional evaluation in all human cognition, offering a naturalistic alternative to normative ideals of rational discourse.

items.title: The Physical Infrastructure of Experience.
items.abstract: Contemporary theories of consciousness share a common methodological deficit: they describe functional correlates of experience without determining the structural conditions under which experience as such becomes possible at all. The present article develops a framework for the physical infrastructure of experience, the set of necessary structural conditions, not sufficient causal mechanisms, that a physical system must satisfy in order to make phenomenal experience possible. Drawing on the theory of causal collapse and the concept of the causal core as interpreter (Stegemann 2026a, 2025a, 2025b), the article argues that three mutually conditioning structural features constitute this infrastructure: (1) criticality, understood as the dynamic regime of phase transitions in which characteristic length scales diverge; (2) non-factorizability, understood as the ensuing impossibility of decomposing the causal structure of the system into independent partial causes; and (3) the causal core as a dynamic attractor in the system’s phase space, providing the reflexive dimension without which integrated causal unity would remain inert. Mathematically, three independent formal strands converge on the same structural situation: the Hammersley-Clifford theorem, the non-analyticity of the partition function, and the violation of the entanglement entropy area law, the last as a formal characterization tool, not a mechanistic hypothesis about neural quantum processes. An explicit demarcation from Integrated Information Theory shows that non-factorizability in the present framework is a categorical structural property, not a scalar measure. Comparison with superconducting coherence sharpens the anti-panpsychist argument, and concrete proposals for empirically distinguishing active from passive criticality are developed. The framework does not claim to solve the hard problem; it claims to determine the physical preconditions without which the hard problem cannot arise at all.

items.title: The Placebo Effect as a Phenomenon of Autocatalytic Organization.
items.abstract: The standard neuroscientific account of the placebo effect identifies the neurochemical systems involved but fails to explain the constitutive transition from semantic context to physiological cascade. The dominant explanatory concept—expectation—does not resolve this gap; it merely relabels the explanandum. This paper proposes an alternative framework based on the theory of autocatalytic organization, drawing on the formal work of Rosen, Kauffman, and Montévil/Mossio. In an autocatalytically organized system, there is no translation between “meaning” and “physiology” because both are aspects of the same self-maintaining process. The placebo effect is reconceived as the integration of a perturbation into self-reinforcing cascades, governed by the topology of the autocatalytic network. This framework is applied to four empirical domains: psychoneuroimmunology (conditioned immunosuppression), open-label placebos, network neuroscience, and the placebome. Concrete, testable hypotheses are derived, including the prediction that perturbation-based measures of network non-factorizability should correlate with placebo magnitude. The clinical implications include a reframing of the drug–placebo distinction, a critique of the factorizability assumption underlying RCT design, and a rationale for individualized open-label placebo interventions.

items.title: The Operator That Cannot Place Itself.
items.abstract: Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi's 1787 objection to Kant's transcendental idealism identified a structural problem that remains unresolved in the tradition of nested ontological frameworks: any system that posits causal relations between distinct ontological levels requires an operator to mediate those relations, but this operator cannot itself be ontologically located without generating an infinite regress. We argue that this problem is not peripheral to Kant's system but constitutive of it, and that its modern descendants, including layered ontologies of mind and body, hierarchical emergence theories, and multi-level realist frameworks, inherit the same defect. We further argue that the problem dissolves, rather than is solved, once the assumption generating it is abandoned: the assumption that ontological levels are real strata rather than epistemic modes of access to a single physical reality. Drawing on the perspectival entity ontology and dimensional logic developed in prior work (Stegemann 2026a, 2026b, 2026c), we show that replacing causal inter-level operators with reflexive epistemic operators eliminates the regress, preserves scientific realism, and reframes classical puzzles, including the Hard Problem of Consciousness and the measurement problem in quantum mechanics, as dimensional category errors rather than metaphysical mysteries.

items.title: The mechanism of phenomenal experience.
items.abstract: The essay develops a reconstructive systems theory of consciousness based on the causal self-closure of biological systems. Consciousness is not understood as a property or effect, but as the epistemic form that inevitably arises when the causal structure of a system is completely self-contained. Physical, biological and phenomenal descriptions are epistemically autonomous forms of reconstruction that are structurally irreducible to each other. There is no translation relation between them, because they represent structurally heterogeneous modes of cognition within a single ontological basis. In contrast to functionalist theories, which presuppose consciousness by definition, this model reconstructs consciousness genealogically: from thermodynamic self-organization to biological autocatalysis to neuronal oscillation dynamics. The central thesis is that consciousness is not an emergent property of complex systems, but the epistemic form that a physical system necessarily assumes when its causal structure collapses completely into itself. For philosophers, this work shows why the hard problem is a category error: Physical and phenomenal description are different epistemic ways of reconstructing the same structure, not ontologically separated domains. For neuroscientists, it combines measurable correlates (oscillation dynamics, perturbational complexity index) with the necessity of subjective experience and explains why global integration implies an internal perspective.

items.title: The Invariance Trap.
items.abstract: Philosophical fallacies arise not only from false premises or ambiguous words. They can also arise when an expression, a function, a structure, or a description is transferred from one context to another. In such transformations, something is typically preserved while something else changes. This paper calls a property invariant relative to a particular transformation when it is preserved across that transition. Depending on the case, what remains invariant may be a linguistic expression, a semantic function, a material structure, a formal relation, or some other feature. The central error occurs when the preservation of one dimension is taken, without independent justification, to establish the preservation of another. This is termed unwarranted invariance transfer. The approach is developed through six types of transformation: expression and meaning, semantic function and causal realization, levels of description, perspectives of attribution, model and object, and metaphorical transfer. The analysis does not claim that every such case is a category mistake in Ryle's classical sense. Rather, it identifies a general inferential form through which equivocations, level confusions, category mistakes, and unwarranted ontological attributions can arise. Functionalism, the Free Energy Principle, and Integrated Information Theory serve as critical test cases for locating the burden of justification and analyzing concrete invariance errors.

items.title: The Functionalist Trilemma.
items.abstract: Functionalism is among the most influential positions in the philosophy of mind. Its central idea is that mental states are determined not by their material constitution but by their functional or causal role. This gives rise to the possibility of multiple realization: if the same functional organization can be realized in biological and artificial systems, then, in principle, the same mental states should also be possible in different material substrates. This paper argues that this inference does not hold for phenomenal consciousness. Functional equivalence initially establishes equivalence only with respect to functionally specified properties. For phenomenal equivalence to follow, an additional bridge premise is required according to which a particular functional organization is sufficient for experience. There are three argumentative possibilities for such a bridge. It may be stipulated definitionally, justified as an empirical generalization, or asserted as a fundamental psychophysical principle, for example as a necessary identity or a fundamental law. In the first case, consciousness is not explained but functionally redefined. In the second case, empirical evidence from biological systems is insufficient to establish substrate independence. In the third case, the transition from function to experience is carried by an additional principle rather than by the functional description itself. This problem can be formalized as a factorization problem. A functional description is an abstraction that maps different realizations onto the same functional class. Functionalism about consciousness additionally claims that experience factors through precisely this abstraction, and therefore remains invariant within every functional equivalence class. This invariance does not follow from the abstraction itself. It is the central additional assumption of functionalism. Functionalism can therefore describe functional equivalence, but it cannot derive phenomenal equivalence from functional equivalence alone.

items.title: The Emergence of Causal Cores.
items.abstract: This article argues that the emergence of causal cores results from fundamental physical and biological principles. The argumentation proceeds in several interconnected steps: First, the thermodynamic framework is outlined, then the biological concretization is analyzed, followed by consideration of information-theoretic aspects, and finally discussion of evolutionary implications.

items.title: The Causal Core as a Structural Principle of Free Will.
items.abstract: The debate on free will remains shaped by metaphysical speculation, reductionist simplifications, and categorical misunderstandings. While classical philosophy often conceived it as a gift of divine grace or the expression of rational autonomy, modern neuroscience and cognitive models tend to deny freedom in favor of deterministic or probabilistic causal chains. This article advances the thesis that the capacity for intentional action is not rooted in an immaterial will, but in a structural center that emerged in the course of biological evolution: the causal core. This core is not a substance but a dynamically integrating system function, thermodynamically initiated, biologically centered, and psychologically accessible. Drawing on thermodynamic principles, the theory of autopoiesis, and system theory, the article traces the causal core’s genesis from autocatalytic chemical cycles and the encapsulation of protocells, through the emergence of the eukaryotic cell nucleus as a morphologically identifiable locus, to its complex integration in neural systems. The causal core stabilizes selective coupling and enables intentional, goal-oriented behavior. By distinguishing biological and psychological levels of description and avoiding the category error of causal reductionism, the article proposes a consistent systems-theoretical model that unites empirical findings with a coherent epistemological framework. The implications for the concept of free will are discussed, along with applications to artificial systems and animal cognition.

items.title: The Causal Core - A centralist principle of causality from the prokaryotic cell to self, ego, and agency.
items.abstract: This article develops the thesis that living systems form a centralist internal asymmetry from their very first appearance, a structure I refer to as the causal core. This core is not a morphological compartment and not a localisable site. It is a functional attractor that emerges from superposed thermodynamic flows within an operationally closed space, constitutes itself in the prokaryotic cell, and recurs in formally invariant fashion at every higher organisational level of the living. The article draws together the empirical evidence for this continuity from five domains, discusses five possible objections, and finally applies the model to self, ego, and agency. These three terms are not reconstructed as independent cognitive modules but as three descriptive directions of the same causal core at the highest level of biological complexity.

items.title: The Biological Foundation of the Soul.
items.abstract: The soul has an image problem. Anyone who mentions it today in a scientific conversation can expect, at best, an indulgent smile. The concept is considered obsolete, a relic of a pre-scientific era in which whatever could not be explained was given a name, and the name was then mistaken for an explanation. And yet the question behind the concept never disappeared. What is it that makes an organism a subject? What is that inner point from which a being acts, perceives, and refers to itself? Science has not explained this point. It has circumvented it. Behaviorism declared inner states scientifically irrelevant: what counts is observable behavior. Cognitivism replaced the soul with information processing: the mind is a system, not a center. Freud operationalized it as the trinity of id, ego, and superego, psychologically precise but biologically unanchored. Modern neuroscience, finally, dissolved the center altogether: what remains are distributed networks, default mode networks, global workspaces, free energy. No place left for a soul. What all these movements have in common: they declared the inner center, the point of reference, either unscientific or dissolved it into functions, without asking whether something real might still lie behind the concept of the soul, something that merely needed a different description. Behaviorism forbade the question. Cognitivism reformulated it. Neuroscience dissolved it into networks. But forbidden, reformulated, and dissolved is not answered. David Chalmers captured this situation in a single phrase in 1995: the hard problem of consciousness. Why is there subjective experience at all? Why isn't it dark in there? Chalmers did not pose a new question; he named an old one that science had systematically circumvented. The hard problem is still considered unsolved today. This article proposes that it is not unsolved, but misconceived. The question “why is there experience?” presupposes that experience is something added to a physical system. The causal core shows that this presupposition is false.

items.title: Resolving the Hard Problem: Consciousness as the Collapse of Causal Separability.
items.abstract: This article proposes a system-theoretical and thermodynamically based model for the solution of the so-called 'Hard Problem of Consciousness'. Instead of asking why neuronal processes generate subjective experience, it is shown that consciousness can be understood as the structural result of a causal collapse in self-organizing systems. The reasoning develops along three evolutionary thresholds: autopoiesis, causal poiesis, and causal collapse. Consciousness does not appear as a property, but as an epistemic state of structural indistinguishability. The article argues that the hard problem is not an unsolved puzzle, but a categorical misformulation.

items.title: Phenomenology, Systems Theory, and Neurobiology of Consciousness: Causal Collapse.
items.abstract: The question of consciousness remains one of the central challenges of philosophy and the interdisciplinary sciences. Phenomenological approaches – especially in the tradition of Edmund Husserl and its further developments in the 20th and 21st centuries – have chosen an approach that refers strictly to experience itself. They try to grasp consciousness as a structure of appearance and to assert it against naturalistic reductions. This essay presents an alternative theory: the model of causal collapse (Stegemann 2025a). It describes consciousness not as a metaphysically grounded subjectivity, but as a structural phenomenon that arises in a recursive system state that can no longer be causally separed. Consciousness is therefore a real, physically describable state of the brain, but not an empirical object in the narrower sense. The "collapse" marks the limit of analytic decomposability – in exactly the same form in which phenomenology insists on the indivisibility of consciousness, but from a different perspective. The aim is to bring this theory into a systematic examination of central representatives of phenomenology – with Husserl as its origin, and with Merleau-Ponty, Waldenfels and Zahavi as modern continuations. The aim is to make it clear that the concept of collapse is not only an alternative approach to consciousness, but is also capable of transferring central phenomenological insights into a system-theoretical-empirical structure – without resorting to corporeality or metaphysical subject.

items.title: Physics of Organismic Storage.
items.abstract: Current neuroscientific models of memory usually view memory as a function, for example as a reactivation of earlier activation patterns, as a symbolic encoding, or as the recognition of stored content. In this perspective, memory is primarily understood as a functional change in state or as the re-availability of semantic or sensory information that is stabilized by synaptic plasticity or molecular modulation. What is usually missing is a physically sound description of what "storage" actually means. In the position represented here, therefore, a radical change of perspective is undertaken: memory is not the reappearance of a stored symbol, but the material, directed restructuring of the system itself. In this sense, memory is not a passive archive, but the active expression of a structural transformation. Storing means that a system has changed irreversibly – and this change is not metaphorical, but physically real.

items.title: Perturbation, Integration, Possibility Space.
items.abstract: Neo-Darwinism describes the filter, not the structure of what gets filtered. It does not explain why highly adaptive phenomena occur: coherent, rapid adaptations across multiple traits simultaneously, which random search in the entire possibility space could not achieve. This paper develops an alternative framework. The central thesis is that autocatalytic systems generate, through their history of perturbations, a structured, non-uniformly distributed variation space whose topology makes certain variations more probable than others. When this pre-structured space is congruent with current selective pressure, the result appears highly adaptive. This congruence is neither guaranteed nor random, but itself a product of system history. The thesis is developed at the cell-biological, epigenetic, and evolutionary-biological levels, empirically anchored, and precisely demarcated from Jablonka's four-dimensions model and from neo-Darwinism. Recent findings on epigenetically driven mutational bias, stress-induced transposon mobilization, cryptic genetic variation, and the G-matrix framework provide converging empirical support.

items.title: Neurally Driven Evolution: Behavior, Niche Construction, and the Acceleration of Variation Structure.
items.abstract: The nervous system invents no new evolutionary mechanism. It accelerates and complexifies an existing one. The first paper in this series showed that autocatalytic systems generate, through their history of perturbations, a structured variation space whose topology makes certain variations more probable than others. The present paper extends this thesis to the level of neural systems. The nervous system is not a fourth inheritance system in Jablonka's sense, but a possibility-space generator operating on a dramatically shortened timescale, which acts on the perturbation structure of offspring through niche construction, without leaving the causal architecture of the basic mechanism. Three empirically grounded channels connect neural processes to heritable variation structure: activity-dependent gene expression inscribed into the somatic genome of neurons; neuroendocrine axes transmitting chronic neural integration states to the germline; and niche construction as the primary indirect channel through which behavior shapes the perturbation environment of successive generations. The Weismann barrier remains intact throughout. The category error committed by Jablonka's behavioral inheritance system is avoided by maintaining strict causal-level distinctions.

items.title: Methodology of Consciousness Theory.
items.abstract: Consciousness research suffers from a methodological and categorical double deficit. While the natural sciences explicitly discuss and justify their methods, consciousness research lacks systematic methodological reflection. This methodological deficit is functionally related to a basic categorical error: the confusion of epistemic levels of description with ontological entities. This level confusion results in three pseudo-problems, which are treated as central research questions, namely the body-soul problem, the hard problem and the what-is-it-like problem. The present article develops a reconstructionist method as a solution to this double deficit. This method avoids the categorical confusion between levels of description and ontology and identifies functional necessities instead of arbitrary correlations. Central is the insight that consciousness does not emerge from dead matter, but from autocatalytic organization. The model of causal collapse describes consciousness as a state of maximally non-factorizable causal entanglement in neuronal systems that arises when a measure of causal separability Σ(t) falls below a critical threshold Σc. The thesis systematically reconstructs the necessary conditions for consciousness: autocatalytic organization as a biological foundation, the causal nucleus as an evolutionary structural principle from the cell nucleus to the default mode network, electrical signal transduction in the nervous system, and finally causal collapse as a mechanism of phenomenal experience. Phylogenetic development shows how the causal nucleus as a structural principle permeates evolution from prokaryotes to early nervous systems to human consciousness. Different forms of consciousness are derived from specific collapse structures: primary consciousness as sensorimotor collapse, self-consciousness as recursive collapse with self-model, intentionality as prospective collapse, and affective consciousness as limbically integrated collapse. The theoretical positioning shows that the model integrates and specifies Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory and plasticity approaches. Empirically, the model is supported by the Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI), functional connectivity patterns, and characteristic differences between states of consciousness. For predictions that are not directly proven, concrete test procedures are proposed. The method transforms arbitrary correlations into functional necessities and opens up new …

items.title: Models and the test of consciousness.
items.abstract: For decades, new theories have been emerging that want to explain what consciousness is. They speak of information integration (Tononi, 2004, 2015), of global availability (Baars, 1988; Dehaene, 2014), recursive predictions (Friston, 2010) or phenomenological structures (Varela, Thompson & Rosch, 1991). Their common conviction is that consciousness can be explained by certain dynamics and forms of organization. But the crucial question remains: How could we tell that such a model not only sounds conclusive, but actually produces consciousness? In the following, it will be shown that all current models of consciousness are subject to a fundamental test. Four aspects must be considered: (1) its generative power, which has not yet been proven, (2) its metaphysical positions, (3) its circular validation between theory and empiricism, and (4) its predominantly interpretive, non-explanatory function.

items.title: Integrated model of causal collapse.
items.abstract: This model assumes that consciousness arises when a recursive system loses its causal separability. The so-called causal collapse describes the transition in which disjoint causal partitioning of the system is no longer possible. Through a corresponding measure of causal entanglement (Σ) and its complement (Ω), consciousness is formally described as a gradual phenomenon that can be modeled across different biological and artificial systems.

items.title: How the World Becomes Present for a Living Being.
items.abstract: Consciousness is approached here as feeling, experiencing, and being there: the felt presence of a living organism within which attention, reflection, and cognitive activities occur. The article develops a biological reconstruction of the conditions under which this state could have taken shape, followed by a philosophical interpretation of its character. It starts from two features of human experience: temporal continuity and wholeness. Seeing, hearing, bodily feeling, and thinking remain distinguishable while belonging to a present that cannot be assembled from mutually independent experiences. Empirical studies trace a progression from local cellular sensitivity and communication between cells to directed neural connections, persistent intrinsic activity, recurrent interactions, bodily feedback, and plasticity shaped by experience. Research on perception, memory, emotion, sleep, anesthesia, and disorders of consciousness specifies contributions to an interconnected and differentiated neural state. Neural nonfactorizability is introduced as a model assumption whose precise physiological conditions require further investigation. Experience and scientific investigation are treated as two ways of knowing the same living individual. Their relation provides no additional causal explanation across descriptions. The philosophical proposal interprets felt presence as the way a living organism is there in its interconnected process of excitation. Consciousness is understood in this sense as a vital function. The question of why experience exists at all is treated as metaphysical from the outset. The article distinguishes empirically testable model claims from philosophical interpretation and considers implications for investigating consciousness in other animals.

items.title: From the Transcendental Subject to the Causal Core.
items.abstract: The relationship between subject and object has been the crystallization point of consciousness research since transcendental philosophy. From Kant to Husserl, attempts were made to understand the conditions of the possibility of knowledge from the structure of the subject. However, with the transition to empirical neuroscience, this question has not disappeared, but has merely been transformed. The transcendental framework continues to have an effect – as an implicit prerequisite of many theories that see themselves as naturalistic. The present text pursues the goal of making this implicit framework visible and overcoming it. He traces the historical development from transcendental philosophy to today's neuro- and systems-theoretical models of consciousness, in order to finally propose an alternative concept: that of causal collapse and the causal core. These terms do not describe consciousness as an emergent product, but as a structural consequence of the self-binding of causal processes. In this way, the classic pair of opposites of spirit and nature is abolished without falling into reductionism.

items.title: From State to Mode: Criticality and Non-Factorizability as Constitutive Properties of Living Systems.
items.abstract: In earlier work, the phylogenetic sequence from autocatalytic autopoiesis through the causal core and electrification to defactorization was developed as a reconstructive derivation of the biological conditions of phenomenal consciousness. Non-factorizability appears there as the result of the fourth tipping point, criticality as its physical realization condition. The present article shows that both properties follow the same logic in the scaling sequence: they are present in autopoietic systems from the very beginning and develop qualitatively new forms with the scaling of the nervous system. This shared logic has remained implicit in previous work; making it explicit is the contribution of this article. The decisive difference from non-living dissipative systems lies in the fact that criticality there is a state a system has, whereas in autopoietic systems it is a mode in which the system operates as a living one. In the nervous system, this mode takes the specific form that realizes non-factorizability as a stable operating condition. The conceptual explanatory gain of this precision becomes apparent at two clinical phenomena: epilepsy and coma can no longer be understood as opposite points on an activation axis, but as structurally distinct failures of the same critical mode in opposite directions.

items.title: From Principle to Function: The Causal Core in the Brain.
items.abstract: The theory of the causal core describes a centristic-causalistic principle that emerges as a universal structural form in open, dynamic systems. This principle is not a material object, but rather a systemic necessity that, under certain conditions, leads to the formation of a central integration mechanism. In biological evolution, this mechanism has manifested as the cell nucleus and later as the brain. This essay investigates how this causal structural principle is concretely realized in the brain, without reducing it to an anatomical region or a "switch." The analysis connects thermodynamic, neurophysiological, and systems-theoretical perspectives and aims to identify causal collapse as the physiological manifestation of the causal core.

items.title: From 2D Object Space to 3D Perspective Structure.
items.abstract: This paper addresses the structural conditions under which objectivity can emerge when multiple perspectives are present. Standard approaches typically presuppose a shared object space and treat differences between observers as secondary deviations. This working paper suspends that assumption and formalizes the transition from a two-dimensional object space to a three-dimensional perspective structure. The formalization introduces a perspective group that acts on objects, allowing perspective-invariant comparison through alignment operations. This mathematical framework generates operators for reflexivity and contextual coherence without requiring external assumptions. The extension from D2 (systematic comparison) to D3 (perspectival alignment) and D4 (contextual integration) provides a dimensional logic that stabilizes cooperation in rational decision-making. This compact technical paper demonstrates the core mechanism of dimensional logic through a specific application: perspective alignment in cooperation problems. It serves as the formal foundation for the framework developed in "Adaptive Rationality through Dimensional Logic" (Stegemann, 2025) and illustrates how perspective-invariant metrics can be operationalized in decision architectures.

items.title: From Autopoiesis to Enaction.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs a conceptual shift from the original theory of autopoiesis to later enactive approaches to cognition and experience. The central claim is that the transition is not a straightforward deduction from autopoiesis. Maturana’s identification of life with cognition expands the concept of cognition from the outset. Later developments add embodied action, autonomy, adaptivity, agency, sense-making, and first-person experience. Each addition addresses a genuine problem, but the sequence risks turning biological regulation into semantic and eventually phenomenal vocabulary without identifying the mechanism that warrants the transition. The paper therefore distinguishes self-production, regulation, cognition, and experience as different explanatory targets. It argues that autopoiesis remains a powerful account of biological individuality if it is not equated with cognition. An alternative continuation is proposed: instead of locating the decisive development primarily in organism–environment coupling, the analysis follows the evolutionary differentiation of the living system itself, especially the emergence of nervous systems, fast signal integration, recursive closure, and a neurally constituted epistemic operational interior. Embodiment and environmental coupling remain necessary conditions, but they are not thereby mechanisms of experience. The result is a reconstruction of the historical divergence between autopoietic theory and later enactivism and a proposal for a biologically grounded route from living organization to cognition and phenomenal experience.

items.title: Epistemic Convergence -- An Integrative Model of Consciousness, Cognition and System Structure.
items.abstract: Our current theoretical landscape for the explanation of consciousness is fragmented. Phenomenology, neurobiology, systems theory, cognitive research, and philosophy of mind each offer perspectives -- but none provides a comprehensive, coherent overall view. The model proposed here is based on four mutually constituting, irreducible perspectives: causal collapse, epistemic relativism, dimensional logic, and autocatalytic self-structuring. The aim is to unfold these four strands not additively, but in a cyclically organized context that is epistemologically grounded, systemically compatible and phenomenologically comprehensible.

items.title: Experience as Self-Reference.
items.abstract: The present article advances a physical identity principle for consciousness: experience is not produced by, correlated with, or supervenient upon a specific class of physical states, it is identical with them. More precisely, experience is identical with endogenously generated, self-sustaining self-reference of the kind that autocatalytic systems necessarily instantiate when the infrastructure conditions identified in Stegemann (2026) are satisfied. This identity is not a contingent empirical finding but a conceptual one: the term ‘experience’ means nothing other than a physical state of the relevant structural type, described from the perspective of the system that is in it. The hard problem of consciousness, why physical processes give rise to subjective experience, is not solved by this principle but eliminated: the question rests on a false presupposition, namely that experience is something over and above the physical state. Once the presupposition is removed, no explanatory gap remains. The identity principle is stated in compact form as ℰ ≡ Πₐₙ, where ℰ denotes experience and Πₐₙ denotes the self-reference mapping of an autocatalytically organized system. The article distinguishes this structural identity thesis from classical type-identity theories, defends it against the multiple realizability objection and the knowledge argument, and draws out its consequences for the scientific study of consciousness.

items.title: DIMENSIONAL LOGIC: LLM EMPIRICS 2026.
items.abstract: Three leading Large Language Models spontaneously operationalize the 4-Dimension system of dimensional logic without any training: -/- D1: Phenomenal (immediate perception) D2: Formal-systematic (predicate logic) D3: Reflexive-metacognitive (Theory of Mind) D4: Contextual-paradigmatic -/- Result: 100% dimension understanding, perfect category error detection, correct transition operators.

items.title: Cognitive Surplus Capacity as the Foundation of Cultural Construction.
items.abstract: This article develops the thesis that the major cultural constructions of humanity (religion, esotericism, art, science) result from a structural discrepancy between cognitive processing capacity and available sensory inputs. While cognitive systems with low neural complexity can operate largely reactively to sensory data, significant surplus capacity necessitates constructive processing beyond the given. These constructions differ not in their cognitive source, but in their methodological constraints: religion dogmatizes its constructions, art makes them explicit as such, science organizes them under conditions of falsifiability. The thesis is developed as a heuristic principle that makes disparate cultural phenomena comprehensible under a unified perspective and is categorially specified to avoid confusions between structural, functional, and phenomenal levels of description.

items.title: Consciousness: An Integrative Model of the Four Fundamental Principles.
items.abstract: Consciousness is defined as the emergent state of a system that fulfills four fundamental principles: (1) autocatalysis as the energetic basis of self-sustaining processes, (2) a causal core as a thermodynamically determined integration center, (3) causal collapse as the fusion of separate causal pathways into an irreducible entity, and (4) plasticity as structural adaptability. The model differs from existing theories in its process-ontological approach: consciousness does not arise through information processing or representation, but through the physical fusion of causal processes. This theory makes specific, empirically testable predictions about neuronal correlates of consciousness and offers new explanatory approaches for pathological states of consciousness, animal consciousness and the limits of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Consciousness as an Expression of Autocatalytic Stability – A New Index for Neuronal Coherence.
items.abstract: The present model assumes that consciousness is not an additive effect of cognitive complexity, but a specific form of systemic integration: a “causal collapse” within the space of recursive processes. This term does not mean destruction, but a temporary indistinguishability of causal paths – a state in which stimulus processing, memory retrieval, and self-modeling can no longer be separated. This collapse is not purely functional, but a structural-energetic phenomenon: It only arises when a system maintains its autocatalytic stability, i.e., when feedback processes are recursively stabilized within a critical range. Such stabilization can only occur in living systems – those that not only consume energy but also regulate it cyclically.

items.title: Consciousness as an Epistemic Singularity: A Systems Theory Approach.
items.abstract: Part I: Philosophical Foundations 1. Rethinking the Problem of Consciousness 2. Gödel's Framework: Undecidability as Self-Boundary 3. Consciousness as an Epistemic Singularity Part II: Systems Theory Analysis 4. The Four Principles of Experience 5. Synthesis: Why Undecidability Leads to Experience 6. Implications for understanding natural intelligence Part III: Technical Implementation 7. Prerequisites for Conscious AI 8. Mathematical Formalization of the Four Principles 9. Architecture and Realization Perspectives 10. Outlook: From Zombie to Conscious Machine.

items.title: What Makes a Person the Same Person? Persistence, Memory, Embodiment, and Continuity.
items.abstract: When someone says that the adult is the same person as the child, at least four claims can be confused: that one numerically identical individual persists, that later mental life preserves psychologically significant connections to earlier life, that a life can be understood as the subject of an intelligible narrative, and that a present individual continues to occupy morally significant relations of care, obligation, or responsibility. Philosophical theories often argue for one of these claims while appearing to settle all four. This paper defends the Non-Substitution Thesis: numerical identity, survival-related continuity, autobiographical intelligibility, and moral standing are distinct relations, and no one of them can simply substitute for the others. That distinction is not a refusal to answer the persistence question. It is a constraint on what a defensible answer must establish. -/- The paper develops a Personal Persistence and Standing Analysis (PPSA-12) and an argument for origin-sensitive, non-branching identity as a condition that any proposed criterion of numerical persistence must respect. Logical countermodels show that the transitive closure of overlapping memories does not by itself establish identity; that duplication can preserve psychological information without multiplying one and the same person; that a causal history can connect stages without making all successors numerically identical to the source; and that neither forgetting nor altered self-narrative alone extinguishes ethical claims. The proposed account is explanatory rather than a complete reductive metaphysics: it identifies necessary structural constraints, tests rival sufficient conditions, and leaves open whether organisms, embodied psychological subjects, or further entities ultimately bear numerical persistence. -/- Sixteen sustained cases range from ordinary aging, the brave officer, amnesia, advanced dementia, brain transplantation, split-brain hypotheses, fission, teletransportation and digital replicas to trauma, social recognition, and Buddhist accounts of continuity without an enduring self. Source-critical comparisons address Locke, Reid, Butler, Hume, Williams, Parfit, Olson, Schechtman, Ricoeur, Lindemann, Vasubandhu, and Indian self/no-self debates without claiming doctrinal equivalence or historical influence where none is documented. Eleven figures, comparative tables, a source-status ledger, an explicitly constructed case corpus, and a …

items.title: Intuition and Object.
items.abstract: The glut of articles, at least since 2009, dedicated to the question whether Kant is a conceptualist or a nonconceptualist continues apace. More in particular, it is striking that people keep on making the disjunction between Kant being either a conceptualist or a nonconceptualist, while he is actually both, in some sense, or neither of course—for if he is both, why the discussion? There is at any rate something artificial about the whole debate: a contemporary framework is imposed on Kant’s arguments, but perhaps there is something wrong with the framework! Nobody seems to pose this question. I argued something to that effect in my early article on the topic in Dutch, published back in 2010, quite early on in the debate on Kantian nonconceptualism, in the Leuven journal Tijdschrift voor Filosofie (Schulting 2010). More recently, in a German-language article in Kant-Studien (Schulting 2015) I made a more concerted effort to point out the problems with both the conceptualist and nonconceptualist readings of Kant’s argument in the Deduction, paying particular attention to the prima facie ambiguous passage at A99ff/B122ff., which conceptualists and nonconceptualists alike cite as evidence for their views. In this chapter draft, which is projected to be a chapter in a final monograph on Kant's Deduction, I rehearse several of my earlier arguments while responding to critiques by Golob, Jankowiak and Blomme of my position on nonceptualism and the related question of objectivity and objective validity. Some of the material is based on texts published earlier in book symposia on the group blog Critique (2017) and in Tijdschrift voor Filosofie in Dutch (2018). This chapter might, if time permits, be rewritten with a less overtly discussion of the debate on my position on NCC, and more specifically on reference and judgement, focusing on how for Kant objects of intuition are fixed.

items.title: Executable Relational Memory: Graph-Organized Learning, Program Composition, and Causal Revision.
items.abstract: We present an executable relational memory architecture in which persistent relational units integrate observations, executable programs, mutable interfaces, and causal dependencies within a shared, graph-organized substrate. Each unit contains a stable three-signal nucleus responsible for activation, while its mutable faces accommodate the procedures through which computational competencies are acquired, tested, composed, executed, and revised. -/- An implemented Genesis organization actively selects informative experiments by identifying disagreements among executable hypotheses, acquires functional relationships from observations, and materializes validated programs as persistent computational units. The architecture maintains independently identifiable positive and negative evidence across contextual projections, enabling contradiction handling, causal revision, and dependency-aware knowledge maintenance. -/- We formalize the operational semantics of this architecture and establish a compositional conservation theorem demonstrating the preservation of observable computational values under admissible contextual reorganization, pure-prefix program factoring, and dependency-certified result reuse. Additional results characterize the effects of finite instruction budgets on operational equivalence and establish information-theoretic bounds for independently retractable evidence. -/- Experimental evaluation confirms the integration of these mechanisms. The original V5 implementation passes all 51 regression tests and acquires 144 executable programs with 1,632 successful checks across four independent worlds. A separate evaluation across 12 newly seeded worlds acquires 144 programs and achieves 1,728 correct checks. In an integrated experiment, five distinct computational tasks coexist within a single memory, producing 100 correct held-out outputs following 25 actively selected observations. A direct mathematical verification suite additionally passes 249,786 targeted comparisons. An experimentally observed Genesis transformation demonstrates that preserving computational output does not necessarily preserve executability under finite instruction budgets. -/- Together, these results establish an implemented and reproducible computational architecture in which relational memory serves simultaneously as a substrate for knowledge representation, executable computation, autonomous competency acquisition, structural reorganization, and causal revision, with …

items.title: Owning a Wrong: It Cannot Be Done in Another’s Place.
items.abstract: After a wrong has been done, what can be done by someone else in the doer's place, and what cannot? This paper separates three things: making good, giving an answer, and owning the wrong. The first two can be done in another's place; owning cannot, and a person can own only his own wrong. From outside, two kinds of material can be read in the act of owning a wrong: saying it in the place where the original words did their work is the act of this occasion; what he does afterward is later material that can go on being read. Later material does not leave that step hanging or void it; changing is his own affair and is not for others to inspect and pass. A correction goes back to where the original words did their work; what is changed is the misstated fact or the mistaken verdict, and what happened stays as it was. Owning a wrong does not cancel the account. Relaying words the person has himself already owned is not owning, in his place, a wrong he has not owned; the phrase "on behalf of" does not by itself tell which of the two is going on. An institution cannot own a wrong; those who can are persons, each his own share; what a predecessor did, a successor cannot own, though he can take the responsibility upon himself of his own accord. What has been owned is not conditional on the other's forgiving, and is not taken back if the other does not forgive; the other person does not thereby owe forgiveness. Lu Xun striking out his own inference in the pages of Yusi in 1924, Samuel Sewall's statement read out in public in 1697, a check sent by Chris Chelios for his teammates, a sentence of Frances Arnold's on retracting a paper, a letter of Chen Xiaolu's and his phrase "on behalf of," and Willy Brandt kneeling in Warsaw are the historical cases.

items.title: The Inauthentic-Authentic Self: Autistic Latina Professors and the Barrier for Autonomy in Academia.
items.pub: In Laura J. Hetrick, Neurodivergent Scholars Speak: Reclaiming Voice in the Academy. Syracuse, New York: Syracuse University Press.
items.venue: Neurodivergent Scholars Speak: Reclaiming Voice in the Academy
items.abstract: This paper develops Phenomenological Dual Masking (PDM), a framework grounded in Latina feminist philosophy and phenomenology to examine how autistic Latinas negotiate authenticity, autonomy, and belonging within institutions shaped by racialized, gendered, and neurotypical norms. Drawing on lived experience, I argue that masking involves the simultaneous concealment of neurodivergence and performance of culturally prescribed Latinidad. This ongoing labor exposes how dominant ideals of professionalism and independence marginalize alternative forms of being. By advancing a relational account of autonomy, I challenge deficit-based understandings of disability and defend neurodivergent Latina experiences as valuable sources of philosophical knowledge and institutional transformation.

items.title: DE LA RENCONTRE AVEC SOI-MÊME DANS L’À-VENIR ET DE LA POSSIBILITÉ DE NE PAS SE TROUVER : de la liberté comme s’angoisser devant soi et de l’être « comme » angoisse « étant-angoisse » pour fuir l’angoisse chez Jean-Paul Sartre.
items.pub: Revue Húmus - Ufrgs (Université Fédérale du Rio Grande Do Sul) / Brésil 16 (49):75-111.
items.venue: Revue Húmus - Ufrgs (Université Fédérale du Rio Grande Do Sul) / Brésil
items.abstract: S’arrêtant sur la liberté comme un se-tenir hors d’atteinte de l’être et un se-garder immunisé contre son action dans un par-delà d’un néant, Sartre signale l’angoisse comme reconnaissance d’une possibilité en tant que sa possibilité et identification de la rupture par rapport à son essence par le néant. De cette manière, s’angoisser devant soi est ce qui s’impose à la liberté dans un mouvement qui renferme le néant en tant que « pourquoi », s’agissant de la reconnaissance par l’existant humain d’une possibilité comme sa propre possibilité. L’angoisse consistant en la saisie réflexive de la liberté par elle-même, l’être émerge « comme » angoisse « étant-angoisse » pour fuir l’angoisse, ainsi que le soutient Sartre, qui signale l’acte originel à travers lequel l’existant humain est pour lui-même son propre néant comme ce qui s’impose à la découverte dans l’immanence absolue en tant que subjectivité pure du cogito instantané, dans un processus qui renferme la question engageant la conscience et son modus essendi comme fondement permettant à l’existant humain de surgir dans le monde comme l’être qui est son propre néant et comme l’être par lequel le néant vient au monde.
