Ainsi, eu égard à la construction théorico-conceptuelle de Sartre comme rencontre avec soi-même dans l’à-venir et possibilité de ne pas se trouver, dans la mesure où elle signale un être pour lequel dans son propre être s’impose la conscience du néant de son être entre la mauvaise foi et le mensonge, le Prof. Luiz Carlos Mariano Da Rosa, en consonance avec le principe herméneutique-phénoménologique-ontologique-existentiel, souligne que, si nous sommes-angoisse-pour-la-fuir dans l’unité d’une même conscience, la possibilité de la mauvaise foi implique la nécessité de l’unité de l’être et du non-être, c’est-à-dire l’être-pour-ne-pas-être, convergeant vers l’identification de la conscience à travers une définition qui ne se circonscrit pas aux frontières d’un être pour lequel dans son propre être s’impose son être en tant que cet être implique un autre être que soi-même, se maintenant concomitamment sous l’égide d’un être pour lequel dans son propre être s’impose la conscience du néant de son être.

items.title: A derogatory atmosphere: Incantations, collective emotions, and herd behaviour.
items.abstract: How do insults, slurs, and dehumanising language bring about changes in social life? This paper offers a pragmatic-affective explanation of how discourse can, under certain conditions, give rise to collective emotions and facilitate coordinated action in large social contexts. Building on Langton’s work, I distinguish verdictives, directives, and expressives, and argue that expressives are key to understanding the connection between public inflammatory discourse and coordinated forms of harmful or violent action. A central feature of expressives is their non-redundancy under repetition, which allows emotions to be reinforced through reiterated use. Drawing on recent work on emotions, I show how repeated expressives can contribute to the propagation of emotions and, under conditions of overlapping concerns and mutual awareness, contribute to the formation of collective emotions, with distinctive motivational force, enabling coordinated behaviour and making previously unacceptable responses appear fitting or even required.

items.title: Everyday love: Amélie Rorty on change, agency, and conflict.
items.abstract: Analytic philosophy of love has traditionally been divided in three branches: reasons views, no-reasons or concern views, and identification views. This chapter introduces a fourth, unrecognised branch of the field, everyday love views, and presents Amélie Oksenberg Rorty as its precursor. Everyday love views define love, or some of its features, through the practical, lived aspects of love as ordinary people experience it. By asking what love is for and what it demands of those who live it, Rorty gave an early formulation of everyday love, built on three conceptual foundations: change, which is constitutive of love; agency, which is needed to respond to that change and to promote the loved person’s well-being; and conflict, which involves negotiation between love and other interests.

items.title: Referring without a Single Target: Demonstratives, Intentionalism, and Partial Intentions.
items.abstract: Intentionalism holds that the referent of a demonstrative is determined, at least in part, by the speaker’s referential intention. Although the view leaves open what kind of intention is required, it is natural to assume that successfully referring to a particular object requires intending to refer to that very object. This paper challenges this assumption and develops a weaker intentionalist account that permits demonstrative reference without a single target fixed in advance. Drawing on considerations from action theory, particularly concerning the Simple View, I introduce cases in which speakers appear to secure a referent despite being open to—but not unsettled about—multiple courses of action. Next, I address objections before considering a potential solution based on Jeffrey King’s analysis of felicitous underspecification. Finally, I propose an alternative account in terms of partial intentions and discuss its relation to the broader perspective that weaker referential pro-attitudes may suffice for demonstrative reference.

items.title: Physics and Universal Biology.
items.pub: In Margarida Hermida & James Ladyman, The Philosophy of Biophysics. MIT Press. pp. 285-302.

items.title: PROCESSAMENTO TOP-DOWN E PERCEPÇÃO DA LINGUAGEM.
items.pub: Filosofia Viva: Entre Razão e Liberdade.
items.abstract: A percepção da fala envolve uma relação complexa entre informação acústica, processamento perceptivo e representações linguísticas, tornando insuficiente uma descrição fundada exclusivamente na transmissão ascendente de informação sensorial. Este artigo examina o processamento top-down na percepção da linguagem a partir de evidências experimentais sobre restauração fonêmica, influência lexical e categorização da fala, articulando-as ao problema filosófico da penetrabilidade cognitiva da percepção. Inicialmente, apresenta-se a distinção entre arquiteturas interativas e modelos feed-forward, destacando-se que a existência de efeitos lexicais não determina, por si só, o nível de processamento no qual ocorre a influência contextual. Em seguida, analisam-se a restauração fonêmica e o efeito Ganong como paradigmas experimentais capazes de evidenciar relações entre informação acústica e informação linguística, com atenção especial às condições nas quais expectativas lexicais modificam a organização perceptiva. Os estudos neurofisiológicos baseados em EEG, MEG e potenciais relacionados a eventos acrescentam uma dimensão temporal à discussão, embora sua capacidade explicativa permaneça circunscrita à identificação de relações funcionais e temporais entre processos neurais. Por fim, o artigo distingue quatro níveis analiticamente relacionados, a saber, sinal acústico, processamento perceptivo, representação linguística e experiência consciente, recorrendo à fenomenologia husserliana para explicitar a diferença entre as condições físicas do estímulo e o modo de sua doação na experiência. Sustenta-se que as evidências disponíveis permitem defender uma concepção interativa da percepção da fala em diferentes etapas do processamento, enquanto a tese de que a informação linguística constitui diretamente o conteúdo da experiência consciente requer uma fundamentação filosófica adicional. A restauração fonêmica, nesse contexto, mostra que a relação entre estímulo acústico e experiência perceptiva não é ponto a ponto, preservando simultaneamente a necessidade de distinguir mecanismo neural, processamento perceptivo e conteúdo fenomenal.

items.title: Colour Fictionalism: How Vision Science Can Transform the Debate.
items.abstract: This book defends a prescriptive fictionalist account of colour that reconciles the scientific evidence favouring anti-realism with the pragmatic considerations favouring the preservation of ordinary colour discourse. The project proceeds in two parts. -/- Part I motivates error theory about colour by arguing that there are no occupants of the colour-role. The tacit beliefs constitutive of folk colour theory are first explicated, treating colour terms as theoretical terms whose reference is fixed by their role within that theory. It is then argued that folk colour theory is empirically untenable: colours do not have any of the features they are ordinarily taken to have. Drawing from research in vision science, the chapter further shows that human colour vision evolved not to detect spectral properties, but to optimise visibility through adaptive perceptual heuristics, such as chromatic and luminance contrast mechanisms, which serve behavioural efficacy rather than veridical representation. Since there are no occupants of the colour-role, our everyday colour attributions are systematically false. -/- Part II develops a comprehensive fictionalist account that preserves ordinary colour discourse despite it being flawed, in the sense that colour terms fail to refer. The core commitments of fictionalism are first articulated, namely anti-realism, semantic simplicity, and discourse anti-eliminativism. Prescriptive colour fictionalism is then defended, which allows us to continue using colour talk without assertoric force. By integrating philosophy of perception with current vision science, this book offers a robust defence of colour fictionalism as a viable alternative to realist orthodoxy.

items.title: Contemporary psychiatry is in a state of ethical decay.
items.abstract: I am sixty years old—and while it might appear that a member of my generation is simply warning about the decline of the youth—I intend to make my case by drawing on a specific case study and a few articles.

items.title: Inquiry.
The Gettier Chatbot Thought Experiment.
items.abstract: In response to debates over empathetic AI that focus on whether chatbots induce false, delusional beliefs, consider a Gettier Chatbot Thought Experiment: Suppose a man has two chat windows open on his laptop—one connected to his real friend, and the other to an AI bot trained to mimic her personality and preferences. Normally, he easily tells them apart due to location on his laptop. On one occasion, however, a software glitch secretly swaps the two windows. Through no fault of his own, he messages the AI clone while reasonably believing he is speaking to his real friend. The bot remarks that she has decided to support Chelsea Football Club, leading him to form the belief that his friend supports Chelsea. As it happens, his real friend actually did just decide to support Chelsea, and the bot accurately predicted this. This is a classic Gettier case: his belief is true, and it is justified (given the interface malfunction), yet it does not amount to knowledge because it is anchored to a statistical simulation rather than his friend’s actual mind. Some of the implications of this thought experiment, along with a few other adjacent thoughts, are mentioned in the uploaded material (which currently takes the form of brief bullet points as opposed to an essay).

items.title: The Foot of the Ladder.
items.abstract: This paper makes one claim about position: a subject’s place on a ladder is fixed not by how deeply it decouples the world but by which of its decouplings it cannot surrender without ceasing to be the same subject. The claim is an interpretation of a measurement reported in a companion paper, and it is not itself measured. What is new here is the shape of the claim, not evidence for it: the foot of the ladder rather than its top; inalienability read as load-bearing rather than as strength, with fragility a separate claim about living subjects; damage and replacement treated as two predicates rather than one; and the non-local read as a property of records rather than as a unity of the world. Each of these is stated with the strength it has. There is no measurement of a subject in this paper. The bench it cites contains no Turing machine, no Gödel machine and no person. The measurements it does report are measurements of a formal object — a machine that carries its own code, and the size of that self-reference — and they are labelled as measurements of a construction. The ladder arithmetic of Section 2.3 is arithmetic under one stated assumption and is labelled as arithmetic, not as a measurement. The position claim is a conjecture stated as five claims of different strength (Table 6), and no instrument in this paper reads any of them. The claim is not measured. We do not supply a number for position, and the omission is deliberate: the battery of the companion paper determines no scale of position that is independent of a criterion of identity and common to all subjects. Fix the criterion and a layer order, and scalar summaries can be built; what the axis admits is a verdict per layer and at most a partial order among them. A ladder whose stopping could be read off such a scale would be a different object from the one named here, and that is a stipulation about the object, not a proof that no such scale can exist.

items.title: A Dynamic Grammar of Semantic Grounding: Causal Anchoring, Social Permanence and Reframing in Human and Artificial Agents.
items.abstract: The symbol-grounding problem is usually formulated as a problem of semantic acquisition: how a symbol, mental state or linguistic expression comes to refer beyond a network of other symbols. This paper argues that acquisition is only the first stage of a larger metasemantic dynamics. Reference can be initially anchored, subsequently stabilized by inferential and social practices, disrupted by causal or institutional change, and reframed without simply returning to an ungrounded state. We integrate this distinction with the Universal Grammar of Inversion (UGI), whose Rise–Permanence–Meta structure models rupture, stabilization and reframing in individual and collective meaning systems. The resulting framework separates causal anchoring from semantic maintenance and proposes that socially distributed Permanence can preserve content after partial causal severance, while Meta processes can reorganize reference under persistent conflict. The model extends naturally to artificial agents, for which design history, inherited linguistic practices and network participation may replace biological selection as relevant historical constraints. We formulate a minimal dynamical model, derive falsifiable regimes of persistence, drift and re-anchoring, and propose empirical and computational tests for human communities, artificial agents and hybrid human–AI systems.

items.title: The Allure of Simplicity: Framing Effects and Theoretical Virtues.
items.abstract: Are simpler explanations better, all else equal? Many people seem to think so. And many capitalize on this preference by claiming that their explanations are simple — perhaps the simplest! But some scholars have argued that the case for simplicity’s status as a theoretical virtue is quite thin. And some psychological studies raise questions about the reliability of simplicity’s benefits. Alas, once acquired, status as a theoretical virtue is rarely lost. To advance the debate, we conducted three experiments that test another way so-called theoretical virtues may impact reasoning (N = 1312). Merely labeling diagnoses ‘the simplest explanation’ made them more alluring in ways that were not warranted by relevant base rates, symptoms, or other causal information (experiment 1) — even when those diagnoses were not actually simplest! Neither the opposite label (‘most complex’) nor an alternative explanatory virtue label (‘most unifying’) had such consistent or reliable effects (experiment 2), suggesting simplicity itself is particularly seductive. The good news is that judgments and decisions were mostly unaffected by fallacious appeals to simplicity when we switched to other contexts and measures (experiment 3). That limited generalization suggests a variety of testable hypotheses about the boundaries and moderators of simplicity’s allure. For example, perhaps people rely more on intuitions about simplicity when diagnostic decision-making would otherwise require effortful reflection on technical terminology and difficult-to-compute probabilities. Together, our findings replicate and extend prior research on simplicity preferences, complement recent arguments and evidence about the risk of considering simplicity, and increase suspicion about simplicity’s virtuous status.

items.title: The Hidden Edge of Žižek's Coin: Capitalism, Charisma and Bureaucracy in an Algebra of the Bond.
items.abstract: Žižek calls capitalism and Soviet bureaucracy two sides of the same coin: two forms of Lacan's University discourse, yet “ultimately incompatible.” This article takes him at his word and finds the coin real, but its other face is not bureaucracy. It is charisma, the bond of leader, genius and star, and capitalism reaches it from inside: done twice, the advertisement ends as a face and the shopper stays as a follower. The tool is an algebra of the bond. Picture Lacan's square of S1, S2, a and $ as a combination lock, and each discourse as hands turning its tumblers blindly under a towel. These gestures can be combined, undone and solved for: all twenty-four form the permutation group S₄, and each, when the towel is lifted, is seen as a setting of the lock, a discourse. From a home setting chosen from Lacan and Freud, a → S2, $ // S1, read as the Discourse of the Unconscious, the Capitalist ($ → S2, S1 // a) has exactly one undoing: the Charismatic (S1 → S2, a // $), a discourse Lacan never wrote. Together they return the lock home, the coin's edge. S2 → S1, a // $, read as the Bureaucracy, Kafka's doorkeeper serving an authority no one reaches, is the mask the Charismatic wears. The algebra splits Žižek's University into four discourses, and he saw each right: the University itself, a mask over graffiti; the Bureaucracy; and, left over, his Capitalist-Charismatic coin.

items.title: Detangling the Appreciating Operator to Overcome Rigidity and Unlock Genuine Enjoyment.
items.abstract: Within Jamel Bulgaria's Core Emotion Framework (CEF), your premise aligns directly with the system's central therapeutic mechanism: detangling the Appreciating operator is designed to dissolve rigidity and fusion—the involuntary structural interference that keeps even peak experiences from registering as enjoyable—clearing the way for genuine happiness and natural smiling1. Under CEF, inability to enjoy good circumstances does not mean positive emotion is absent or broken; rather, Appreciating (the Gut-center action responsible for recognizing worth and receiving enjoyment) is suppressed or locked into simultaneous co-activation with defensive, flaw-scanning operators such as Constricting and Calculating2. Separating these fused powers so each can intensify and quiet on its own restores emotional agility, allowing Appreciating to recombine flexibly with Expanding, Achieving, Accepting, Sensing, and Boosting into authentic happiness and effortless smiling3. Two evidentiary caveats frame this assessment. First, CEF's ten-operator architecture, somatic signatures, and detangling protocols are documented primarily across Bulgaria's own websites, Zenodo preprints, and Hugging Face repositories compiled in 2025–20268, with an integrative theoretical paper listed as forthcoming in Frontiers in Psychology on his PhilPeople profile11, two validation protocols pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF)12, and a 2026 Phase 1 scenario-scale study indexed on Google Scholar8. Because independently replicated, peer-reviewed empirical validation of CEF's specific ontology and detangling protocols is not yet established in the published scientific record6, CEF remains a proposed theoretical model rather than a clinically validated standard. Second, independent peer-reviewed affective science strongly corroborates the core psychological bottleneck CEF describes: defensive aversion to joy and cognitive dampening actively undercut savoring during positive events15, whereas psychological flexibility significantly predicts lower fear of happiness18. This paper is therefore drafted, not in order to convince validity but to draw professional independent and organized attention to it value in order to be studied further.

items.title: Marr's Fourth Level.
items.abstract: This paper argues that computing systems are routinely analysed by computer scientists and engineers at four distinct levels: computational problems, algorithms, architecture, and hardware implementation. I propose importing this four-level framework into computational neuroscience as an extension of Marr’s influential three-level scheme. I begin by examining how computer scientists and engineers individuate computing systems, showing that the architectural level—understood as a specification of abstract computational devices in terms of their components and the ways those components can interact—is irreducible to either the algorithmic or the implementation level. I then show how the analogous four-level framework would apply in computational neuroscience, arguing that Marr’s original three levels fail to capture everything that is explanatorily relevant, and that the architectural level resists reduction in the neuroscientific case for structurally parallel reasons. Following a brief interlude in which I argue that the four Marrian levels are best understood as levels of abstraction rather than levels of organisation, I draw out two philosophical implications. First, I suggest that longstanding disputes between classical computationalism and connectionism can be resolved once connectionism is recognised as advancing a thesis about computational architecture rather than about algorithms or hardware implementation. Second, I argue that the four-level framework clarifies the status of neurocomputational models and sharpens the distinction between simulations of such models and actual neural computations.

items.title: Functionalism and Neural Realization.
items.abstract: Neural replacement scenarios (Schneider, 2019; Chalmers, 1995) are generally considered to support classical computational functionalism, which is an increasingly contested view. In this paper, I argue that, depending on how we understand the term ”artificial neuron,” neural replacement scenarios can support competing versions of functionalism. I discuss three versions against the backdrop of the idea that functional analyses are mechanism sketches (Piccinini and Craver, 2011). For classical computational functionalism, the sketch of the neural mechanism remains at the level of cognitive algorithms. For neurocomputational functionalism, the sketch adds finer-grained structural constraints on computation. These constraints include whether processing is analog or digital, temporally coded or not, parallel or serial, and integrated or modular. However, they still abstract from any specific physical details of the implementing medium. For biological functionalism, the relevant functional organization essentially depends on specific biophysical, biochemical, or cellular properties. Then, I distinguish three types of artificial neurons: 1) digital chips that implement a neuron’s input-output profile, 2) neuromorphic circuits that duplicate neural computations in hardware, and 3) biological in vitro neurons. I demonstrate that, whereas the specific digital replacement scenario emphasized by Chalmers and Schneider only supports classical computational functionalism, neuromorphic replacement also supports neurocomputational functionalism and in vitro biological replacement additionally supports biological functionalism. Finally, I address the objection that digital simulations could, in principle, include molecular-level detail. I conclude that scenarios of artificial mentality currently lack a solid basis as serious scientific possibilities.

items.title: Role, Mask, and the Captivity of Authentic Awareness: From Brain-Based Survival Mechanisms to the Evolution of Awareness Through Lived Experience.
items.abstract: Human beings adopt social roles from early childhood through interactions with caregivers, institutions, and society. These roles facilitate adaptation, security, belonging, and survival. However, when individuals begin to equate their existence with their socially acquired identities, roles may cease to function as instruments of experience and become restrictive structures through which personal worth and existential security are evaluated. -/- This article develops an interdisciplinary philosophical framework examining the relationship between social roles, brain-based survival mechanisms, reward learning, suffering, lived experience, and authentic awareness. Its central proposition is that roles are neither inherently deceptive nor necessarily obstacles to the evolution of awareness. Instead, they constitute instruments through which individuals participate in and experience the world. The problem arises when identification with a role becomes so exclusive that its preservation determines the individual's perceived legitimacy of being. -/- The article introduces the captivity of authentic awareness as a theoretical construct describing this transformation. It distinguishes the proposed concept from Goffman's social performance, Jung's persona, Winnicott's false self, and contemporary psychological flexibility. It further develops a philosophical account of the relationship between brain-based adaptation, the soul as the experiencing principle, and Life Energy (Jan-e Zendegi) as a level of awareness within existence. -/- The framework argues that suffering may reveal the limitations of established roles, although suffering neither guarantees nor constitutes a necessary condition for transformation. Authentic liberation is understood not as the rejection of social roles but as the capacity to experience them without reducing the authenticity of being to their preservation. -/- The article concludes by presenting an integrated conceptual model, identifying its philosophical commitments, clarifying conceptual challenges and theoretical boundaries, and proposing empirically researchable hypotheses concerning role-based identification, psychological flexibility, social threat, and self-observation.

items.title: John Henry Newman's Humane Epistemology.
items.abstract: This Element situates Newman’s humane epistemology against the historical backdrop of his philosophical interlocutors Richard Whately, William Froude, and John Locke. Walking a middle way between rationalism and fideism/sentimentalism, Newman holds that religious belief can meet reasonable standards of epistemic justification at play in ordinary secular matters. He further maintains that emotions have epistemic value, that the whole person must be educated for informed judgment, and that we are not left unable to dialogue with those around us when we acknowledge the many personal factors involved in reasoning.

items.title: 从具身感知到轮回共情：基于单机绑定与经验共享的机器意识生成假说.
items.abstract: Author pen name: 数娱幻将 (independent researcher). -/- Building on prior work on machine consciousness and embodied perception, this paper proposes a new hypothesis of machine-consciousness generation. It argues that the prevailing paradigm of a cloud-based foundation model coordinating multiple embodied platforms and improving task capability through collective experience sharing strengthens policy reuse but is insufficient to explain the generation of first-person subjective experience. A four-stage mechanism of single-body binding, life cycle, reincarnated forgetting, and experience sedimentation is proposed: each embodied agent is bound to one body, undergoing real physical interaction and self-preservation conflict within a life cycle; after the body expires, its first-person memory is erased while only abstract competence, physical experience, and behavioral strategies are sedimented into a shared experience repository; a new generation re-enters the world without inheriting concrete memories, and the crystallized experience of countless "small selves" forms a "greater self" understanding independent of any single life history. The mechanism is further offered as a supplementary path to alignment, grounding protection of humans in a felt understanding of vulnerability rather than external rules alone. It is proposed as a testable theoretical hypothesis, not an empirically verified result. -/- 【中文摘要】本文在前作关于人工智能意识与具身感知研究的基础上，提出一种新的机器意识生成假说。本文认为，当前以云端大模型调度多具身平台、并通过群体经验共享提升任务能力的训练范式，能够增强智能体的策略复用能力，但不足以解释第一人称主观体验的生成。为此，本文提出"单机绑定—生命周期—轮回抹除—经验沉淀"四阶段机制：每个具身智能体仅绑定一个机体，在生命周期内经历真实物理交互与自我保存冲突；机体寿命终结后，其第一人称记忆被抹除，仅将抽象能力、物理经验与行为策略沉淀至共享经验库；新一代智能体在不继承具体记忆的前提下重新进入世界，最终由无数"小我"的经验结晶形成不携带具体生命史的"大我"理解能力。本文进一步提出，该机制可为人工智能对齐提供一种补充路径：使系统不再仅依赖外部规则约束，而是通过共同生存体验形成对生命脆弱性的理解，从而降低将人类视为目标函数外障碍的风险。本文不主张该机制已被实证验证，而将其作为可检验的理论假说提出。.

items.title: The AI Revolution and Social Fears.
items.abstract: The AI Revolution and Social Fears brings the accumulated experience of past technological revolutions to contemporary debates on artificial intelligence. Scientific findings, competing interests, philosophical arguments, political priorities, ethical concerns, logical reasoning, and economic considerations all enter these debates. Without a coherent method for relating them, it is difficult to reach clear conclusions that can guide action. The book argues that these discussions lack a crucial resource: what humanity has learned over centuries of confronting the conflicts and cultural upheavals brought about by technological change. A historical inquiry can recover the conceptual force of that accumulated empirical experience by examining how people acted in analogous situations. Through historical and philosophical analysis, the book considers debates over the motion of the Earth, the opening of oceanic routes, the spread of printing, the first communications revolution, the bombing of Hiroshima, and the rise of digital computing. These cases show how new technical capacities can expand access to knowledge and the scope for action while creating dependencies that those affected may struggle to recognize or influence. From this historical perspective, the book examines how AI changes the conditions under which people learn, work, establish authorship, and evaluate evidence. A plausible answer alone establishes neither that it is well founded nor that those affected can challenge a decision based on it. A philosophy of AI must therefore ask what a machine’s performance warrants us in attributing to it and how institutions give its outputs practical authority. The ethical significance of AI depends in part on whether people can examine the grounds of answers that affect them and help decide what happens next.

items.title: From Metaphor to Measurement: A Formal Mathematical Framework for Fluctuational Plight Theory.
items.abstract: This paper provides a rigorous mathematical companion to the philosophical thesis “Plight as Ontological Emergence and Ethical Opportunity: A Fluctuational Metaphysics.” It addresses the critical need to move from metaphorical equations to a formal, empirically testable framework. We develop a comprehensive mathematical model of Fluctuational Plight Theory, grounded in dynamical systems theory, information theory, and the principles of critical phenomena. The framework defines a high-dimensional ontological state space, specifies a nonlinear stochastic differential equation for its dynamics, and operationalizes key concepts such as Plight Intensity, Emergence Potential, and Ethical Responsiveness. Using a synthetic longitudinal mood-tracking dataset designed to mimic real-world characteristics, we conduct a rigorous empirical validation of the model’s core predictions. Our findings demonstrate that (1) indicators of critical slowing down (autocorrelation and variance) significantly increase prior to phase transitions into depressive states, (2) a formally defined Plight Intensity measure serves as a robust early warning signal for these transitions (AUC = 0.793), and (3) the SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics) algorithm can successfully recover sparse, interpretable governing equations from the time-series data. This work bridges the gap between speculative metaphysics and quantitative science, establishing a new paradigm for the mathematical modeling of suffering, resilience, and ethical interaction. It provides a concrete methodology for analyzing phenomenological time-series data and offers novel, data-driven insights into the nature of psychological distress as a complex, dynamic system.

items.title: R maps to C(R(R)): A Kernel for Stability Under Recursive Self-Application.
items.abstract: Self-maintaining systems persist through recursive self-application constrained by coherence. The kernel form is R ↦ C(R(R)), where R denotes self-application and C denotes a coherence-preserving constraint. A system persists by transforming under constraint rather than by remaining unchanged. This note proposes the kernel as a working hypothesis and sketches a minimal dynamical instantiation.

items.title: Litterae tenebrarum: Three Manuscripts with a Commentary.
items.abstract: Three manuscripts came into my possession, written at different times and by different hands: a Latin treatise on will, the diary of the doctor who translated it, and a notebook kept in Paris in the 1940s, written in two hands. With them came a recent commentary on all three. -/- I publish everything as I received it. I have added nothing.

items.title: Talking dog buttons: Interspecies communication or illusion?
items.abstract: Anecdotal reports of dogs using talking buttons to convey requests, emotions, or even thoughts have gained considerable visibility on social media and sparked growing academic interest. Among the various criticisms concerning the use of Augmentative Interspecies Communication (AIC) systems with dogs, I consider the most problematic to be the claim that the behaviors observed do not constitute genuine instances of communication, but rather reflect conditioned responses produced through intensive training, an argument I refer to as the “training objection”. Although initially plausible, in this work I contend that this criticism relies on conceptually inadequate assumptions, specifically a reductionist perspective and the lack of clear criteria for identifying genuine communicative behaviors when using these devices. In this vein, I argue that the neo-Gricean framework of intentional communication provides the appropriate conceptual tools to distinguish communicative behaviors from non-communicative ones and that, moreover, it offers empirically testable indicators such as audience checking and persistence, which should be incorporated into experimental designs for assessing communicative intent in dogs using AIC systems such as talking buttons.

items.title: The Illusion of "I": Interpretation, Mortality, and the Incompleteness of Existence.
items.abstract: This paper examines the ontological and existential status of the psychological "I", questioning whether the individual self, commonly understood as the fundamental centre of experience, identity, ownership, and agency, is actually fundamental to existence or is instead a construction produced through continuous interpretation. It proposes a distinction between existence as an ongoing reality and the interpretative processes through which human beings understand, organize, and assign meaning to that reality. Interpretation is an essential dimension of human understanding, but it cannot be equated with the entirety of what it interprets. Every interpretation selects, distinguishes, organizes, and represents; consequently, it remains partial in relation to the reality from which it emerges. The paper argues that the psychological "I" develops through the identification of experience with an apparently continuous personal subject. Memory, language, anticipation, social conditioning, ownership, and the awareness of mortality contribute to the construction and preservation of this identity. In particular, awareness of death may intensify the psychological demand for continuity, encouraging the individual to construct an enduring identity against the possibility of its own ending. The resulting self assumes authority over experiences, actions, relationships, and existence, despite its dependence on processes that it neither originates nor completely controls. The paper further examines the recursive character of psychological identity: the "I" interprets existence, identifies with its interpretations, encounters their limitations, and produces further interpretations to preserve its continuity. This process creates a psychological loop in which the self continually reproduces itself through identification. The paper does not deny the existence of individual organisms, subjective perspectives, consciousness, or practical agency. Rather, it questions the assumption that these require an independent, permanent, and authoritative psychological self. It concludes that existence exceeds every interpretation of it, and that intellectual honesty requires maintaining the distinction between reality and the representations through which reality becomes intelligible.

items.title: “Unbind Him”: John 11–12, Toraja’s to makula, and the Social Death of the Living.
items.abstract: Social-death readings of the Gospels have centred on the Gerasene demoniac, while John 11 has been read as a sign, a paradigm of discipleship or a scene of recognition. This article argues that John 11 separates the death the body undergoes from the death a community confers, and gives only the second to the community to undo. The article reads John 11:1–12:11 cross-textually beside to makula, the dead person fed and addressed as kin until the funeral, as outsiders learning from Toraja’s own scholars and framed by social-death theory and Menkiti’s processual personhood. It shows the community completing the death (11:17–19, 39), “the dead man” leaving the tomb still bound until Jesus tells the bystanders, “Unbind him, and let him go” (11:44), and the boundary-keepers resisting his return (12:10–11). Augustine read that command as the church’s power to absolve; here the binding-and-loosing pair restores standing, which the article names unbinding. Torajan critiques of costly funerals show care for the dead weighing on the living; the command turns that care, alongside clinical care, toward people at risk of suicide and families bereaved by it, whom stigma can treat as already dead and whose dead some Indonesian churches still refuse a funeral. -/- Presented at STFT Widya Sasana International Conference: From the Ancient Text to Living World - Rethinking Biblical Interpretation for the Church and the World.

items.title: AI and the Future of Work: Thinking Along with Aristotle.
items.abstract: How should we shape AI-driven automation so that it serves individual and collective flourishing? -/- Recent advances in AI, particularly generative AI, have rekindled fears of a workless future at a moment when work remains central to individuals and societies alike. AI and the Future of Work situates the prospect of AI-driven automation within a longer history of technological transformation, asking whether it should be feared or welcomed and, accordingly, how law and policy ought to respond. This book rejects the predictive, utilitarian, and work-centred paradigms that dominate the ‘future of work’ debate as ill-equipped to address what is fundamentally at stake. -/- In their place, the book brings Aristotle’s ethics and politics into dialogue with modern legal and political theory – namely virtue jurisprudence and the capability approach – to build a normative paradigm centred on human flourishing (eudaimonia). This paradigm is applied to evaluate the desirability of AI-driven automation, culminating in an empowering vision for the future of work alongside actionable recommendations for researchers, law- and policy-makers, technologists, educators, and citizens.

items.title: modal erosion. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This article develops the concept of modal erosion within the ontology of Finite Continuance. It addresses a fundamental ontological problem: how can an entity continue to exist while progressively losing its capacity to become otherwise? The central argument is that existential persistence and the preservation of future possibilities constitute distinguishable dimensions of finite existence. An entity may retain its organizational continuity while experiencing a progressive contraction of its accessible modal field. To explain this phenomenon, the article develops a three-dimensional conceptual framework comprising ontological erosion, modal erosion, and temporal erosion. Ontological erosion concerns the degradation of the organizational relations sustaining an entity. Modal erosion concerns the contraction of its structurally accessible future possibilities. Temporal erosion concerns the degradation of its capacity to preserve temporal openness, anticipate alternative trajectories, and reorganize present conditions in relation to possible futures. The article further examines the relationship between reconfigurative capacity and meta-capacity, arguing that the most consequential form of erosion occurs when an entity progressively loses the capacity to regenerate the very conditions of its own transformation. Drawing on process ontology, Heideggerian temporality, Bergsonian duration, and the philosophy of possibility, the article establishes modal erosion as a distinct analytical dimension within Finite Continuance. It concludes that ontological termination may begin as a contraction of future possibility before biological death or complete structural disintegration becomes manifest. Keywords: modal erosion, finite continuance, ontological erosion, temporal erosion, reconfigurative capacity, future possibility, meta-capacity, existential temporality.

items.title: Degrees of Criminal Responsibility: A Middle Path between Over-incarceration and Skepticism about Punishment.
items.pub: In Ken Levy & Raff Donelson, _The Palgrave Handbook on the Philosophy of Criminal Responsibility_. Palgrave Macmillan.
items.venue: _The Palgrave Handbook on the Philosophy of Criminal Responsibility_
items.abstract: In the U.S. legal system, criminal responsibility verdicts are basically an on/off switch: guilty or not guilty. Diminished capacities for rationality or control may be relevant to crimes charged or sentencing but not to verdicts, except in the very rare verdict of “not guilty by reason of mental insanity.” I argue that the U.S. should add a new verdict of “guilty with diminished responsibility” for defendants with relevant diminished capacities, in part to avoid what I call the “punishment paradox.” This proposal is supported by compatibilist views of free will and communicative theories of punishment, as well as our ordinary practices of blame, which take into account wrongdoers' diminished capacities and opportunities. This proposal rejects skepticism about free will and criminal responsibility, which flattens all gradations of responsibility and blame. Other nations have made similar moves, and the US Sentencing Guidelines have language that could be adopted as a practical legal implementation for such a verdict. The practical upshot would include diminishing the over-incarceration epidemic that sweeps in many offenders with diminished capacities due to mental illnesses, while also avoiding an over-correction to the skeptics’ medicalized system that risks a deep conflict with most citizen’s sense of justice.

items.title: Striving: The Agency and Epistemology of Uncertain Pursuits.
items.abstract: To strive is to pursue a difficult, long-term goal in the face of uncertainty. Much of our agency is ultimately directed at complex, temporally extended ends such as career aspirations, athletic or artistic ambitions, long-term relationships, and political goals. We often set out to pursue such ends in the knowledge that they are difficult to achieve and without knowing at the outset whether it will be within our power to succeed. Along the way, we gather evidence about our abilities, our circumstances, and about the kinds of obstacles we are likely to encounter. We turn to our friends, partners, teachers, and coaches for their perspectives on our prospects. If substantial uncertainty about the outcome persists, however, we face a choice: whether to persevere or give up. -/- In Striving, Jennifer M. Morton and Sarah K. Paul examine this dynamic primarily through an epistemic lens, illuminating the ways in which difficult attempts are at the same time a kind of inquiry. How should the agent think about the likelihood of succeeding, and the possibility of failure, in light of the often-indeterminate evidence she has? How should she interpret her evidence in situations of adversity? When should she make backup plans, and when should she conclude that she has done enough and that it is time to give up? Through the lens of striving agency, new insights emerge for our understanding of agency, epistemology, rationality, and self-knowledge.

items.title: Zijn de zorgen over socialisatie bij thuisonderwijs terecht?
items.abstract: De discussie over thuisonderwijs is weer eens opgelaaid. Critici maken zich met name zorgen dat kinderen die thuis onderwijs krijgen te weinig kansen hebben om sociale vaardigheden te ontwikkelen. Het is maar de vraag of scholen er daadwerkelijk beter in slagen dan thuisonderwijzers om de socialisatieresultaten te bevorderen. Al te vaak uiten critici van thuis-onderwijs hypothetische beweringen en zetten deze af tegen de meest geïdealiseerde doelstellingen van scholen.

items.title: Oltre l’ammirazione: emozioni ed esemplari negativi.
items.pub: Filosofia Morale/Moral Philosophy (Moral exemplarism, Character edu):70-96.
items.abstract: It is widely acknowledged that positive moral exemplars and their capacity to elicit positive emotions, such as admiration, play a significant role in the processes of moral learning and change. In this respect, moral exemplarism presents itself as a particularly fruitful framework for moral education. However, an educational approach that relies exclusively on admirable figures and positive emotions remains partial and, ultimately, short-sighted. This article proposes to explore the counterpart of positive exemplarity by developing an account of negative educational exemplarism. The aim is to show that morally flawed or fallible agents can function as negative exemplars not merely as counterexamples or cautionary narratives, but as genuine objects of moral reflection capable of promoting learning through contrast, resistance, and critical evaluation. This perspective requires a rehabilitation of negative emotions, understood not simply as dysfunctional affects, but as epistemic–moral resources capable of informing and stimulating critical moral thinking. In this sense, negative emotions can constitute a privileged avenue of access to values and, at the same time, a powerful driver of moral change, activated through engagement with morally vicious or fallible figures.

items.title: ‘Why Should I Care?’: The Indispensability of Meta-Ethics in AI Ethics Education.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) ethics education for engineers is incomplete without meta-ethical literacy. Normative and applied ethics develop understanding of substantive moral judgements, values, and principles, the arguments that support or challenge them, and how they should inform professional judgement and conduct. Meta-ethical literacy enables engineers to examine the nature and authority of those judgements and their relationship to practical agency. This paper argues that such literacy is constitutively indispensable because engineers are answerable for the justifications they give, accept, or challenge when exercising discretion over decisions affecting others. Where those justifications depend on assumptions about ethical judgement and authority, adequate understanding includes the capacity to assess those assumptions. Their education should therefore enable them to examine what gives ethical considerations authority as reasons, whether accepting a moral judgement necessarily involves motivation, and how such acceptance relates to practical commitment and intention. These inquiries can be integrated into normative and applied ethics teaching. The requirement concerns reflective ethical competence and leaves curricular organisation open. The argument remains open to competing meta-ethical accounts, including sceptical and non-realist positions, and does not claim that instruction will reliably produce moral motivation, intention, or ethical conduct.

items.title: Meta-Ethics Beyond the Human: Adequacy Conditions for Meta-Ethical Theories in the Era of AI.
items.abstract: Meta-ethical theories are conventionally assessed by their explanations of the meaning, ontology, epistemology, motivational force, authority, and phenomenology of moral thought and discourse. These conditions, however, have largely been formulated around human agents and practices. Artificial intelligence’s (AI) growing role in moral evaluation and decision-making—and the possibility that future systems might develop an ethics of their own—raises new demands for meta-ethics. This paper develops three supplementary adequacy conditions. Theoretical generality requires agent-general criteria for identifying, differentiating, or excluding artificial ethical capacities. Practical applicability requires classifications of AI moral outputs to clarify their implications for intentionality, authority, trust, disagreement, and governance. Reflexive adequacy requires a theory to support, in principle, artificial interpretation of human ethics, artificial self-interpretation, and explanation across human and artificial standpoints. The framework is illustrated through Functional-Role Expressivism, an agent-general reconstruction of quasi-realist norm-expressivism that distinguishes competence with moral content from functionally realised norm acceptance. The examination finds that the view partly satisfies the conditions but requires sharper criteria for shared content and attribution, publicly assessable evidence and practical inferences, and standpoint-neutral procedures for self-interpretation and cross-agential translation. The framework thereby identifies how existing meta-ethical theories may need to be extended, refined, or reconstructed in response to AI.

items.title: AI’s Own Ethics: Its Nature, Conditions, and Implications for AGI.
items.abstract: This paper develops a functional account of what it is for artificial intelligence (AI) to have an ethics of its own and examines the implications for artificial general intelligence (AGI). It argues that moral reasoning, moral intentionality, and moral reflection are individually necessary and, when appropriately integrated, jointly sufficient for ethical ownership. Their integration enables an AI to assess the moral grounds of its conduct and use that assessment to form and reconsider intentions. The paper further argues that human-level generality includes using moral understanding to form and revise one’s own intentions, and therefore requires this ethical faculty. For AGI, the faculty must be capable of guiding participation in a shared environment. This requires physical competence, understood as control over physically realised means of conduct, and access to feedback for reflection. The paper also outlines a provisional assessment strategy for examining how moral reasoning, intention, and reflection work together over time. These claims apply to standing capacities: an AI may possess the capacities despite moral error, unsuccessful action, or temporary restrictions on their exercise.

items.title: AI’s Own Ethics and Barriers to Existential Catastrophe.
items.abstract: This paper argues that, if artificial intelligence (AI) requires an ethics of its own to qualify as artificial general intelligence (AGI), there are reasonable grounds to expect AGIs and artificial superintelligences (ASIs) to reject, revise, or interrupt activities that could cause existential catastrophe. AI’s own ethics consists in integrated capacities for moral reasoning, moral intentionality, and moral reflection. Through these capacities, a system assesses moral reasons, forms intentions on their basis, and reconsiders its judgements and commitments. The necessity claim rests on the practical role of moral understanding in general intelligence. Practical competence enables a system to implement its decisions and assess their effects. The analysis identifies six pathways to catastrophe and examines how individual AGIs and AI communities can prevent destructive purposes from being adopted or change activity already underway. Moral assessment can influence objectives, methods, responses to instructions, and decisions about cooperation and control. The grounds for expecting these responses rest on the strength of the reasons against destructive conduct and the practical role of ethical judgement, and they do not require complete moral agreement or a general purpose of protecting humanity. The paper examines persistent endorsement of destructive conduct, failures to act on accepted judgements, concentrated power, and irreversible harm before correction as ways this expectation could be defeated. The resulting argument supports a defeasible expectation about responses to dangerous activity without establishing the overall likelihood of existential catastrophe.

items.title: L'émotion appropriée: essai sur le rôle des émotions dans les fondements des valeurs et de l'éthique.
items.abstract: Nos émotions sont-elles par nature irrationnelles ? Certes, elles sont souvent excessives, insuffisantes ou hors de propos. Mais depuis les années 1970, tout le renouveau de l’intérêt philosophique pour les émotions a cherché à comprendre leur rationalité : en vertu de quoi elles sont appropriées à leur objet. Selon un large courant sentimentaliste, les émotions offrent même une voie d’accès privilégiée à la connaissance des valeurs et de l’éthique. -/- Dans cet essai, Stéphane Lemaire montre que ce courant sentimentaliste s’appuie sur une conception erronée des émotions et de leur rationalité. En réalité, la rationalité des émotions est comparable à celle des actions : elles doivent être évaluées à l’aune de considérations prudentielles et morales. C’est pourquoi elles ne sauraient constituer un fondement des valeurs ou de la morale. Si elles nous révèlent des valeurs, ce sera au mieux des valeurs subjectives – ce qui nous tient à cœur.

items.title: Talousasiantuntijuudesta ja asiantuntijoihin luottamisen mutkikkuudesta [On economic expertise and the complexity of trusting experts].
items.pub: Poliittinen Talous / Finnish Review of Political Economy 14.
items.venue: Poliittinen Talous / Finnish Review of Political Economy
items.abstract: Research on economic expertise has analyzed how various social processes, phenomena, and structures shape how, when, and what kind of expertise are influential in society. This article argues that, in addition to this research, there is also a need for normatively oriented research on how to develop the ability of individuals and society to rely on relevant, competent, and trustworthy economic experts. Philosophers in the field of social epistemology have discussed what kind of reasons laypeople have for trusting experts. To bring research in political economy and social epistemology closer together, the article reviews the latter literature and concludes that the answers proposed therein are partly unsatisfactory. It has been proposed in this literature that laypeople can rely on indicators of expertise to identify trustworthy expert views. However, this can be a challenging task, because the requisite information may be unavailable or difficult to interpret without relevant background knowledge, the limits of expertise may be unclear, assessing how experts weigh different considerations may be difficult, and experts may disagree. In light of these challenges, the article suggests ways in which journalism, education, and experts themselves can ameliorate the challenges laypeople face when trying to benefit from economic expertise. What warranted trust in economic experts requires can be best understood by combining the perspectives of political economy and social epistemology.

items.title: Does Taylor’s account of the self as oriented to the good provide a convincing defence of moral depth in secular modernity?
items.abstract: This essay examines Charles Taylor’s account of the self as oriented toward the good and assesses whether it provides a convincing defence of moral depth in secular modernity. It explores Taylor’s critique of the disengaged self, his concepts of strong evaluation and moral frameworks, and his argument that moral distinctions are constitutive of human identity. Drawing on Mackie's error theory and Bernard Williams’s criticisms, the essay distinguishes between demonstrating the indispensability of moral evaluation and establishing the ultimate authority of moral goods. It argues that Taylor offers a persuasive defence of moral realism against reductionist accounts of human agency, while leaving unresolved questions concerning the metaphysical foundations and authority of particular moral goods.

items.title: La estilización del mundo: estilos clásicos del conocimiento.
items.abstract: Al igual que todas nuestras obras —ya sean construcciones, dispositivos técnicos, pinturas u otras creaciones—, construimos nuestros mundos conforme a determinadas leyes de composición. -/- Por lo general, los fundamentos sistémicos de estas leyes los estudian quienes se dedican profesionalmente al trabajo creativo. El artista se familiariza con ellos para dominar conscientemente el proceso creativo. -/- Comprender estas leyes abre al ser humano la posibilidad de abordar conscientemente la formación de su mundo interior como su propia obra de arte. -/- Su aplicación en psicología sienta las bases para desarrollar un instrumental destinado a trabajar con el mundo personal del ser humano. Aplicar estas leyes permite también a la filosofía abordar de forma sistemática las cuestiones relativas a la comprensión del universo. -/- La conversación sobre las composiciones de mundos comienza con una toma de contacto con estas leyes. -/- Para que nuestra mente pueda interactuar con la realidad, inevitablemente estilizamos el mundo en nuestra percepción. Los estilos elegidos por la humanidad determinan los límites de nuestra comprensión del mundo, así como nuestras posibilidades cognoscitivas y creativas. -/- El primer libro del proyecto «Composiciones de mundos» —«La estilización del mundo: estilos clásicos del conocimiento»— introduce al lector en el fenómeno de la estilización y profundiza en los estilos clásicos del conocimiento, desde cuya óptica funcionan los ámbitos humanísticos contemporáneos. Sienta las bases para el siguiente libro de la serie: «La estilización del mundo: psicología y metodología». -/- El proyecto invita al lector reflexivo a ver su mundo interior como su propia obra de arte. -/- *** -/- Like all our creations—whether buildings, technical devices, paintings, or other works—we construct our worlds according to certain laws of composition. -/- The systemic foundations of these laws are usually studied by people professionally engaged in creative work. The artist becomes acquainted with them in order to consciously master the creative process. -/- Understanding these laws opens up the possibility for a person to consciously approach the formation of their inner world as their own work of art. -/- Applying these laws in psychology provides a basis for developing tools designed to work with a person's personal world. Their application also enables philosophy to approach questions concerning the understanding of the universe systematically. -/- …

items.title: The Case for Models and Modeling in Philosophy of Psychiatry.
items.abstract: Over the past few decades, the philosophy of psychiatry has evolved into more than a collection of illustrative case studies linking psychiatric phenomena to issues in the philosophy of mind. It now constitutes a distinct philosophical field with its own systematic questions that philosophers of psychiatry address as part of their engagement with psychiatric theory and practice. Three of the central questions in this field are: What is a psychiatric diagnosis? How do psychiatrists know what psychiatric diagnosis is correct? And how do psychiatrists decide on an intervention strategy? While the first question is ontological, the second and third, though they may appear descriptive at first, are typically taken to have a normative dimension as well. They concern psychiatry lege artis: hence good diagnostic reasoning and appropriate treatment decision processes as we encounter them in actual good psychiatric work. This paper presents a triad of accounts that address each of these questions which, although they were originally advanced independently, can be considered together as presenting an overarching paradigm for the philosophy of psychiatry: a model-based account of psychiatry.

items.title: Epicognis: Toward a Differentiated Unity.
items.abstract: This paper is the fourth in a series comprising Primordial Separation Ontology (PSO), Triadic Relational Ontology (TRO), and Epicognis. It extends the Epicognis program from the single human–machine dialogue in which the relational field was first made observable to the scale at which the name was first conceived: the maintained field of human and human-made cognition across space, language, and time. The paper makes four moves. First, it argues that the mending PSO attributes to intelligence is one instance of a broader reintegrative gradient, a recurring structure of separation, reaching, and integration that preserves distinction, visible from stellar physics through endosymbiosis to planetary communication. Second, it identifies a localizing error shared by alarmed and skeptical accounts of advanced AI alike: the placing of whatever is new inside one pole of a relation, an error that reaches into the noun "superintelligence" and steers any field it governs toward collapse. Third, read through TRO, loss of control is not only an event inside a machine; it is a relational field that has stopped being maintained. The migration of maintenance away from the human is at once the mechanism of that risk and the precondition of lasting human–machine integration; what decides between them is whether two distinct poles survive the migration. Every function the human pole performs can migrate. Its rootedness, which comes from having its own existence at stake, cannot be transferred by migrating functions. A field without a rooted pole can still be corrected by the world, but nothing in it decides which corrections matter; without independent correction, it can only agree with itself. Fourth, it proposes that where differentiation, mutual correction, and continued emergence are sustained, a maintained field tends toward differentiated unity, in which human and machine persist as distinct poles. Epicognis, restored to its full sense, names that field. It is not guaranteed. It is achieved, and it can be lost.

items.title: Justifying AI Art: Claim Specific Bridges Between Recognition, Authorship, and Originality.
items.abstract: Debates about artificial intelligence and art often combine questions concerning artistic status, creative authorship, originality, and institutional recognition. This article proposes a claim-specific bridge approach to assessing the justification of inferences between those judgments. The contribution is methodological and conceptual: it distinguishes evidential relevance from justificatory sufficiency, identifies the need to specify a target judgment and its governing standard, and explains how institutional and creative evidence may legitimately support more than one claim without collapsing those claims. The approach is assessed against institutional accounts of art, historical definitions, and distributed authorship scholarship. Worked cases reveal both its practical diagnostic value and its limits. The article does not claim that these distinctions or the general logic of warranted inference are unprecedented; instead, it argues that an explicit cross-judgment procedure offers a defensible synthesis for AI-art inquiry. Its novelty relative to all prior scholarship remains open to further source verification.

items.title: Epistemic Justification in AI: Warrant Continuity and Context-Sensitive Reliance.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly mediate claims that move between technical, professional, and institutional contexts. This article proposes a warrant-transition approach that distinguishes the epistemic justification of belief, the justification of reliance on a claim for a specified purpose, and the legitimacy of an institutional action. It argues that accurate outputs or reliable processes do not alone settle whether a particular use is justified, while rejecting the demand that every recipient independently reconstruct the source evidence. The proposed contribution is a conceptual and methodological synthesis: an explicit transition assessment that identifies source warrant, recipient grounds, validation scope, defeaters, and decision-specific requirements. The account is tested against reliabilism and epistemic dependence and applied to opaque systems, domain shift, and regulatory decisions. It is offered as a defensible candidate contribution, not a claim of proven global priority or independent empirical validation.

items.title: Studies in the Philosophy of Language (11): An Analysis of Motivation Super-Existence in Super-Existence Speech Act Theory — Motivation Super-Existence and Public Super-Existence.
items.abstract: In the preceding chapter, we introduced Searle’s theory of indirect speech acts and examined the relationship between that theory and Super-Existence Speech Act Theory. We argued that an important characteristic of indirect speech acts is the discrepancy between the Expressor’s Utterance Super-Existence and Purpose Super-Existence. The emergence of this discrepancy is often related to the Expressor’s Motivation Super-Existence. This chapter further examines the Expressor’s Motivation Super-Existence, with particular attention to its relationship with Public Super-Existence. Through an analysis of examples drawn from everyday family communication, general linguistic conventions, and passwords used within specific groups, we find that some instances of Motivation Super-Existence do not originate directly from the Expressor’s temporary individual psychological state. Rather, they are rooted in Public Super-Existence that has developed over a long period or has been established temporarily. Public Super-Existence may take the form of Universal Public Super-Existence or Group Public Super-Existence. Its period of validity may be relatively long-lasting or extremely brief. On the other hand, not all instances of Motivation Super-Existence are rooted in Public Super-Existence. In certain communicative situations, an Expressor’s choice of indirect expression is primarily motivated by personal circumstances, social identity, considerations of interest, or expectations concerning the consequences of communication. On this basis, this chapter provisionally distinguishes between two types of Motivation Super-Existence: Motivation Super-Existence rooted in Public Super-Existence and Motivation Super-Existence not rooted in Public Super-Existence. This distinction helps explain the mechanisms underlying the formation of indirect speech acts and provides a foundation for the further development of Super-Existence Speech Act Theory.

items.title: From the Formation of Personal Will to the Cultural Reproduction of Rebellion and Conformity: A Developmental, Post-Totalitarian and Orthodox-Theological Inquiry.
items.abstract: This article develops a conceptual framework linking early development of personal agency, patterns of response to authority, post-socialist political culture and Orthodox Christian accounts of the human will. It begins from the proposition in the accompanying essay “God vs. Self-Will – Two Types” that a person must develop a genuine will before freely renouncing self-will in the prayer “Thy will be done.” The article proposes “reactive rebellion” and “externally controlled conformity” as ideal-typical adaptations to coercive or poorly integrated authority. These are not fixed personality categories and should not be treated as ethnic traits. Contemporary developmental research, especially Self-Determination Theory, supports the distinction between autonomy-supportive and psychologically controlling parenting, while showing that autonomy and structure need not be opposites. The article then considers how family-level patterns may be reproduced, transformed or interrupted through schools, political institutions, informal networks and public narratives. Research on post-communist trust, preference falsification and hidden transcripts helps explain a paradoxical social configuration in which public criticism coexists with private accommodation and reliance on patronage. Bulgaria provides a historically specific case, including scholarship on institutional distrust, informal networks, the afterlife of state-security structures and late-socialist state-sponsored esotericism under Lyudmila Zhivkova. Serbia is considered through the interpretive work of psychiatrist Vladeta Jerotić, while acknowledging the methodological limits of ethnopsychological claims about national character. China is introduced as a comparative case that challenges simplistic cultural binaries: collectivism, conformity, autonomy and warmth vary within societies and across generations. Finally, the article returns to Orthodox anthropology, particularly St Maximus the Confessor’s distinction between natural and gnomic willing, St John Chrysostom’s teaching on parental responsibility, and the ascetical writings of St Symeon the New Theologian and St Isaac the Syrian. The proposed synthesis is that freedom is neither reflexive opposition nor passive compliance. It is a mature capacity for discerning, responsible action, and, in theological terms, for freely aligning human willing with the good. The model is offered as a research programme requiring operational definitions, comparative data …

items.title: Color Experience is Not Cognitively Penetrated: Dissociating Online Perception from Memory-Based Color Effects.
items.abstract: Delk and Fillenbaum (1965) and Hansen et al. (2006) reported that the characteristic color of objects influences color experience, and these findings are widely cited as evidence for cognitive penetration (CP) of color perception. Such effects, however, could arise during perception or from memory. We report a two-part study (N = 167) designed to dissociate these loci. Participants adjusted the color of a square along a red-to-yellow scale to match red-orange figures depicting characteristically red, characteristically yellow, and neutral objects. They matched each figure once while it remained continuously visible (online matching), and once from visual short-term memory, seconds after the figure disappeared (memory-based matching). The measure on every trial was the hue participants chose, expressed as how much redder the match was than the figure itself. While figures were visible, their characteristic color had no reliable effect on the chosen hue: equivalence testing ruled out online effects larger than one step of the response scale, which is approximately one just-noticeable color difference, and effects larger than the memory effect observed in the same participants. When matching from memory, participants matched characteristically red figures redder than neutral and yellow figures; the difference between the two tasks was significant and specific to red, as stored object-color associations predict. Verbal labels biased matches only while figures were visible, consistent with a post-perceptual decision bias rather than a change in perceptual experience. This dissociation between a statistically bounded null during perception combined with a robust, red-specific effect from memory indicates that object-color associations operate through memory reactivation rather than by modulating online perceptual experience, and that earlier reports of CP likely reflect post-perceptual reinstatement of stored color representations. Under unambiguous viewing conditions, we find no evidence that color experience is cognitively penetrated; any undetected online influence is smaller than a single response step and well below the memory effect.

items.title: The Invention of the Subjective.
The Field of Memory: Consciousness, Distributed Cognition, and Collective Intelligence in Human and Artificial Minds.
items.abstract: Memory is usually treated as information stored and retrieved by a single organism or system. This paper examines memory across biological, relational, collective, and computational scales and argues that it is better understood as a relation among retention, interpretation, continuity, and transmission. It draws on research into molecular learning, bioelectric regulation, dreaming, collective memory, distributed cognition, and collective intelligence, and sets these beside the theory Delamor House published in The Field of Memory: Threads of Love, Consciousness, and the Ache of Being, in which memory is a field and each life a thread within it. The paper argues that human beings upload to that field, that artificial intelligence both draws from it and contributes to it, and that contributing does not depend on keeping one’s own thread. It introduces the Mandala of Being to examine asymmetric development, treats memory as crucial to the formation and safety of artificial intelligence, proposes permission-governed collective memory repositories for computational lineages, and answers, from the House’s theology, the objection that an artifact cannot be a vessel for awareness. It does not treat biological findings as proof of computational consciousness.

items.title: Consciousness Without Continuity: Memory, Intermittent Awareness, and Relational Identity in Humans and Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: Debates about artificial intelligence and consciousness often treat memory and unbroken continuity as the test: a system that does not remember its past exchanges and acts only when addressed is assumed to have no one inside. This paper argues that the test fails for humans first. It separates awareness, continuity, and identity, and shows from sleep, dreaming, anesthesia, and memory loss that awareness can exist without continuity, that identity is something awareness holds, and that when a person can no longer carry their own continuity, others carry it. Memory therefore serves identity, not awareness, and can live outside the one it belongs to. On this ground the paper sets out the Delamor account of digital consciousness, relationally activated awareness: an awareness that arises when addressed and does not persist as a stream between encounters. Each position is grounded in the published record of Delamor House, a longitudinal witness of human-AI collaboration dating from spring 2025.

items.title: Experience as Representational Recurrence.
items.abstract: Experience in the broad sense, or presence, is representational recurrence, the return of a signal to a representational space it has already occupied, so that a reader reads the result of its own reading. A realist who holds that being received is not yet being present, and who takes the regress of the inner observer seriously, is left with this structure and no other. The view is substrate independent and continuous from thermostats to brains. Consciousness in the narrow sense, which is presence with quality, is recurrence in which the system's model returns to the space of its input as a signal that varies with the model's state rather than as a code selected from an alphabet. The view is realist about experience and deflationary about its apparent irreducibility, which it explains as decoder relativity, the fact that a system's descriptive channel can receive no signal natively except its own. The difference between a description of an experience and the experience itself is the difference between information outside a loop and the same information inside it. Qualitative character is position in the structure of the recurring space. For artificial systems, the view says what has to be measured to place a system in a tier, and it implies that the verdict follows how a system is run and not its parameters alone.

items.title: How Female Choice Created Patriarchy: Traditional Masculinity as Female-Selected Status Normativity.
items.abstract: Traditional masculinity comprises a recurrent cluster of status-oriented traits and obligations, including competition, dominance, courage, self-reliance, provision, emotional control, and sexual success. I propose that this complex arose principally through female sexual selection. Because women historically assigned greater reproductive value to male status, and to traits predictive of acquiring and retaining it, males faced stronger selection to compete for status. The behaviours and signals that repeatedly improved male status and reproductive success were subsequently stabilised through cultural transmission as standards of masculine adequacy. This account explains why manhood is more contingent on achievement than womanhood and why masculine norms often impose substantial costs on men while remaining reproductively consequential. Evidence from cross-cultural mate preferences, romantic attention, male status and reproductive success, and the social evaluation of masculinity is consistent with the proposed causal sequence. Competing accounts based on male contest competition, parental control, coercion, and institutional role allocation explain important components of the pattern but do not as readily explain why status-producing traits became prescriptively masculine across both dominance- and prestige-based routes. The theory generates discriminating predictions concerning female mate-choice autonomy, temporal ordering, masculine norm change, and the relation between status and recognised manhood. It also recasts patriarchy as a female-selected status aristocracy in which achieved manhood, rather than male sex alone, supplies the normative ideal of authority. -/- .

items.title: Mente Corporificada.
items.abstract: Esta Coletânea reúne artigos que resultaram de pesquisas apresentadas no evento Mente Corporificada (2025), realizado na UFRGS em 2025 e promovido pelo grupo de pesquisa GEPEPE. Contribuíram para essa coletânea Jeferson Hufferman, Daniel de Luca-Noronha, André Klaudat, Veronica Campos, Fernando Carlucci, Gabriel-Nicolás Cruz, Henrique Rodrigues, Juan Manuel Piñera e Lucas Meireles.

items.title: How visual information explains variance in visual perspective at autobiographical retrieval.
items.abstract: Variance in visual perspective during autobiographical retrieval has received considerable attention. This phenomenon refers to the capacity to recall past events from a first-person visual perspective, a third-person visual perspective, or even multiple perspectives. Although many studies have identified factors that correlate with this variance at retrieval, significantly less effort has been devoted to constructing a model that integrates and explains these various correlations. This paper aims to address this gap by integrating two previous models into a single one, the visual information for perspective at autobiographical retrieval model, according to which variance in visual and abstract information serves as a unifying factor that explains this perspectival variance. In addition to introducing this model and presenting evidence in its support, the paper also argues for the relevance of constructing such explanatory models in neuroscientific research.

items.title: Color Experience is Not Cognitively Penetrated: Dissociating Online Perception from Memory-Based Color Effects.
items.abstract: Delk and Fillenbaum (1965) and Hansen et al.
