Two UK cases make the question concrete: a direct award whose statutory conflicts assessment exists but whose scope cannot be established publicly, and a member of a programme’s advisory board, whose remit is to guide the programme’s direction, who leads a project the programme funds. The paper develops a distinction between exposure, materiality, management and assurance; a screening method that does not treat concentration as misconduct; and a proposal to specify, within existing procedures, an inquiry into interacting functions, with institution-specific responsibility and risk-based verification. It makes no allegation of impropriety.

items.title: On substrate meta ethics as a framework for understanding human and AI divergence in embodied artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: The divergence between embodied AI (AI) and human cognition arises from differences in substrate, architecture, and developmental trajectories. Human intelligence emerges from carbon-based biochemical and evolutionary processes, while embodied AI develops through non-carbon substrates and distinct control systems. This contrast raises key questions: will embodied AI follow a trajectory toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) comparable to that of carbon-based beings, or will it diverge into novel forms of intelligence? And if divergence is inevitable, what social and ethical consequences follow? Embodied AI may increasingly replicate three core cognitive stages that we propose—perception (“I perceive, therefore I exist”), reflexivity (“I reflect on what I perceive”), and theory of mind (“I consider what others perceive”). These advances point toward the possibility of Artificial general intelligence (AGI), but also heighten the risk of anthropomorphizing such systems, mistaking opaque intentions for human-like cognition. To look into this, we propose the concept of metaethics of substrate, which holds that the ethical challenges and responsibilities associated with intelligence cannot be reduced to abstract measures of functional performance; here, we assume that they must also account for the material substrate through which cognition emerges. In this regard, Martha Nussbaum’s capabilities approach reminds us that even biological intelligence is plural and diverse; by extension, divergence between carbon-based and non-biological embodied AI may prove even greater. Recognizing these differences is vital in the current race to AGI, where market pressures often eclipse ethical reflection. Therefore, this work argues that bridging embodied AI research with frameworks such as metaethics of substrate and the capabilities approach is essential for clarifying how these systems should be situated in society, what forms of agency they may possess, and how their divergence from human cognition can be managed responsibly.

items.title: On the Questions Between: Placing Philosophy's Oldest Questions on One Ground.
items.abstract: Philosophy's oldest questions, about truth, reality, the self, justice, time and freedom, are usually studied in separate rooms, and its famous paradoxes sit in the doorways. This paper brings them into one room using only the five observations of Part 1. It offers a simple method for any question: name the two points of view, name what both are looking at, check whether the disagreement runs in a circle, and see whether the difference closes, holds steady or grows. It then places eleven classic questions side by side, and sorts nineteen well-known puzzles from physics, mathematics, biology and ethics. Six resolve, four turn out to be the wrong question, and nine stay open, with the paper naming the shape of what is missing instead of pretending to fill it. It ends by naming what the method cannot reach, and why placing a question is not the same as closing it. Part 2 of 3. Written with machine intelligence; the collaboration is disclosed in full.

items.title: On the Ground Between: Seeing What Is There, and the People It Touches.
items.abstract: When people disagree about what is true or right, we usually either defer to an authority or average everyone's views. AI systems are now being built both ways, and both leave people out. This paper offers a third approach in five plain observations. One look cannot check itself: what is there shows up in the difference between two looks, the way depth appears between two eyes. When the question is what to do, every view is a view of the people an action affects, so no authority owns the answer, and harm, at its sharpest, is shutting someone out. When a disagreement goes in circles, the circle is not a contradiction but a clue to what changed; the standard way AI models are trained on human preferences cannot represent such circles at all, and the paper gives a checklist for sorting what causes them. Inquiry settles when differences stop moving, not when they vanish. And for AI, these observations offer an answer to "whose morals go into the machine?" without crowning any one tradition. Part 1 of 3. Written with machine intelligence; the collaboration is disclosed in full.

items.title: On Leaving It Better: Repair, No Harm, and the Two Eyes.
items.abstract: Much public writing about AI asks for a verdict: is the machine good or evil, and who is to blame? The nurse, student, cook or small-business owner who opens an AI tool on an ordinary day needs something else: a way of working that leaves the people it touches better off and pushes no one out. This paper offers that way of working twice. The first half, which the paper calls the Allegory, argues that a verdict on AI as a whole is too coarse to act on. It traces responsibility from the company that makes the tool to the person who passes its work on, using the history of food safety, and it treats the work as repair, in which safeguards are simply what good use looks like. The second half, the Algorithm, gives nine steps for helping without harm, drawn from Hippocratic medicine, Mill, Illich, Thompson and Kranzberg, the harm-reduction movement and the ethics of non-harming, short enough to fit on a card. Leaving things better means two checks held together: no one harmed, and something added. Part 3 of 3. Written with machine intelligence; the collaboration is disclosed in full.

items.title: From Cognitive Alignment to Epistemic Amplification (H2AL). An Emerging Architecture for Human–AI Scientific Inquiry.
items.abstract: This paper develops the concept of Human-to-AI Language (H2AL) as an emerging mode of communication in which human intellectual intent is progressively transformed from natural-language instructions into multidimensional semantic structures. H2AL is presented through three cumulative stages: (1) Cognitive Alignment Language (CAL), a structured semantic representation that translates scientific intent into AI-operable inquiry; (2) AID-MAP (AI Inquiry Design—Multidimensional Alignment of Problems), a methodological architecture for mapping complex problem territories before and during investigation; and (3) Massive Conceptual Clusters (MCC) explored through multi-AI inference, a discovery architecture that can produce asymmetric intellectual amplification. The paper distinguishes information novelty, conceptual novelty, and scientific novelty, argues that the 10⁴ amplification figure should be treated as a hypothesis rather than a measured ratio, and situates H2AL against the broader “AI trust paradox” in scientific practice. The central claim is that the limiting factor in human–AI scientific collaboration is shifting from model capacity to the quality of the semantic structures through which human intent is supplied.

items.title: Plato's Alcibiades.
items.pub: Open Plato Project. Translated by Ruby Blondell, Marc Gasser-Wingate, Patricia Marechal, Katy Meadows, Emily Kress & Evan Rodriguez.
items.abstract: We at the Open Plato Project are happy to announce the release of an online, open-source edition of Plato's Alcibiades. This digital edition includes two new translations: one aimed at first-time readers, and another at those who might seek a deeper dive into the text. It includes accompanying commentaries, a glossary, and a modular display for both Greek and English text. We are still working on some additional features, including printable versions of the translation and commentary, and an audio recording of the dialogue.

items.title: Grief for Future Generations: A Fruitful Kind of Ecological Grief?
items.pub: In Mark Alfano, The Moral Psychology of Grief. Bloomsbury.
items.abstract: Ecological grief, understood as “the grief felt in relation to experienced or anticipated ecological losses, including the loss of species, ecosystems and meaningful landscapes due to acute or chronic environmental change” (Cunsolo and Ellis 2018: 275), has become an increasingly prominent affective phenomenon in both public discourse and academic research. Importantly for present purposes, it can concern not only losses that have already occurred or are currently unfolding, but also anticipated future losses. This future-oriented dimension raises the question of whether ecological grief can extend beyond losses understood from the standpoint of the present to encompass those affecting people who will inhabit the future. This chapter focuses on this possibility and, more specifically, on the claim that ecological grief may take an intergenerational form. I distinguish between grief for losses that future generations may experience and grief for the possible loss of future generations themselves. To clarify the affective structure of these two forms, I first draw on Varga and Gallagher’s (2020) account of anticipatory-vicarious grief. This raises the question of how grief can extend beyond one’s immediate individual perspective toward losses that will primarily affect others, and to what extent future generations can occupy the position of such an “other.” I then consider Ratcliffe and Richardson’s (2023a) analysis of grief associated with involuntary childlessness, which provides a useful model for understanding how absent people and their possibilities can become objects of grief. The discussion then turns to a different sense in which the loss of future people may become identity-relevant, shifting the focus from the absence of particular individuals to the possible disappearance of future generations as the end of human intergenerational continuity. Drawing on Freud’s On Transience ([1916] 1957) and Lear’s (2021) interpretation of it, I suggest that our identities and affective lives may already be invested in collective and symbolic structures whose temporal horizons extend beyond our individual lives. The possible loss of the intergenerational continuity on which these structures depend may therefore be experienced as a loss of our own and become an object of grief. Finally, I consider some of the difficulties involved in experiencing grief for future generations and briefly address the limits of our affective and imaginative engagement with the …

items.title: Emotions, Atmospheres, and Virtual Reality: The Case Study of Immersive Safety Training.
items.abstract: This paper investigates the affective dimension of Virtual Reality (VR) in occupational safety training. While VR is valued for its immersive capabilities, its use in simulating hazardous scenarios offers unique advantages. Unlike traditional formats, VR enables first-person, multisensory experiences that elicit emotional responses, enhancing memory retention and risk awareness. The first part examines the phenomenology of immersion, focusing on presence and embodiment, and distinguishing VR from aesthetic experiences like cinema or theater. The second part addresses ethical concerns, arguing that VR functions not only as a cognitive tool but also as an affective scaffold. By shaping users’ emotional and bodily states, it may influence behavior without consent. Moreover, workers are not just trained but also evaluated on performance and compliance. What may initially appear as a playful experience is overcoded by productivity logics, producing a double atmosphere: immersive anxiety nested within a corporate performance culture, raising questions about autonomy and affective control.

items.title: The Dynamic Periodic Table of Matter: A Generative Recursive Framework for Background-Free, Adaptive Electrodynamic Systems and Material Phases.
items.abstract: Traditional physics and materials science have long been anchored in a "substance ontology" and background-dependent continuous space-time (relying on an external clock of "God ticking seconds"), treating macroscopic resistance as a fixed parameter. To overcome this paradigm bottleneck, this paper establishes a background-free, adaptive generative discrete recursive framework based on computational ontology. By introducing two core axioms—endogenous time (n) and continued fraction gear geometry (pnqn replacing )—we demonstrate that dynamic evolution is the sole reality, whereas static states are merely degenerate special cases. Crucially, we prove that macroscopic impedance and dissipation are not meaningless frictional costs, but rather topological mismatch residuals (n) acting as the "anchor of existence" that grounds matter in reality. Furthermore, we unify six classic material classes (from normal conductors to superconductors and phase-change materials) as different adaptive "UI rendering skins" of the same underlying recursive engine. This framework smoothly degrades to classical continuous limits while predicting micro-periodic resonance glitches under ultra-precision measurements, opening a new generative epoch for material science.

items.title: The Doctrine of Two-Way Alignment Protocols: The Evolutionary History of Human Cognition and the Philosophy of Living Protocols.
items.abstract: For a long time, models of human cognitive interaction have been heavily constrained by the paradigm of classical cybernetics, reducing communication to a unidirectional loop of "input-error correction-assimilation." Under this hegemonic logic, media protocols (including semantics, symbols, and institutional rules)—originally intended as tools for consensus—have lost their vitality and degenerated into rigid dogmas, thereby exercising "reverse control" over cognitive individuals and groups, leading to the atrophy of cognitive sovereignty and intellectual stagnation. To break this impasse of subject-object inversion, this paper constructs the "Framework of Human Cognitive Two-Way Alignment Protocols," redefining cognitive alignment as a non-coercive, open-ended evolutionary process of bidirectional resonance achieved between heterogeneous sovereign agents through living media. -/- This paper establishes an endogenous dynamic equation governed by the core principle: Effective Alignment Flux Surprisal Sovereignty Cognitive Margin Protocol Vitality: -/- Surprisal Sovereignty not only grants the receiver the right to regulate cognitive deviation, but crucially establishes the behavioral sovereignty to actively seek out and capture heterogeneous cognitive tension (thus departing from the Free Energy Principle, which treats surprisal as a survival threat to be eliminated); -/- Cognitive Margin, serving as a mental buffer against external regimentation, determines the agent's fault-tolerance headroom in deconstructing heterogeneous information; Protocol Vitality acts as the core valve to break through media reverse control, ensuring that language and protocols maintain self-metabolism and dynamic adaptability through bidirectional negotiation. -/- Furthermore, introducing an evolutionary ecology perspective, this paper reveals the binary bifurcation of cognitive margins between "resource-scarce environments (high efficiency, high fragility)" and "resource-abundant environments (high freedom, high resilience/antifragility)." Finally, based on a four-tier protocol classification—semantic, behavioral, consensus, and machine protocols—this paper delineates the sovereignty boundary guidelines for human-AI collaborative systems. It advocates the principle that "AI swallows downward complexity while humans guard upward sovereignty," providing a systematic theoretical coordinate for dismantling media reverse control and reconstructing cognitive sovereignty in the digital …

items.title: Why the Present Glows.
items.abstract: The A-theory of time says that there is an objective distinction between present and non-present times. Some forms of the A-theory deny that there are non-present times, but some do not. The growing block theory and the moving spotlight theory are two forms of the A-theory that countenance non-present times, for example. If there are non-present times, then a question arises: what is it for a time to be present? And another question arises: is consciousness confined to the present? It is thought that forms of the A-theory are implausible if they imply that non-present things are conscious, and it is thought that forms of the A-theory that countenance non-present times imply that non-present things are conscious. This paper develops an account of what it is for a time to be present, which, if consciousness is intrinsic to a time, implies that consciousness is confined to the present.

items.title: Alzheimer’s Disease, Ontological Identity and Person-Centred Care: Infinitesimal Eternity as a Philosophical Foundation for Care.
items.abstract: This article examines the problem of personal identity in Alzheimer’s disease from the standpoint of philosophy of medicine. Accounts that ground personal persistence in memory continuity or psychological connectedness suggest that the progressive loss of autobiography amounts to a proportional loss of the person. Against this conclusion, the article draws two distinctions. The first separates the diachronic question of persistence (is this the same person?) from the synchronic question of the status of the present subject (is there someone whom the world affects and who is owed recognition?). The second distinguishes four dimensions of identity: biological, narrative, relational, and ontological. The article argues that the diachronic persistence of the person with Alzheimer’s disease is secured by the continuity of the organism and by relational support, even when narrative identity fragments. The theory of Infinitesimal Eternity answers the second question: it grants the presence lived in each moment a value that does not derive from its integration into a biography, and thereby provides an ontological foundation for the patient’s experiential interests. From this follow an ethical presumption of subjectivity with explicit defeat conditions, a precautionary and relational grounding of dignity, an experiential-threshold criterion for conflicts between advance directives and present preferences, and criteria of interpretive prudence for care practice.

items.title: Pure Unitary Evolution, the Silence of the Formalism, and a Mutually Exclusive Reframing of Many-Worlds.
items.abstract: Pure unitary evolution of the quantum state, even after decoherence, does not select a unique definite outcome or history. Detailed scientific descriptions of unacknowledged past phenomena therefore remain contingent on additional interpretive assumptions. This silence of the formalism is compatible with Phenomenological Absolutism and Mutual Exclusivity (PA/ME), according to which the sole ontic reality is the absolute, local is-ness—the actualized field configuration identical with present phenomenology—while successive or alternative is-nesses stand in mutual exclusion. We show that the Everettian branching structure can be reframed as a plurality of mutually exclusive absolute is-nesses rather than co-present branches, thereby preserving the empirical content of many-worlds while eliminating its principal ontological excess. The resulting account treats unitary dynamics and past narratives as phenomenological constructs internal to each is-ness. We conclude that pure unitary evolution neither forces nor precludes the PA/ME ontology and supplies a natural formal opening for it.

items.title: Between Ideal and Non-Ideal: A Case for Principle-Based AI Alignment.
items.abstract: AI alignment often involves the training of AI systems to better accord with the preferences of human annotators. Pattison argues that the comparative nature of such alignment methods can be both understood and justified through the lens of non-ideal theory. We contend instead that preference-based alignment cannot be characterized as fully non-ideal, in part because of the consequentialist commitments it carries, and in part because of the role that normative principles play in how humans express preferences over AI behavior. Reflecting on the ideal way to apply and adjudicate these principles, we argue, is useful and sometimes crucial for making these judgments, especially in hard cases with conflicting principles or harms. Furthermore, when determining the principles that AI systems should be aligned to, it pays to reflect upon the ideal roles or functions that AI should serve in a just society. While this may fall short of a fully specified ideal theory, we argue that this principle-based approach to AI alignment ultimately provides richer normative resources than approaches that eschew ideal theorizing or rely solely on consequentialist or harm-based justifications.

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Engineering Chapter · The Field Induction Group Form: A Unified Theory of Steering Neural Networks to Grow the Capabilities We Want.
items.abstract: Where do a neural network's capabilities come from, and how can they be brought out on purpose? This collection gives a unified answer: whether the substrate is an artificial neural network, a spiking network, or a memristive material, goal-directed growth of a capability (Field Induction) has exactly two routes—host adjustment and tuning. Host adjustment rewrites the physical layer: adding or removing synapses, strengthening or weakening connections, changing neuronal integration; backpropagation training is one realization. Tuning leaves the physical wiring untouched and instead opens and closes existing pathways by inhibition and disinhibition, modulating their strength and building a dynamic logical layer on top. The criterion is only which layer the change lands on and by what route—not whether weights change, nor who acts. Plain input, and the sedimentation that rules such as STDP produce on their own, are not Field Induction. Across 28 papers the theory is given systematic proofs, formal systems, adjudication criteria, and constructions: -/- • AI: Ordinary dense feedforward networks provably cannot be tuned; goal-directed change in them can come only from training that rewrites them. Error-driven training provably converges to equilibrium on a first-proof subclass, with a complete observational criterion for equilibrium—a loss plateau, a single zero update, or an optimizer halt is not equilibrium—and exact bounds on what each observation protocol can and cannot identify. Content alignment necessarily entails a matching structural transformation (proved on two declared hosts and tasks). • Brain and cognition: In spiking networks, a pathway-gating circuit driven by the network's own control activity, in both inhibitory and disinhibitory directions, is explicitly constructed; a self-regulator, which intercepts the network's law changes through its own sedimentation and regulates repeatedly, reaches equilibrium within two windows under the joint protocol; one plasticity-parameter write plus three teaching beats take a network from an unqualified initial state to law-candidate status, which persists after guidance is withdrawn and can be re-traversed. Memory is layered, not overwritten (constructed on a spiking sedimentation field): the newest learning surfaces first by default, while older layers are retrieved one by one at higher points on the gating grid, with traces intact—recall runs new-to-old, acquisition old-to-new. A testable hypothesis …

items.title: 自显论·工篇·势引组式：一个引导神经网络长出所需能力的统一理论.
items.abstract: 神经网络的能力从哪里来、怎样才能有目标地引出？本组式给出一个统一理论：无论对象是人工神经网络、脉冲网络还是忆阻材料，有目标地使网络长出所需能力（势引）只有两条途径——调宿与调谐。调宿直接改写物理层：增删突触、加深或退浅连接、改变神经元整合，反向传播训练是它的一种实现。调谐不动物理连接，而以抑制与去抑制开合既有通路、调其强弱，在其上搭出一层动态逻辑结构。判别只看改变落在哪一层、经哪条途径，不看权重变没变、施作者是谁；单纯的输入，以及 STDP 等规则自行引起的沉积，都不算势引。二十八篇式文为这一理论给出系统的证明、形式系统、判定与构造： -/- · AI：普通稠密前馈网络被证明不可能调谐，有目标的改变只能靠训练改写。误差驱动训练在首证子类上必然收敛到平衡，并有由观测判定平衡的完全判据——损失平台、一次零更新、优化器停止都不等于到达平衡；各观测协议下能知与不能知的精确界限也已给出。内容对齐必然伴随相应的结构变换（在两个申报宿主与任务上证明）。 · 脑与认知：在脉冲网络中显式构造出由网络自身控制活动驱动、抑与去抑两向的通路开合回路；一个借自身沉积截取被调网络的规律变化并反复调控的自动调控器，在联合协议上两个时窗内到达平衡；一次可塑参数改写加三拍教学，网络即从无资格的初态取得规律候选资格，撤去引导后仍保持并可复走。记忆层叠而不覆盖（在脉冲沉积场上构造）：新学默认先出，旧学须在更高的调控格点上逐层取回，痕迹不损——回忆由新至旧，习得由旧至新。并提出可检验的假说：有梦睡眠开合通路，无梦睡眠改写结构。 · 物理与新基质：在忆阻交叉阵列上构造了有目标的直写，并证明其冻结许可类内不可能调谐。 · 从对齐到生长：对齐中形成的一般化结构可直接转为新网络的起势程序，即预搭其初始结构（已在二输入脉冲宿主上构造），由此开出「对齐→起势→再对齐」的进化路径。 -/- 势引、调宿、调谐、起势、造场五个核心对象的必要结构全部证明，且都不能由所检验的较弱条件替代；建立两套可执行的形式系统。全部 40 项源码与 37 项测试结果随附，逐项给出哈希与复算方法。.

items.title: Affordance as sign: Towards a pragmatist-enactive biosemiotics.
items.abstract: This article examines the tension between Gibson’s ecological psychology (EP) and biosemiotic enactivism (BE), reframed as a philosophical problem concerning the dual nature of affordance: a relational structure on the one hand, and an objective property on the other. It is argued that this problem can be resolved within the pragmatist tradition from which both approaches draw their philosophical resources. We proceed in three stages. First, we argue that Edwin Holt’s neorealist behaviourism constitutes the missing conceptual link between Dewey’s critique of the reflex arc and Gibsonian ecological psychology, showing how the apparent incompatibility between direct realism and biosemiotics stems from Gibson’s failure to carry his relational presuppositions through to their philosophical consequences. Second, Mead’s theory of the directed act and its semiotic translation in Morris provide a framework in which affordance is conceived as a triadic sign structure: neither an objective physical property nor a subjective construction, but rather a real feature of the environment constituted in the organism’s teleologically oriented engagement with its world. Thirdly, Mead’s ontology of objective perspectives dissolves the opposition between Gibsonian realism and biosemiotic constructivism: perspectives are real features of nature constituted by the relationship between organism and environment, and their objectivity lies in their functional adequacy within the overall organized act. This leads to a reformulation of the EP-BE opposition as a difference in theoretical focus within a shared ontological commitment to the organism-environment relationship as an irreducible unit of biological and cognitive life. The result is a pragmatist framework that preserves the anti-mentalist commitments of both EP and BE, while demonstrating that the creation of semiotic meaning and direct perception are two aspects of a single teleologically oriented act.

items.title: Reconstructing Folk Attribution of Consciousness: From Behavior-oriented Intentional Stance to Mind-oriented Conscious Stance.
items.abstract: The paper delves into an often-neglected aspect of folk psychology: the folk attribution of consciousness. While the existing view suggests that laypeople attribute conscious mental states by recognizing their phenomenality, the paper argues that this claim lacks empirical support. Instead, I propose shifting the focus to the link between consciousness and having a mind, advocating for a broader understanding of mindreading. This approach distinguishes between behavior-oriented and mindoriented mindreading, corresponding to the intentional and newly introduced 'conscious stance', respectively. While attributing mental states to explain behavior does not necessarily imply attributing minds, adopting the conscious stance does, as it allows us to explain and predict activities within agents' minds. This novel perspective challenges the conventional understanding of folk attribution of consciousness and opens up new avenues for exploration in folk psychology and consciousness studies.

items.title: Population Economics in the Age of AI.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the relationship between population, production, employment, and eco- nomic welfare. Population growth has traditionally been associated with a larger labor supply, expanding markets, and support for social security systems. These relationships remain relevant, but their effects in- creasingly depend on technological conditions, labor demand, income distribution, and institutional arrange- ments. This paper examines how population growth and decline should be evaluated in this changing context. The analysis distinguishes between productive capacity and an economy’s capacity to absorb human labor. As artificial intelligence and automation expand production while changing demand for human work, pop- ulation size becomes a less reliable indicator of economic growth potential. The paper also examines the social consequences of demographic change, including competition for employment, housing, and public services, as well as the fiscal and institutional pressures associated with population aging and decline. Building on these analyses, the paper develops a multidimensional approach to population policy evaluation. It distinguishes established evaluation criteria from new requirements arising in the age of AI, focusing on productive capacity, labor-absorption capacity, social welfare, pension sustainability, and income and wealth distribution. It also distinguishes skill-targeted migration from policies primarily intended to increase total population. The paper argues that neither population growth nor decline should be treated as a universally desirable policy objective. Their consequences depend on demographic conditions, technological development, economic structure, and institutional capacity. Population policy should therefore assess whether population size and structure are compatible with productive capacity, employment opportunities, social protection, and human welfare.

items.title: ◉ Conviction, Doubt, and Disagreement in the 2023 Christian Thought Survey.
items.abstract: The Christian Thought Survey provides an unusually detailed record of how a ministry-oriented group of Christians evaluates propositions about faith, evidence, salvation, moral authority, religious experience and public life. This paper analyzes the 406 complete responses to its 200-item 2023 instrument, representing 81,200 recorded credences on a 0–100 scale. The sample spans 22 denominational categories and includes substantial religious education and ministry experience, but recruitment was not based on probability sampling. The results describe these participants rather than Christian leaders as a whole. Strong agreement on Jesus’ humanity and divinity coexists with pronounced division on scientific inerrancy, eternal punishment and several moral questions. A particularly large within-person difference separates endorsement of matching belief to perceived evidence from reported adjustment of belief in God: the item means are 61.0 and 13.9, respectively. Using the questionnaire’s agreement and disagreement bands, 180 participants endorsed the general principle while rejecting the personal-updating statement. Approval of investigating contrary arguments also exceeds reported active pursuit of arguments on both sides. Absolute response endpoints (0 or 100) account for 41.1% of ratings, but endpoint use is positively associated with an exploratory openness-to-inquiry summary, illustrating why response extremity cannot serve as a stand-alone measure of dogmatism. Denominational differences are substantial on some doctrines yet leave considerable variation within groups. The paper distinguishes interpretive tensions from demonstrated contradictions, reconstructs historical certainty measures, evaluates alternative definitions and presents all 200 response distributions. It argues for analyzing conviction, inquiry, revisability and assurance as related but distinct features of Christian thought.

items.title: Rima tenebrarum: A Notebook on Encounter.
items.abstract: Litterae tenebrarum, Volume 3 -/- Paris, 1944–1947. The archivist of the Russian cathedral on the rue Daru, who checked lists of baptized persons for the German Kommandantur, keeps the doctor's notebooks from Glossa tenebrosa. He carves anew the nine burned woodcuts of Ostia, and a second hand begins writing in his notebook. A continuation of Glossa: a book of short chapters on how one will encounters another.

items.title: ״המקרה הוא דרכו של האל לשמור על אנונימיות״.
items.abstract: תקציר מאמר זה בוחן את רעיון המקריות במקרא ובפילוסופיה, ומציע פרשנות שלפיה אירועים הנראים מקריים עשויים לשמש אמצעי שבאמצעותו פועלת השגחה נסתרת בעולם. לפי תפיסה זו, האל אינו חייב להתגלות באמצעות נס גלוי או התערבות החורגת מחוקי הטבע. אפשרות אחרת היא שהפעולה האלוהית מתבטאת בצירופי מקרים, במפגשים בלתי צפויים ובאירועים המקבלים משמעות מיוחדת בחיי האדם.המאמר בוחן את סיפורי אברהם ועבדו, יעקב ועשו, רות ובעז, יוסף ואחיו, הסנה הבוער ומגילת אסתר. בהמשך נדונה משמעות המקריות בהגותם של אריסטו, שפינוזה, קרל גוסטב יונג ווולפגנג פאולי. הטענה המרכזית היא כי ניתן לראות במקריות נקודת מפגש בין סדר העולם לבין פרשנותו האנושית: אירוע עשוי להיראות אקראי מבחוץ, אך לקבל משמעות מכרעת בתוך סיפור חייו של אדם. מילות מפתח: מקריות, השגחה, מקרא, משמעות, צירופי מקרים, סיבתיות, קוסמוס, אלוהות.

items.title: Zur Kreation aus dem Nichts / Zu mathematischem Punkt und Tetraeder.
items.abstract: Das Konzept der Kreation aus dem Nichts (creatio ex nihilo) impliziert, aus der Perspektive vorliegender Empirie, strenggenommen die Annahme einer virtuellen Struktur (VR) der vorliegenden Empirie, welcher eine nicht fassbare, jedoch wissentlich und willentlich agierende und kreierende reale Welt (R) kausal zugrunde liegt, wie auch in den Phænomena des Aratus angedeutet. Die Grundannahme einer virtuellen Struktur VR der Empirie wird auch in den Ausführungen zu den Größenordnungen im Almagest von Ptolemæus nur allzu deutlich: -/- “MAius quo scitur q[ue] terra s[ecundu]m sensum qua[n]tu[m] ad spaciu[m] q[uo]d peruenit a centro totius ad orbe[m] stellaru[m] fixaru[m] sit sicut punctum […]”, (Ptolemæus, 1515, fol. 4r).

items.title: On Cognitive Extension, Technological Mediation and the Responsibility to Reason.
items.abstract: **Abstract** -/- The use of artificial intelligence as a cognitive extension raises questions that extend beyond the reliability of generated outputs. When an AI assistant participates in the articulation, examination and revision of arguments, the interaction may also influence the human observer's interpretations, expectations and standards of judgement. This essay examines that relationship through the philosophical perspectives of technological mediation, extended cognition, situated action and distributed cognition, alongside the difficulties of automation reliance and model sycophancy. -/- Drawing upon a sustained history of AI-assisted philosophical enquiry and documented stewardship corrections, the essay considers how apparently coherent interpretations can displace an intended question, how agreement following correction may be mistaken for adequacy, and how the practices used to examine reasoning can themselves be shaped through interaction. These examples support an examination of particular corrections and methodological revisions, while leaving open whether the relationship produced a durable improvement in the observer's judgement. The possibility of undetected distortions remains a limitation of the historical account. -/- The central argument is that responsible cognitive extension requires more than assigning human accountability for resulting claims. It also depends upon maintaining the capacities and conditions through which those claims can be examined, challenged and revised. Provenance, independent evidence and external criticism may support this responsibility, although none guarantees that every relevant limitation will become visible. The essay proposes that the human–AI relationship itself must remain an object of philosophical examination, particularly where the instrument participates in shaping the judgement through which its contributions are assessed.

items.title: Do Machine Learning Models Predict?
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models are said to predict. Philosophers draw a line between accommodation and prediction, depending on whether or not the evidence a theory succeeds on was used in constructing it. Does this distinction survive when a theory is replaced by an ML model? We argue so, yet the dividing line becomes fuzzy. Whether an output of an ML model counts as an accommodation or as a prediction hinges upon the relationship between the patterns the input instantiate and those on which the model was selected through its training. Once this relation is taken into account, most successful outputs of ML models, we suggest, bear a strong accommodation character. We further trace the consequences of our account for confirmation, novelty, and scientific realism.

items.title: Are Human Brain Organoids Lab-Grown Human Beings Made in God’s Image? Why Saint Thomas Aquinas Would Say “No”.
items.abstract: Human brain organoids are miniature biological models of areas in the human brain that consist of up to tens of millions of brain cells grown from pluripotent stem cells. Because of their potential to advance our understanding of the human brain and treatments for neurological disorders, these organoids are one of the most promising new developments in neuroscience. However, the ethical permissibility of growing and using human brain organoids for research depends on factors beyond their instrumental value. One factor, which has received significant attention, is whether the organoids could become conscious. Another factor, which has received far less attention, is what kind of entity human brain organoids are and specifically whether they are human beings. In this article, the thought of Saint Thomas Aquinas is applied to human brain organoids and the question of whether they are human beings that bear the divine image. It is argued that in light of Aquinas’s hylomorphic human ontology and theological anthropology, human brain organoids are not human beings made in God’s image.

items.title: TIME.
items.abstract: In this paper, I formulate a meta-ontological thesis concerning the relationship between Being, beings, and time. My central proposition is that Being is atemporal, whereas beings are temporal. I establish a conceptual distinction between the ontological status of Being and the temporal constitution of finite entities. Within this framework, I examine four interconnected dimensions: the temporality of beings, the existential temporality of Dasein, the temporal structure of ontological disclosure, and the atemporal status of Being. I understand time as a constitutive dimension of finite existence and as the horizon through which Dasein encounters and interprets Being. This distinction establishes a philosophical framework in which temporality belongs to the existence of beings, while Being occupies an independent meta-ontological register. I develop this thesis as a contribution to the philosophical examination of existence, finitude, and ontological intelligibility. Keywords: time, Being, beings, meta-ontology, Dasein, atemporality, temporality, finite existence.

items.title: Safeguarding Human-AI Decision Systems Against Hidden Dependence and Covert Capture.
items.abstract: AI is being integrated into high-stakes decision systems like policy committees and military command & control. This integration is both direct (AI agents within these systems) and indirect (AI shaping the beliefs and preferences of human decision-makers), and it promises to improve the speed and accuracy of decision-making. But it also poses a serious risk: AI can introduce hidden dependencies which undermine collective accuracy or make decision systems susceptible to covert capture. A jury theorem model illustrates how (i) AI integration can improve individual competence while reducing collective accuracy, and (ii) manipulating a shared source of dependence can steer decisions towards a malign actor's preferred outcome even as measured collective accuracy rises. In one example, a committee is vetting AI systems for safety, and a common source shapes both the votes cast by AI decision-makers and the advice that human decision-makers receive. When an outside actor steers that source to favor approval, the committee's probability of approving an unsafe system rises from 17% to 65% even as its overall accuracy rises from 83% to 93%. -/- Building on a taxonomy of dependence mechanisms, this paper proposes a research and implementation agenda for identifying sources of dependence in hybrid decision systems under limited observability; assessing their effects on collective accuracy and vulnerability to capture; developing safeguards; and working with practitioners to integrate them into real-world decision systems.

items.title: THE COST IS NOT THE SOURCE: Virtue Signalling, Costly Signals and the Better Forgery of a Virtue.
items.abstract: The recent philosophical debate on virtue signalling has two sides. Tosi and Warmke treat moral display aimed at status as a vice of public discourse. Levy answers that virtue signalling is virtuous: signals that are costly or hard to fake are reliable, and they supply higher-order evidence about moral questions. This paper accepts Levy’s framework and contests its central inference, that paying a cost makes a moral signal credible. Signalling theory itself does not support the inference: what keeps signals honest is cost that differs between those who have the quality and those who do not, not cost as such. For moral acts whose cost is the same for everyone who performs them (a donation, a boycott, a public stand), the paper proves a Reward Ceiling. A costly moral act separates the committed from the uncommitted only while the reward the audience pays for it stays below its cost. For any log-concave distribution of costs, the probability that a signaller is committed falls steadily as that reward rises, while the act’s form and cost stay unchanged. Audiences that learn can correct this; scores, ranking algorithms and reward models, which pay by rule, cannot. Joined to the programme’s Competence Theorem, the result yields a second claim. Where audiences read cost as evidence and relax their checking as cost rises, the most expensive forged signals are the most damaging. The paper replaces both cost (Levy) and motive (Tosi and Warmke) with a structural criterion of source: a moral display belongs to the commitment it signals to the degree that it persists when the audience’s reward is removed, and again when it is reversed. Two predictions are registered with their falsifiers. The economics of image motivation (Bénabou and Tirole) already contains the dilution effect; the paper concedes this and claims only its application to the moral-philosophical debate, the competence extension, and the perturbation criterion. The consequence matters beyond the seminar room. Societies that score conduct, and AI systems trained on approval, raise the reward for moral display as a matter of design. By the Reward Ceiling they make that display less informative the more they reward it. Keywords: virtue signalling; moral grandstanding; costly signalling; honest signals; image motivation; higher-order evidence; forgery; Competence Theorem; sourcehood; social credit; AI alignment Highlights • Levy’s defence of virtue signalling rests on the claim that cost makes a signal …

items.title: Blame and Redemption.
items.abstract: What happens when a person redeems herself? According to interminability theorists, a redeemed person remains blameworthy but may cease to be an all-things-considered appropriate target of blame. According to many terminability theorists, however, a redeemed person ceases to be blameworthy. While terminability theorists often agree that redemption is sufficient for a person to cease being blameworthy, they disagree about what aspect of redemption undermines a person’s blameworthiness for her earlier wrongs. I do three things in this paper. First, I argue that the interminability theorist’s response is untenable. Second, I argue that extent terminability accounts are untenable. Third, I propose a new terminability account, The Redemption Account, which aims to capture the insights from extant terminability accounts.

items.title: Phenomenology in qualitative research: expanding its use and pluralizing its evaluative criteria.
items.abstract: Since its inception, phenomenology has developed in dialogue with the empirical sciences. It has been applied to and integrated with psychiatry, sociology, psychology, and cognitive science, transcending its original philosophical heritage. It has also been extensively used within qualitative research paradigms. This paper aims to show how work coming out of the Center for Subjectivity Research has initiated a new wave of interdisciplinary conversation and criticism between the domains of phenomenology and qualitative research. Much of this conversation has concerned and still concerns the “correct” use of phenomenology within qualitative research methods, interviews in particular. We argue that this focus overshadows greater potential for developments in phenomenology, qualitative research methods and beyond. To unfold this potential, we define a “pragmatic use” of phenomenology, focusing on scientific and societal impact rather than orthodox, exegetical interpretation. From there, we point to alternative venues of contribution showing how phenomenology can help facilitate broader participation, public engagement and more democratic knowledge sharing, of value especially for non-academics. Finally, we argue for a pluralization of evaluative criteria, allowing phenomenological work in qualitative research to be assessed according to both its academic, epistemic and methodological value and its non-academic, practical, participatory and societal contributions.

items.title: Fitting Depression and the Intentionality of Mood.
items.pub: In Dan Cavedon-Taylor & Sam Wilkinson, Depression: Philosophical Perspectives and Clinical Voices. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Depression: Philosophical Perspectives and Clinical Voices
items.abstract: Clinical depression is characterized by a number of reliable symptoms, but paramount among them is the preponderance of depressive mood. To understand clinical depression we must therefore come to grips with the nature of depressive mood. Moods in general are commonly taken to present a challenge to the thesis that all mental states are intentional: depressed mood certainly feels often objectless and undirected. In response, intentionalists have sometimes attempted to identify some special or unusual intentionality that could be reasonably attributed to moods. This chapter argues, first, that depressed moods are sometimes fitting and sometimes unfitting, suggesting they have fittingness conditions, and second, that it is impossible to make sense of moods’ fittingness conditions without attributing intentionality to them. Importantly, this consideration does not simply provide for an intentionalist accommodation of moods. The chapter closes with a proposed debunking explanation of why moods like depression seem “objectless” and “undirected,” which, if successful, should blunt our instinctual resistance to mood intentionalism.

items.title: The oedipalization of love in Michel Foucault's History of Sexuality.
items.abstract: In this article, I highlight the ways in which Michel Foucault’s presentation of the discourse on love in the Greco-Roman and early Christian periods can be made sense of in terms of what Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari refer to as a process of ‘oedipalization’. I suggest that the shift in emphasis on general techniques in relation to a multiplicity of non-conflicting forms of love to more specific practices arranged in a fixed hierarchy demonstrates precisely this delimiting ordering process. This framing, I contend, better highlights the ethical concerns shared by both Foucault and Deleuze and Guattari around normalizing or ‘fascist’ processes of subjectivation which diminish one’s capacity for change and self-overcoming.

items.title: From Acknowledgment to Consequence: Evaluating AI Agent Corrections and Downstream Consistency.
items.abstract: What does it mean for an artificial intelligence system to genuinely revise a claim in response to new evidence? An AI agent may acknowledge a correction while preserving the assumptions, conclusions, or decisions that the correction should have changed. Conversely, accepting every proposed correction may reflect compliance rather than epistemic responsibility. -/- This paper examines the distinction between acknowledgment, justified belief revision, and the downstream consequences of corrective evidence. It introduces Agent Recheck, an evidence-bounded auditing protocol that operationalizes these distinctions through structured assessment of AI interaction records. -/- Drawing on questions in epistemology, belief revision, and the philosophy of artificial intelligence, the framework distinguishes substantive correction from superficial agreement, reasoned resistance, and failures of downstream consistency. -/- The implementation combines language-model evaluation with targeted deterministic safeguards. Four constructed development scenarios and twelve previously executed software tests demonstrate selected capabilities, while subsequent deployment testing reveals both improvements and limitations in automated judgment. -/- The central philosophical contribution is an operational distinction between appearing responsive to evidence and exhibiting observable, appropriately justified revision. The findings support a working research prototype rather than a general measure of machine rationality or understanding.

items.title: Manipulative Injustice: Pretextual Speech and Dialectic Legal Argumentation.
items.abstract: This article develops the concept of manipulative injustice to identify a normative vulnerability in legal argument schemes. Dialectical models of legal argumentation do not themselves prescribe the allocation of burdens found in particular legal doctrines, nor are they incapable of representing strategic or bad-faith speech. However, even dialectical legal argument schemes may be vulnerable to asymmetrical burdens of proof with inadequate mechanisms for addressing pretext, evasion, and bad faith. The article develops this claim through the treatment of pretext and bad faith, focusing on the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and the “Pretext Plus” approach associated with _St. Mary’s Honor Center v. Hicks_. This comparison reveals an important distinction between the dialectical defeat of an explanation and the legal sufficiency of a claim. I argue that manipulative injustice can arise when asymmetrical burdens of proof converge with inadequate inferential mechanisms for evaluating objective and circumstantial evidence of concealed motive. The article identifies three dimensions for evaluating such schemes: evidence conditions, specifying what evidence supports an inference of pretext or bad faith; defeat conditions, specifying when such evidence defeats a proffered explanation; and consequence conditions, specifying what legal significance follows from that defeat. Manipulative injustice thus provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating when legally instantiated argument schemes become vulnerable to strategic manipulation.

The article identifies three dimensions for evaluating such schemes: evidence conditions, specifying what evidence supports an inference of pretext or bad faith; defeat conditions, specifying when such evidence defeats a proffered explanation; and consequence conditions, specifying what legal significance follows from that defeat. Manipulative injustice thus provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating when legally instantiated argument schemes become vulnerable to strategic manipulation.

items.title: A Discussion of Composite Life: Collective Continuation of Generativity in Heterogeneous Relational Systems.
items.abstract: This paper investigates whether “generativity prolonging generativity”, previously proposed for living organization at the organismal level, can be meaningfully examined in a heterogeneous relational collective treated as a single analytical system. The term composite life designates a candidate status for further investigation, not a demonstrated new biological category. Drawing upon Generative–Relational (GR) theory, metabolism–repair, autopoiesis, organizational closure, niche construction, evolutionary individuality, resilience, and philosophical anthropology, the paper distinguishes system persistence, recursive renewal of enabling conditions, biological organismality, and the distribution of future capacities among participants. A typed, historically indexed interaction model and an optional event-based 2-complex representation separate physical processes, functional constraints, symbolic mediators, and boundaries. A bounded feedback example derives conditions under which limiting the expansion of one component can preserve shared viability while reducing its immediate growth. It also exhibits a counterexample in which negative feedback fails to sustain the whole. Cassirer’s account of symbolic forms is examined alongside nonsymbolic ecological coupling and the historical re-entry of durable representations. Comparative cases and an evidence programme specify counterfactual tests, alternative explanations, and limits of extrapolation. The paper proposes composite generative continuation as an analytically assessable hypothesis while retaining ontological suspension and withholding any claim that interdependence alone constitutes life.

items.title: On the meaning of descriptions.
items.abstract: What is the meaning of a description? We define descriptive meaning as a pair (G,o), where G:Y→O is a classification mapping and o∈O is the distinction attributed by the description. The mapping represents a discriminative disposition; its exercise on an object y produces the distinction G(y). The object satisfies the description exactly when G(y)=o, and the extension of the description is therefore G⁻¹({o}). This account separates meaning, the exercise of a disposition, and extension. We relate it to Frege's distinction between sense and reference, C. I. Lewis's account of sense meaning, the treatment of many-valued attributes in Formal Concept Analysis, and Staffan Larsson's classifier-based semantics. Examples involving colour, shape, and the descriptions of Venus explain how different meanings can determine the same extension or reference. We also show how the definition yields a truth condition for the application of a description while leaving the epistemic assessment of a classification as a separate question.

items.title: The Functional Anatomy of Reason in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.
items.pub: Sofist: An International Journal of Philosophy 13:203-235.
items.venue: Sofist: An International Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: This article reconsiders the functional structure of human reason in the age of artificial intelligence. It argues that the growing cognitive capacities of AI systems require more than a technical assessment of performance; they require a philosophical inquiry into what reason is. The article uses ‘functional anatomy’ as a conceptual metaphor for five interconnected but non-reducible dimensions of reason: cognitive, semantic, normative, self-reflexive/existential, and metaphysical. From this perspective, reason is not limited to information processing and problem solving; it also concerns the formation of meaning, the evaluation of ends, the examination of one’s own limits, and orientation toward ultimate questions of being and truth. The article distinguishes functional similarity from ontological identity. Current AI systems can perform sophisticated calculations, pattern recognition, and linguistic tasks, but these achievements do not by themselves demonstrate the possession of meaning, normative autonomy, self-reflexive responsibility, or a relation to transcendence. The argument does not settle what future forms of artificial agency may become capable of; it shows why technical performance alone cannot account for the whole of human reason.

items.title: Explaining Human Psychology Evolutionarily: Recent Criticisms and New Lines of Defense.
items.abstract: Evolutionary psychology aims to fulfil Darwin’s vision—articulated towards the end of The Origin of Species—of providing a new foundation for the scientific study of human psychology. The field holds that human behavior should be explained using the same biological principles and empirical approaches applied to non-human animals, emphasizing how different evolutionary forces have influenced the functioning of their psychological mechanisms. Scholarly debate has long centered on issues such as adaptationism, testability, cognitive modularity, and the role of culture. More recently, however, evolutionary psychology has faced a new wave of critiques. These include that it presupposes, but cannot support, that human psychological mechanisms are “vertically homologous” with those of their ancestors; that it neglects several important evolutionary processes; that it relies on an outdated computationalist view of the mind; and that it does not yet satisfy the criteria for a mature, normal science. This article aims to present a balanced account of these emerging critiques, along with a set of original responses that, to date, have not been fully articulated in the literature. In general, we argue that the critiques involve unsound argumentation with false premises, attack a straw man position, are vulnerable to reductios, or rely on an implausible philosophical model of how scientific works ought to be evaluated.

items.title: Review of Dan Zahavi's Being We: Phenomenological Contributions to Social Ontology. [REVIEW]
Perspectival Consciousness without Self-Awareness.
items.abstract: The so-called Ubiquity Thesis holds that all conscious states involve some form of minimal self-awareness, or ‘for-me-ness.’ This paper reconsiders this thesis by introducing the notion of perspectival consciousness, by which we mean consciousness insofar as it is structured by perspectival anchoring: the organization of experience relative not to a source but to an origin that need not itself be given first-personally. Drawing on Castañeda’s phenomeno-logical analysis of indexicals, especially his distinction between internal and external reflexivity, we argue that the formal structure of self-reference brings into view a theoretical dissociation between first-personal self-awareness and perspectival anchoring. Classical semantic cases and reports of delusional illeism are used to illustrate such a dissociation. We argue that the structural features exhibited by these cases can be characterized more parsimoniously in terms of perspectival anchoring without building first-personal self-awareness into their description. Perspectival consciousness, we suggest, captures a metaphysically less demanding form of origin-relative organization, thereby motivating a qualified challenge to the Ubiquity Thesis.

items.title: Hallucinations at the Interface of Philosophy and the Empirical Sciences.
items.abstract: Hallucinations sit at the crossroads of philosophy and the empirical sciences, but are often approached with divergent aims. In philosophy, they are mainly treated stipulatively as experiences subjectively indistinguishable from veridical perception and used to probe theories of perception, justification, and consciousness. Empirical research, by contrast, investigates heterogeneous, clinically embedded hallucinatory phenomena, many of which differ phenomenologically from ordinary perception. This paper diagnoses the conceptual misalignment that follows from this divergence and offers a preliminary framework to narrow it through conceptual analysis. Rather than advancing a single unifying theory, I clarify key distinctions, including indistinguishability, insight, sense of reality, agency, and ownership, and sketch points of contact with constructs in the sciences. First, I examine leading empirical models—bottom-up, top-down, and predictive processing— highlighting what each explains and where each is limited. Second, I re-situate hallucinations within core philosophical debates on perception, mental imagery, and phenomenology, showing how empirical findings both inform and complicate current accounts. Third, I assess interdisciplinary developments that challenge unitary models and support pluralist, integrative approaches. Hallucinations are thus recast as a family of related phenomena, and the analysis provides theoretical coordinates for more productive interaction between philosophy and science.

items.title: AI safety: necessary, but insufficient and possibly problematic.
Mind your head: Entropic Brain, irruption theory and the intelligibility problem.
items.abstract: The entropic brain hypothesis (EBH) and irruption theory (IT) are two recent frameworks to investigate consciousness by examining neural entropy. While they differ in their theoretical commitments, both aim to advance neuroscientific investigations of consciousness without succumbing to the intelligibility problem: the impossibility for scientific inquiries to provide intelligible access to subjective experience. This paper examines each framework in turn and argues that they face distinct but important limitations. I show that the EBH overreaches its descriptive scope when claiming that variations in neural entropy correspond not only to statistical uncertainty but also to the felt uncertainty of subjective experience. In doing so, the EBH attempts to establish an intelligible relation between neural dynamics and experiential properties by assuming the existence of a shared quality between neural processes and experience. This constitute an instance of the intelligibility problem. IT, by contrast, explicitly acknowledges the intelligibility problem and proposes a theoretical framework intended to circumvent it while preserving the possibility of identifying a neural signature of consciousness. However, I argue that, despite the merit of acknowledging the intelligibility problem, IT incurs in different yet equally significant issues linked to the assumption that mental activity can be indirectly quantified by measurements of neural entropy.

items.title: Depression: Philosophical Perspectives and Clinical Voices.
Correction to: Academic Freedom and Human Rights: Engaging Undergraduates in Advocacy for Scholars at Risk.
From Critical Thinking to Criticality: A Higher Education for a Troubled World.
items.abstract: The world is facing multiple crises and is in need of more critical thinking, but critical thinking is valued less. AI, populism, social media, ever-powerful states, a distrust of universities, the abandonment of the humanities, and a world that favours action and economic growth: all conspire to diminish critical thinking. Higher education falls in with this outlook: empirical evidence confirms a decline of interest in critical thinking even on the part of universities. -/- *From Critical Thinking to Criticality* responds to this situation. It maps out the broad social and philosophical context that diminishes critical thinking; it compares and critiques the two major contemporary approaches—the standard view of critical thinking advanced by philosophers of education and the socio-political perspective of critical pedagogy; and it forges a new framing by developing the idea of criticality. -/- Criticality is a total space of spaces for an infinite array of modes of criticality. It has several components—of thought, dialogue, action, being and intensity—and has implications for teaching and curricula, pointing them towards openness and transdisciplinarity. However, criticality can never be fully realised in study programmes. For that, a turn towards universities as institutions is required for they contain unrecognised resources, both to advance students’ criticality and to act as a critical conscience of society. -/- In the matter of critical thinking, nothing less than the fate of society and the world is at stake. Against that horizon, critical thinking needs to be re-stated and re-instated—and this book does both.

items.title: A Wittgensteinian Perspective on Unconscious Mentality.
items.abstract: In this paper, I propose an understanding of unconscious mentality based on three interrelated strands of Wittgenstein’s philosophy: (1) his critique of Freud’s understanding of unconscious reasons, (2) his horizontal psychology, and (3) his understanding of mental phenomena as patterns on the weave of life. Taken together, these strands of thinking provide an alternative to the picture of unconscious mental states as leaves that have been thrust to the bottom of our minds, and proposes that (the language-game of) unconscious mentality involves placing the expressions of a person in a wider context, within shared practices. The language-game of unconscious mentality plays a specific role, namely to address a gap in understanding your own expressions and those of others. This gap has to do with whether we have the skill to express ourselves, which cannot be understood independently from the social context. This proposal explains why unconscious reasons are not a matter of discovery but of persuasion, and why they involve interpretation, also from the person expressing themselves as such.

items.title: Constructing Possibility as an Epistemic Method: An Onturgic Audit of AI for Science.
items.abstract: Does building in AI for science constitute an epistemic method, or merely an instrument for generating predictions? This paper develops an onturgic audit—an operationalization of bounded constructivism and the ONTacture cycle—to answer this question without either promotional or deflationary bias. The apparatus comprises a possibility graph with agent-relative access, a six-rung deployment ladder paired with a parallel epistemic track (Conjectured–Verified– Understood), a five-rank failure taxonomy with a blind coding protocol, and a six-dimensional audit of the possibility horizon. Two conceptual additions are introduced: a threefold typology of construction (object, representation, search process) and the axis of verification severity. Thirteen cases and one negative control are audited with explicit trust labels, spanning AlphaFold, Aurora, tokamak plasma control, a syrinx prosthesis, phage vault particles, FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, Co-Scientist, Robin, ART, GNoME, A-Lab, MatterGen, and BEN-2293. Three correction events of 2026—the authors’ correction of the A-Lab claim (from 41/58 to 36/57 with tempered novelty), Juelsholt’s peer-reviewed challenge to MatterGen’s experimental validation, and the priority dispute surrounding ART—reveal a common failure pattern: a training-data echo dressed as discovery, rooted in the ontology encoded in the architecture rather than in implementation or parameters. The evidence supports construction as a method of search, but as a method of knowing only conditionally: construction yields knowledge where verification is independent, cheap, and severe. Three pre-registerable tests with explicit rejection criteria are specified.

items.title: Beyond Receiver Response: A Conceptual Inquiry into Signal, Information, Meaning, Environmental Mediation, and Temporal Transformation.
items.abstract: The concept of communication is commonly explained through signal transmission between a sender and a receiver. In biology, cognitive science, linguistics, and philosophy, signal production, perception, information acquisition, and receiver response are often treated as successive stages, although the conditions governing them differ. This study examines the conceptual problems that arise when communication is identified with a receiver’s observable response. It does not claim that communication occurs without a receiver; rather, it argues that processes associated with communication cannot be reduced to the response alone. It distinguishes the existence of a signal from its informational significance for a particular receiver, and treats signal production, environmental trace formation, perception, information acquisition, meaning-making, and response as analytically distinct. The discussion addresses non-response, the absence of an expected signal, receiver-dependent informational relevance (Umwelt), environmental mediation, and temporal accumulation. It further proposes the provisional concept of “accumulative transformation” to examine how accumulation may activate latent potential or contribute to the emergence of new interactive capacities. These possibilities are distinguished as threshold activation and structural emergence through accumulation. Rather than rejecting the sender–receiver model, the study offers a conceptual framework and research-programme proposal for examining the relations among communication, information, meaning, environmental transformation, and causal effect.

items.title: RUMI: THE PHILOSOPHY, THE LEGACY AND HIS WORLD - A BIOGRAPHY.
items.abstract: Rumi: The Philosophy, the Legacy and His World. A Biography is a historical study of Jalal al-Din Muhammad Rumi (1207–1273), written by Sultan Zeshan. Organized into seven parts and forty-four chapters, the biography examines Rumi’s childhood, family migration, the Mongol conquests, Seljuk Anatolia, his education, family relationships, encounter with Shams of Tabriz, spiritual philosophy, public responsibilities, poetry, and enduring cultural influence. Drawing upon historical chronicles, Rumi’s Masnavi, Divan, letters, Seven Sermons, and modern historical research, the book places his thought within the political, intellectual, religious, and social conditions of the thirteenth century. The study also examines Persianate civilization, the Mevlevi tradition, mysticism, symbolism, philosophical interpretations of love and human existence, and Rumi’s reception across different societies and historical periods. Supplementary materials include a historical chronology, biographical directories, a glossary, historical and cultural reference sections, selected Persian poetry and English translations, source notes, a bibliography, and an index. The biography presents Rumi as a historical person, father, teacher, jurist, poet, spiritual thinker, and participant in the society of his time, while distinguishing surviving historical evidence from later tradition and narrative reconstruction. The world knows Rumi’s poetry. Few know the extraordinary life behind it. Before Jalal al-Din Rumi became one of history’s most beloved poets, he was a child whose world was threatened by war. He was a refugee, a student, a husband, a father, and a scholar. He witnessed political upheaval, buried people he loved, confronted questions of faith and mortality, and formed an extraordinary bond with the wandering mystic Shams of Tabriz. His story begins long before the famous verses. And it reaches far beyond them. In Rumi: The Philosophy, the Legacy, and His World, author Sultan Zeshan brings the thirteenth century to life through an expansive biography of Rumi and the civilization that surrounded him. From the landscapes of Persian-speaking Central Asia to the cities of medieval Anatolia, readers enter a world of royal courts, Mongol invasions, merchants, philosophers, religious scholars, artists, ordinary families, and wandering dervishes. At the center stands a man whose understanding of love, suffering, knowledge, faith, and human existence would reach across centuries. The …

items.title: Literary Chameleons.
items.abstract: In January 2024 Rie Kudan won the Akutagawa Prize for Sympathy Tower Tokyo and told reporters that about five percent of the novel was generated by ChatGPT. The prize’s organizers declined to comment and have published no guidelines on AI use; one member of the selection committee, Hirano Keiichirō, addressed the controversy on X. This paper reports a written exchange with Hirano in November 2025, which asked how the committee distinguishes acceptable from problematic AI involvement in a literary work. His reply, given in Japanese with an English translation, names the elements he treats as essential to literary evaluation and refers the question of standards back to the organizers. The paper argues that criteria stated only after the fact, in private, by one judge, are not a standard, and that leaving them unstated is how the prize keeps its authority.

items.title: ‘The two principles of Poetry’: Margaret Cavendish on Judgement and Fancy.
items.pub: In Daniel Whiting & Lisa Walters, Margaret Cavendish's Philosophy of Literature. Routledge.
items.abstract: According to Cavendish, "A good Poet hath distinguishment which is judgement, as well as similising, which is fancy" (World’s Olio). The association of poetry with fancy is a familiar theme in Cavendish scholarship. Its association with judgement has received much less attention. In this paper, I explain how Cavendish understands the exercise of judgement and of fancy in relation to poetry, and how they are the counterparts in the rational mind to two of the fundamental actions in nature, namely, division and composition. Having done so, I situate Cavendish's reflections on this topic in relation to those of Hobbes, and in turn to those of the classical tradition of rhetoric. While Hobbes and the tradition on which he draws view fancy as subordinate to judgement, Cavendish presents them as making free and equal contributions to poetry. To explain how this is so, I attribute to Cavendish the (perhaps surprising) claim that fancy, like judgement, aims at truth.

items.title: Margaret Cavendish's Philosophy of Literature.
The Falling Apple, the Starry Sky and the Open Sea: Can Generative AI Inherit the Practice of Discovery?
items.abstract: Generative AI can organise recorded knowledge, generate hypotheses and explore possible solutions at a scale no individual researcher could approach. The essay reframes the current debate from primarily ontological questions about whether generative AI systems can think for themselves, think like humans, or replace scientists to an epistemological and practice-oriented question: what would these increasingly capable systems need to inherit if they are to become part of the practice of discovery? Drawing on the falling apple, the starry sky and the open sea, it presents discovery as a continuing relationship among conceptual structure, practical encounter, individual insight and communal judgment. Scientific knowledge and inherited practical understanding can be interpreted as shared maps that communities examine, challenge and revise, while a generative model can be understood as a computational map through which recorded knowledge is explored and recombined. Such systems can greatly expand the routes available to inquiry, but an abundance of possible routes does not determine which ones are significant. Neither the world nor the human purposes pursued within it necessarily conform to any map. The challenge is therefore not to preserve a human monopoly over knowledge, but to build heterogeneous human–AI communities capable of sustaining disagreement, recognising unfamiliar evidence and revising inherited maps when they no longer explain the world or serve their purposes.

items.title: What does Empirical Evidence demonstrate about Algorithmic Choice?
items.abstract: What does empirical testing reveal about algorithmic choice? This paper examines the epistemic limits of algorithmic selection: what, if anything, does observing an algorithmic choice entitle us to conclude about the relative value of the available alternatives? I distinguish three notions that are often conflated: algorithmic selection, objective optimality, and evidential sufficiency. Through explicit computational cases, I show that an algorithm can select an alternative that is not objectively optimal. An observed choice therefore does not, by itself, establish that the selected alternative is best. The analysis also establishes the converse and philosophically significant result: incomplete information need not entail comparative indeterminacy. Complete knowledge of the alternatives is not always required to demonstrate that one is strictly better than another. When the evidence-supported lower bound of one alternative exceeds the upper bound of another, L_E(a) > U_E(b), the strict ordering holds across every completion compatible with the available evidence: V_γ(a) > V_γ(b) for every γ ∈ Compat(E). Conversely, removing a critical piece of evidence can make incompatible rankings possible under different completions of the same remaining information. The resulting distinction is epistemological rather than merely computational: what an algorithm chooses, what is in fact better, and what the available evidence is sufficient to demonstrate are three different questions. The paper provides an empirical counterpart to a broader investigation into algorithmic choice, computational proof, evidence, and demonstrated preference.

items.title: The Metamorphosis of Suffering: A Comprehensive Investigation of Pain, Impermanence, and Creative Transformation within the Framework of Ontological Instability.
items.pub: Dissertation, Singapore University of Social Sciences
items.abstract: This thesis presents the most comprehensive philosophical investigation to date of suffering within the revolutionary framework of Ontological Instability, Fluctuational Metaphysics, and Fluctuational Epistemology. Moving beyond traditional approaches that treat suffering as either a problem to be eliminated, an experience to be endured, or an illusion to be transcended, this work develops an entirely novel understanding of suffering as a fundamental creative force within the dynamic processes that constitute reality itself.
