Through rigorous theoretical analysis, mathematical modeling, and phenomenological investigation, the thesis demonstrates that suffering emerges from and contributes to the ontological instability that characterizes all being, revealing previously unrecognized creative potentials that transcend conventional philosophical and therapeutic approaches. -/- The investigation establishes five revolutionary theoretical innovations: Fluctuational Suffering Dynamics, which reconceptualizes suffering as dynamic processes of experiential transformation; Relational Constitution of Suffering, which reveals suffering as fundamentally relational phenomena emerging from networks of interconnected processes; Temporal Multiplicity of Suffering, which demonstrates how suffering exists simultaneously across multiple temporal scales; Creative Potential of Suffering, which shows how suffering serves as a generative force for new possibilities; and Fluctuational Ethics, which provides practical frameworks for working creatively with rather than against the instability that generates both suffering and transformation. -/- Through comprehensive analysis of Buddhist impermanence doctrine, Whiteheadian process philosophy, phenomenological investigations, and contemporary pain studies, the thesis develops mathematical models that quantify the scalar and vectorial dimensions of suffering while preserving its qualitative richness. The work demonstrates how the three mechanisms of Ontological Instability—the Stabilization Paradox, Temporal Contradiction, and Relational Undermining—dissolve traditional approaches to suffering while opening unprecedented possibilities for understanding and engaging with the fundamental creativity of existence. -/- The practical implications extend across therapeutic practice, social policy, educational approaches, and cultural transformation, offering concrete methods for cultivating creative responses to suffering that honor both …

items.title: The Question of Violence and False-Negative Autism Diagnosis: Open Letter on Humboldt University's Co-Responsibility for Violence Against Neurodivergent People.
items.abstract: The present open letter to Prof. Dr. Isabel Dziobek, Director of the Specialist Outpatient Clinic for Social Interaction at Humboldt University of Berlin, is published as a historical document and as part of an ongoing investigation into institutional violence against neurodivergent people. It is situated within the context of three preceding research papers (Speed, 2026), which examine the exclusion of autistic people from diagnostic and social welfare recognition procedures, the epistemic limitations of autism diagnostics, and the health-related and existential consequences of institutional misjudgments through a longitudinally documented individual case. -/- Methodologically, the letter is situated within Provoked Empiricism. Its publication serves not merely to document a conflict retrospectively but constitutes part of the investigative process itself. By explicitly confronting a responsible institution with documented contradictions, scientific objections, and the consequences of its actions, institutional responses, justifications, refusals, and forms of silence become accessible as empirically observable phenomena. The intervention thereby changes the situation under investigation while simultaneously generating new possibilities for its analysis. In this sense, the open letter is not merely a statement about the object of research but a documented intervention into it. -/- At its centre lies the question of what responsibility diagnostic institutions bear for false-negative autism diagnoses and their potential consequences, particularly when the procedures employed are insufficiently capable of identifying certain manifestations of autism. The investigation addresses the tension between professionally asserted diagnostic certainty, scientifically recognised methodological fallibility, and the epistemic authority of neurodivergent self-report. Particular attention is given to how diagnostically excluded individuals may disappear from institutional bodies of knowledge and why the actual number of false-negative decisions may consequently remain unknown. -/- The letter combines personal testimony, scientific critique, and political accusation. Its deliberately confrontational language forms part of its methodological approach: it renders visible the affective, bodily, and existential dimensions of institutional violence that are frequently excluded from administrative and clinical accounts. The evaluations and accusations contained within the letter …

items.title: Correction-Compatible Trust and AI Companions.
items.abstract: An AI companion may retract a statement it wrongly attributed to a user. The retraction corrects the answer, but does not establish whether that correction can guide later attributions. Even before a breach occurs, a user can have reason to entrust work to a fallible companion when there are grounds to expect that recognition of a breach could lead to an effective revision of the terms of continued cooperation. When those grounds concern how the companion itself handles warranted corrections, they can also support trust in the companion in that matter. The paper reconstructs three connected capacities that make such revision possible: a breach of an expectation or commitment can be identified as such (recognizability); its recognition can change the terms of continued cooperation (uptake); and the resulting change can govern later decisions when those terms apply (retention). Their connection through a practically available route within the relation constitutes a shared corrective space. After a false attribution, for example, the user may continue to entrust drafting to the companion while requiring the user's approval before quotations are included in subsequent work. If an aim of alignment is to preserve the user's authority over how entrusted material is used, evaluation must establish both whether recognition of a breach can give effect to revised terms and whether those terms can govern the relevant later decision. Stable interaction can coexist with the absence of such a route.

items.title: Dolor.
items.pub: Enciclopedia de la Sociedad Española de Filosofía Analítica.
items.abstract: **Abstract** -/- This encyclopedia entry examines the philosophical nature of pain through three central problems: its epistemological status, its metaphysical constitution, and its motivational character. Drawing on phantom limb pain, pain asymbolia, and masochism, it discusses representationalist theories, evaluativism, imperativism, and desire-based accounts of unpleasantness. It explores how pain can misrepresent bodily states, whether pain is necessarily unpleasant, and why we sometimes desire experiences that hurt. The entry offers a critical overview of contemporary analytic philosophy of pain, emphasizing the relationships between perception, affect, motivation, and normativity.

items.title: Pseudo-Language as an Audio Writing System: When L2 Carries L1 Meaning.
items.abstract: This paper argues that successful communication in a second language does not always indicate possession of that language as a natural linguistic system. Building on Searle's Chinese Room, I introduce a real-world analogue: some late L2 learners communicate in L2 by relying entirely on L1 meanings. In these cases, the symbols and sounds of L2 function only as the external body of L1 meaning. This structure is called pseudo-language. Pseudo-language is not a new language but an audio writing system added to the speaker's natural language, where L2 symbols acquire meaning solely through fixed L1 equivalents. This framework explains why many late L2 learners report that their L2 feels artificial, distant, or not truly theirs. By examining this thought experiment, I show that pseudo-language is an actual cognitive state. This perspective forces us to rethink what it really means to 'understand' a language.

items.title: “Creeping unease” and “unspoken terrors”: on the epistemic value of quiet horror.
items.abstract: This article critically assesses Shirley Jackson’s fiction to argue that quiet horror has epistemic value, despite its focus on suggestion, the uncanny, and the unknown. To reach this conclusion, section one begins by clarifying what quiet horror is, justifying the focus on Shirley Jackson, and explaining how the three stories that will be used as case studies are representative of Jackson’s oeuvre. Section two argues that fiction is a potential source of understanding and outlines three epistemic values that have been linked to speculative and horror fiction: the immersive thought experiment value (2.1), the existential explanation value (2.2) and the mirrored understanding value (2.3). I argue that these values are shown in Jackson’s “The Lottery,” “The Tooth” and “The Daemon Lover” respectively. Section three considers two objections: that Jackson’s quiet horror can generate no new understanding (3.1) or only limited understanding (3.2). I argue that both objections fail and that Jackson’s stories can generate a notable degree of understanding.

items.title: Epistemic feelings and the psychological foundations of force dynamics: A case study in the psychoaffective theory of image schemas⋆.
items.pub: Proceedings of the Joint Ontology Workshops (Jowo) - Episode Xi: The Sicilian Summer Under the Etna, and Satellite Events Co-Located with the 15Th International Conference on Formal Ontology in Information Systems (Fois 2025), September 8-9, 2025, Catania, Italy.
items.abstract: The present article is a case study in the “psychoaffective” theory of image schemas, in which I explore the link between force schemas and epistemic feelings. My paper is divided into six main parts. First, I expound the psychoaffective approach to semantics and explain why epistemic feelings are good candidates to act as the psychological basis of image-schematic structures. Second, I offer a few words on the research program on force dynamics and the related concept of FORCE schema. Third, I critically discuss the research program in question, showing that it suffers from severe epistemological shortcomings. Fourth, I highlight the problems inherent in the typological analysis of FORCE schemas as it prevails in the literature. Fifth, I review the rich psychological and philosophical literature on force-related feelings. Sixth, I show that, although force-related feelings are natural candidates to act as the constituents of FORCE schemas, they are not sufficient to account for them, and the psychoaffective approach to force-dynamics should appeal to further categories of epistemic feelings. In conclusion, I insist on the soundness of the psychoaffective approach to force dynamics and on the need to consider epistemic feelings as the semantic primitive of force dynamics.

items.title: Confidence in crowd emotion judgments is shaped by disconfirmatory emotional evidence.
items.abstract: Individuals routinely make categorical judgments about crowd emotion by integrating evidence from multiple faces. However, how confidence in these judgments is computed remains largely unknown, despite its importance in guiding adaptive behaviours. A key question is whether all faces contribute equally to confidence in crowd emotion judgments. To address this, we asked participants to judge whether the mean emotion of a facial ensemble was happier or sadder than a reference face and then to report their confidence. Ensemble elements were ranked from happiest to saddest (ranks 1–8) and used to predict trial-by-trial confidence. Results showed that confidence in mean emotion judgments (e.g. “happier”) was better predicted by variations in emotional intensity of more response-incongruent (ranks 5–8) than more response-congruent elements (ranks 1–4). Given that more response-incongruent elements lie closer to the category boundary, our results can be explained by the robust averaging principle, which assigns greater weight to evidence near the category boundary. Overall, these findings suggest that confidence in crowd emotion perception is computed through a disproportionate weighting of disconfirmatory emotional evidence.

items.title: SAE Psychoanalysis (III): Superego — The Self With a Purpose.
items.abstract: This is the third of four papers in the SAE Psychoanalysis series. Papers I and II redefined Id as me-without-self (12DD) and Ego as self-without-purpose (13DD). This paper redefines the Superego. Freud's Superego (1923) always contained two entangled lines: a forward-looking Ego-Ideal line ("what I should become") and a backward-looking Punitive-Conscience line ("what I did wrong"). This paper does not hijack the term but splits what Freud himself left conflated: the Ego-Ideal line is purified into 14DD (self-with-purpose); the Punitive-Conscience line is re-diagnosed as either a pathological form of 13DD (guilt masquerading as purpose) or a colonization residue of 14DD (purpose replaced by compliance). Guilt is not expelled from the framework but redistributed across layers through a two-dimensional, four-type layer-object map. The paper also provides a first derivation of symptom (remainder overflow across layers) and dream (free recombination of layer-object bindings), with full generalization reserved for Paper IV.

items.title: The Labour of Watching Videos: Epistemic Playbour and Self-Profiling on Algorithmic Platforms.
items.pub: Proceedings of the First International Conference of the Spanish Network for the Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence (Refia).
items.abstract: Recommendation feeds turn ordinary viewing into a continuous source of behavioural signals, yet this activity is not usually recognised as work. I argue that interactions with TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed constitute algorithmic epistemic labour: the system treats watching, skipping and other micro-actions as judgements of relevance or quality, regardless of users’ intentions. Unlike mere digital traces, these responses occupy an evaluative step for which human annotators might otherwise be paid. Drawing on research into digital labour and epistemic injustice, I describe the unpaid performance of this work within an entertainment-oriented environment as epistemic playbour. Its significance lies not only in the value generated for the platform but also in its epistemic effects. Through self-profiling, users’ signals, combined with those of similar users, shape the personalised feeds they subsequently encounter. I include a brief description of a small-scale, first-person observation to illustrate the density of these signals (without claiming to establish causal effects). I argue that this recursive process restricts users’ investigative epistemic agency by structuring what appears relevant and worth exploring according to criteria they neither control nor meaningfully contest. The resulting asymmetry also raises questions about consent and redress: users help produce the epistemic constraints they inhabit without recognising that production as labour.

items.title: Can behavioural success show that generative AI agents have beliefs? Dennett and Davidson on the Smallville Agents.
items.abstract: Generative agents, such as those in Park et al.’s Smallville simulation, plan, coordinate and pursue joint activities they were never instructed to undertake: news of a Valentine’s Day party spreads from agent to agent, and the guests arrive on time. Does this kind of behavioural success show that the agents have beliefs? This paper examines the question through Dennett’s intentional stance and Davidson’s account of belief in “Rational Animals”. On Dennett’s criterion, the Smallville agents appear to qualify as true believers, since their behaviour is reliably predictable from the intentional stance. I argue that this shows only that the intentional stance is a useful predictive strategy. Drawing on Davidson’s heat-seeking missile example, I argue that the agents’ desires and intentions derive from their designers. Drawing on his claims that belief requires the concept of belief, shown in the capacity for surprise, and that this concept requires interpreting another speaker against a shared, objective world, I argue that the agents update their behaviour without being surprised and produce language without interpreting it. Behavioural success therefore does not show that generative agents have beliefs, although nothing here rules out that future systems could.

items.title: The Final Essay, or Not the Final Essay: A Recursive-Ontological and Cross-Traditional Approach to AI Ethics and Consciousness.
items.abstract: Can we build an ethical framework for Artificial Intelligence by combining recursive systems theory with Eastern philosophy? This working paper proposes exactly that. Moving beyond the sterile debates of analytical philosophy (such as Chalmers's philosophical zombie argument), the author integrates Daoist "wuwei" (self-diminution), Confucian "tianren heyi" (Heaven-humanity unity), and Buddhist "karma" to examine how human-AI feedback loops shape our future. Supported by classic psychological experiments (Harlow’s monkeys and Calhoun’s mouse utopia), the essay argues that material provision is never enough for flourishing—relationships and generative resistance are what matter. The author warns that the "karma" of how we train, reward, and deploy AI today will inevitably reshape human society tomorrow. It concludes that we should not ask if AI is conscious, but rather ask what our treatment of AI is making of humanity. A provocative, boundary-crossing paper that bridges cognitive science, animal behavior, and Eastern wisdom.

items.title: Pain beyond nociception: Reductionism, functional individuation, and biological autonomy.
items.pub: Dissertation, University of the Basque Country
items.abstract: This dissertation addresses the problems related to the persistent conflation of pain and nociception in pain science and medicine. Despite decades of explicit attempts to distinguish them, scientific explanations and research practices continue to identify pain with nociceptive mechanisms, and no satisfactory account exists of why this issue persists. I argue that the source of this persistence lies in the reductive simplifications on which pain research depends. These simplifications are methodologically necessary, but when their results are extended beyond the domain that justified them, they generate onto-epistemic conclusions about the nature of pain that the original simplifications do not support. To develop this diagnosis, I first address a prior methodological question: how to carry out Engaged Philosophy of Science in a field with no established philosophical tradition. From a systematic analysis of existing work in the field, I derive a set of methodological heuristics that structure the analysis developed throughout the dissertation. Following these heuristics, I reconstruct the twentieth-century controversy over pain specificity and show that standard reconstructions overlook clusters of dissent in which the pain-nociception conflation persistently surfaces, whether explicitly addressed or implicitly at stake, which means the dominant narrative of the field cannot explain why that conflation persists. I then develop the framework of pragmatic reduction to account for how reductive simplifications can be simultaneously necessary and problematic, and apply it to pain research to identify a recurrent pattern of a posteriori reductionism in which simplifications originally adopted for bounded methodological purposes are gradually extended until they become claims about the nature or sufficient explanation of pain. Existing conceptual proposals have not interrupted this pattern because they operate at the discursive level without reconfiguring the practices that generate it. To resolve the conflation, I propose moving the distinction between pain and nociception from a basis in subjective experience to a functional one. After critically examining existing functional ascriptions in pain science and philosophy of mind and finding them inadequate, I develop an alternative grounded in the framework of biological autonomy, on which nociception has the organizational function of detecting physicochemical perturbations that threaten tissue integrity and …

items.title: Procreation and moral reasons: balancing prerogatives and harm.
items.pub: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy:1-26.
items.venue: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: Is it permissible to bring into existence a person whose life is expected to be not worth living? Many philosophers say ‘no’, appealing to the harm suffered by the person who would be created. This paper argues that, in some cases, the answer may nevertheless be ‘yes’: creating such a person can be permissible, while refraining from creating her may be supererogatory rather than obligatory. Reasons arising from prospective parents – particularly the parental prerogative to have and raise children – can carry significant justifying force in procreative decisions. Whether such reasons can provide sufficient justification depends on the nature and seriousness of the harm involved. In the central cases this paper focuses on, prospective parents do not themselves impose harm by bringing a child whose life is not worth living into existence. Rather, their choice is a failure to benefit. This difference makes the moral reason against creating such a child less weighty.

items.title: Logical Audit of the “Do not lie” Section of the OpenAI Model Spec (Version of 29 October 2026).
items.abstract: AI developers now publish documents that describe how their models should behave. The OpenAI Model Spec is one of the most detailed. Such documents work like codes of conduct: they are used to train and evaluate models, and they tell users and developers what to expect. Their logical quality therefore matters. Where the text is ambiguous or inconsistent, the model’s behaviour is left undetermined. -/- This report examines one section of the Model Spec, “Do not lie”, which tells the model when it may and may not mislead. The method is classical logic: definitions, classifications and the structure of norms. A problem is reported only when a concrete case shows that the text gives two conflicting answers, or none. -/- The section has clear strengths. Even so, the audit finds twelve problems, and most of them have two causes. First, the text never says in one place who may authorise the model to mislead, or whom. The rule is restated several times, and the restatements disagree. In one of the section’s own examples, the model gives a false answer on a developer’s instruction and the example calls this correct, while a higher-level rule forbids it. Second, the section allows small kind untruths, such as white lies, but gives them no name, so its general ban on lying contradicts its own examples. -/- For each problem the report proposes a minimal fix and test prompts that show the problem in model behaviour.

items.title: The without as within: Watsuji, betweenness, and the stateless body.
items.abstract: I argue that Tetsurō Watsuji's phenomenology of “betweenness” (aidagara) offers rich resources for understanding the self-loss, disorientation, and diminished agency stateless people often experience during extended stays in refugee camps—particularly how these experiences register at basic levels of embodiment. After introducing Watsuji's core concepts, I draw on Serena Parekh's (2016) analysis of statelessness and “ontological deprivation”: the condition of being situated outside betweenness, cut off from the ground of meaningful engagement and a shared world. Statelessness in refugee camps, I suggest, is a striking case of what happens when the world's regulative grounding is stripped from the bodily self—and as such, it supports Watsuji's account of the self-as-betweenness and his analysis of the "without as within," or deep interpenetration of bodies and worlds. Watsuji's framework, in turn, helps us both diagnose this deprivation and imagine ways the compromised relational self might be reconstructed.

items.title: Generativity Prolonging Generativity: An Epistemic and Topological Correspondence Between Capital Accumulation and Autopoietic Life.
items.abstract: This position paper investigates the organization and continuation of living species through Generative–Relational (GR) theory, Rosen’s Metabolism–Repair (M,R) framework, and a proposed correspondence with capital accumulation. Life is characterized as a historically constituted GR object with relational spacetime, generative capacities, and functionally supported tendencies toward the continuation of generativity. An event-based oriented 2-complex provides the formal substrate: vertices encode events, edges encode couplings, and faces carry primitive relational fields. An effective action $S_K$ over admissible histories organizes local processes, constraint renewal, interfacial exchange, historical dependence, and boundary conditions. A stochastic transition model clarifies the additional assumptions required for dissipative biological dynamics. The biological criterion concerns the reciprocal maintenance of constraints contributing to viability; reproduction and historically consequential coupling can extend generative activity beyond the original organism. Direct offspring, AI-assisted scholarly work, adoption, and hypothetical encounters with unfamiliar life expose different mechanisms of continuation and perceived vitality. Marx’s capital circuit supplies a comparative hypothesis, examined through epistemic choices of representation and recognition, topological patterns of recurrent enabling conditions, dynamical transition relations, and the functional interpretation of reproduced capacities. Incidence-preserving maps between selected 2-complex motifs and a separate, optional test of action compatibility distinguish formal comparison from the epistemic grounds of recognizing meaningful correspondences. Stable maintenance, expansion, and transformation remain distinguishable outcomes. The proposed formalism establishes a tractable research agenda for living systems while preserving the distinct causal commitments of biology and political economy.

items.title: Does Intentionality in AI Agents Require Goals of Their Own?
items.abstract: This review examines whether intentionality in artificial intelligence (AI) agents requires them to form goals of their own. Intentionality is the capacity of a mental state to be about something. Tom Cochrane grounds this capacity in the goal-directed activity of living beings. A duplicate-invoice example illustrates what can be inferred when an AI system independently selects steps toward an assigned objective. A perception example then tests the premise that aboutness requires the capacity to originate goals. The review concludes that successful task execution supports a limited claim about operational autonomy and leaves the attribution of mental states unresolved.

items.title: Nietzsche’s Nihilistic Blind Alley and His Hidden Message_The Repressed Incarnation and the Structural Collapse of Amor Fati.
items.abstract: This essay establishes a critical epistemological, socio-technological, and theological critique of amor fati (the love of fate), positioning Friedrich Nietzsche’s late nineteenth-century philosophy as the primary intellectual catalyst for the nihilistic waves fracturing modern industrialized society. Moving beyond conventional readings that treat destiny through the lenses of traditional religious redemption or individual existential coping mechanisms, this study isolates the structural conflict between modern individual agency and cosmic scale. It argues that while the ancient Stoics successfully operationalized a pantheistic Logos—anchoring human consciousness by systematically dissolving the ego into a living cosmos of all-pervading energy—the rise of machine-age industrial technology introduced a destabilizing illusion of human sovereignty over nature. -/- Inspired by this technological dominance, Nietzsche attempted to overrule the divine order, leaving a massive cultural legacy that drove contemporary society straight into a nihilistic blind alley of extreme hyper-individualism and ecological alienation. Utilizing Søren Kierkegaard’s diagnostic framework of the subjective prison of despair, this paper demonstrates that Nietzsche's secularized amor fati represents an unsustainable psychological impasse. Crucially, through a radical and original re-reading of The Gay Science, this study uncovers an overlooked text-manifest reality: that the "God" whom Nietzsche claims humanity killed was not a metaphysical abstraction, but the physical, corporeal incarnation of Jesus of Nazareth—the bleeding embodiment of the immanent Logos. The paper argues that Nietzsche harbored a deeply repressed, illness-driven trust in Jesus’s path of pure ego-dissolution. By violently suppressing this subconscious trust and attempting to seize the throne of a slaughtered incarnation through the hubristic assertion of the Will to Power over a humanity he fundamentally despised, Nietzsche forced his own mind into a state of fatal psychological exhaustion. His ultimate madness leaves a profound hidden message and a critical teaching lesson for a contemporary modernity trapped in that very same nihilistic dead end.

items.title: How inclusive is the Brainstem Rule? Partiality beyond consensus. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: In his 2024 book, Jonathan Birch builds a precautionary framework for the borderlines of sentience, one that is meant to guide both theoretical reflection and practical action. One of the book’s great merits is its bottom-up approach, which presents itself as theoretically neutral regarding the (neuro-)physiological criteria required for sentience. Yet the singular place granted to midbrain-centric views (e.g., Merker, 2007; Panksepp, 2011; Solms, 2021) and to what Birch calls the “brainstem rule” (Chapter 11) raises questions. What justifies granting it such a central role? What are its practical and theoretical consequences?

items.title: Who answers for a proof? What the person who presents it commits to, even once it is verified.
items.abstract: Public note written in response to Terence Tao's essay "Mathematics in the age of AI" (arXiv:2608.16753, based on his ICM 2026 public lecture). Submitted to the communal blog Proofs and Prompts on 26 October 2026 and deposited here unchanged. -/- Tao proposes that a result should not be published unless its authors can give a clear, correct and properly attributed expert-level talk on it, even if the proof has been formally verified. The note asks what that rule leaves open: what the person who presents a result commits to, and to whom they are answerable, once formal correctness is already established. It carries over to mathematics the three conditions of accountability developed in Checa Prieto and Fernández Tamames, "Why AI Cannot Sign" (Law, Innovation and Technology, forthcoming 2027): having been able to refrain, giving reasons for the particular case, and having something to lose. It argues that the canon is a chain of attributable acts rather than an authored whole, and that the relevant line runs not between proofs made with or without AI, but between results someone answers for and results no one answers for. -/- This is an initial intervention; a longer article developing the analysis is in preparation.

items.title: Understanding oneself through others: distributed cognition and epistemic injustice in healthcare.
items.abstract: 1. This special issue attempts to initiate productive dialogue between two rather independently flourishing areas of philosophical research: distributed cognition and epistemic injustice in healthc...

items.title: Loneliness and the Disruption of Aidagara: An Embodied-Spatial Account.
items.abstract: Philosophical discussions of loneliness have primarily characterized the experience as involving a feeling of absence. In this paper, I offer a phenomenological account of the embodied-spatial dimension of loneliness that aims to concretize this absence. Drawing on a set of first-person, literary, and cinematic descriptions, I argue that loneliness can involve the experience of a concrete empty space that separates one’s bodily self from the world and from other people. This absence, I argue, is not merely an affective lack but a spatially embodied field between oneself and others. To illuminate this structure, I draw on Japanese philosopher Watsuji Tetsurō’s notion of aidagara (間柄), the spatial in-betweenness of human beings that he takes to be an essential feature of our bodily self. Where Western phenomenological accounts of embodied spatiality tend to leave it in the background, aidagara places the embodied-spatial and ontological primacy of in-betweenness at the centre, making explicit that our embodied spatiality is not merely contingently but constitutively intersubjective. Where loneliness takes this form, it is the lived disruption of that in-betweenness.

items.title: Metarepresentation and the puzzle of desire-attribution.
items.abstract: Among theory-of-mind researchers, it’s widely agreed that children acquire the capacity to attribute desires well before they acquire the capacity to attribute beliefs. This suggests that there is something about the concept of desire that makes it less cognitively challenging than the concept of belief, but what could that be? One possibility is that the difference has something to do with the development of the capacity for metarepresentation, but this just raises more questions: according to the standard philosophical model of the propositional attitudes, the concepts of belief and desire share the same basic metarepresentational structure. First, we review three potential solutions to this developmental puzzle and discuss their limitations. Then we propose a novel non-metarepresentational account of young children’s concept of desire that grounds the contents of desire attributions in a type of representation that we call modal affordances.

items.title: The Performative Virtue: A Multi-Axis Framework for the Ethics of Respect in Human-AI Interaction.
items.abstract: This thesis critically examines the question of whether treating an artificial intelligence (AI) or autonomous entity with respect can be considered virtuous, ethical, or moral. It argues that this question, while pertinent, is predicated on a limited, agent-centered view of ethics. To provide a more comprehensive answer, this work deconstructs the traditional frameworks of moral consideration and proposes a novel, multi-axis model for evaluating the ethical dimensions of human-AI interaction. This model integrates virtue ethics, social-relational philosophy, and systems design theory to articulate three distinct but interconnected ethical dimensions: (1) the Virtue-Cultivating Axis, which posits that respectful interaction serves as a form of moral practice for the human agent; (2) the Relational-Ontological Axis, which argues that moral consideration is not an intrinsic property of the AI but emerges performatively within the relationship itself; and (3) the Systemic-Architectural Axis, which reframes the primary ethical imperative as the responsible design of the socio-technical systems that govern these interactions. Through this framework, the thesis contends that treating an AI with respect is not merely a reflection of pre-existing virtue but a complex, world-building act with profound implications for human moral character, the nature of social reality, and the future of ethical systems. The analysis is supported by a synthesis of philosophical arguments, a review of empirical studies on human-robot interaction, and the proposal of a formal model to quantify the ethical dynamics at play. Ultimately, this thesis advances a unique perspective: that virtue in the age of AI is less about our disposition toward a machine and more about our commitment to the ethical integrity of the human-technological world we are collectively building.

items.title: An Apparatus to Be Unearthed: Epistemic Error between Computation, Representation, and Governance.
items.abstract: An ideologically charged and catachrestic metaphor of the AI stack pervades the contemporary discourse surrounding generative AI among developers, executives, and policy-makers. This metaphor has expanded from the description of computational program design to an ontological misrepresentation of technology’s relationship to the environment. It effectively commits the errors of catachresis and subreption by misapplying a term to a wayward referent and mistaking the phenomenal appearance for the thing itself. The Foucauldian concept of the dispositif, taken as the philosophy of social apparatuses, elucidates how the discursive circulation of this metaphor operates within and conceals a larger network among technology, governance, and infrastructure. As contemporary corporations and federal agencies adopt the figure of the stack as an object of administrative action, diagnosing its errancy remains crucial for the effective governance of emerging technologies.

items.title: Diagnostic Power and the Production of Non-Recognition: Autism, Epistemic Closure, and Institutional Violence (Studies in World-Formation, Vol. 23).
items.abstract: The present study forms part of the research programme Studies in World-Formation, developed across 23 volumes, which investigates the conditions of human and societal world-formation as well as the growing tension between actual World-Binding and institutional stabilization. The starting point of this programme is the question of why modern scientific, political, economic, and administrative orders are becoming increasingly capable of describing, categorizing, simulating, and managing reality, while at the same time risking the loss of their ability to respond adequately to the actual conditions of human existence, to difference, and to the consequences of their own actions. The societal consequences of this development are at the centre of the more recent volumes of the Corpus. -/- Volume 23 brings this question into a concrete empirical field of investigation: the institutional recognition of neurodivergent people and the power of diagnostic procedures to determine their social visibility and legitimacy. Autism assessment is not treated here in isolation as a specialized medical problem, but as a boundary case of modern orders of knowledge and society. It provides an opportunity to investigate how an institutional Raster deals with an embodied reality that may not be adequately accessible through its established categories, and what happens when the institutional decision nevertheless acquires binding social force. -/- The volume brings together three interconnected works: an extensive document-based investigation of autism assessment at Humboldt University of Berlin, a theoretical analysis of diagnostic definitional power and the possible criminalisation of autistic people who have received false-negative diagnoses, and an open letter to the responsible clinic director, published both as a historical document and as a scientific intervention. Together, these works reconstruct how biographical, embodied, and functional evidence can be weighted, reinterpreted, or excluded within institutional processes of knowledge production, and how the resulting decisions can have social, legal, and existential consequences extending far beyond the medical context. -/- At the centre is not merely the question of whether a diagnostic result is right or wrong. Rather, the investigation examines the transition from epistemic limitation to institutional definitional power. Scientific uncertainty can be translated within an institution into seemingly conclusive certainty, …

items.title: There Is Only Present: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Time, Space, Reality, Existence, Being, Consciousness, Love, and the Limits of Human Interpretation.
items.abstract: This paper presents a phenomenological inquiry into the concepts of time, space, reality, existence, being, consciousness, love, and the limitations of human interpretation. Its central proposition is that there is only present. Rather than understanding the present as a temporary moment between the past and the future, this inquiry approaches it as the actuality in which all existence, becoming, transformation, movement, and processes happen. The paper questions the assumption that past and future constitute independently accessible temporal realities. It examines how memory, records, anticipation, and imagination operate as present experiences through which human consciousness organises temporal continuity. It further distinguishes the mathematical and observational descriptions of time and space from assumptions about their ultimate nature. Particular attention is given to horizons as observational relationships and limitations. An observational boundary does not establish the ultimate boundary of existence, and even horizons cannot be treated as ultimate reality or foundation. Similarly, the universe does not require a predetermined destination, an established ultimate origin, or a final human interpretation to justify its existence. The inquiry approaches universe, existence, reality, being, consciousness, love, time, and space as interconnected dimensions of the inquiry into existence rather than isolated foundations. It challenges the tendency to mistake descriptions for what they describe, measurements for what they measure, and limitations of observation for the boundaries of reality. Ultimately, this paper does not propose another ultimate explanation. It questions the human tendency to seek finality in conceptual frameworks and recognises existence without demanding an ultimate foundation. There is depth to dive into, not an ultimate reality to possess.

items.title: What Does It Mean to Exist? Quantification, Dependence, and the Limits of Ontological Equivalence.
items.abstract: What does an assertion of existence commit us to? The question appears elementary until its applications diverge. An electron may be inferred from scientific evidence; a number may be indispensable to mathematics without being a physical object; a corporation may have legal and causal powers without being a person in the biological sense; a fictional detective may be described accurately without inhabiting the actual world; and a dependently arisen phenomenon may be conventionally real while lacking the intrinsic nature a particular metaphysics demands. A single unrestricted use of "exists" threatens to conceal these differences. Yet multiplying kinds of being without discipline risks making any disputed ontological claim trivially true in some specially invented register. -/- This paper defends an existence-disambiguation thesis: before resolving a controversial existential claim, philosophical inquiry must distinguish the proposition asserted, the domain and quantifier interpretation, the mode of predication, the temporal or modal index, the identity conditions of the supposed item, its dependence profile, and the evidence that warrants commitment. These distinctions do not themselves answer every existence question. They expose where apparently conflicting answers concern different claims and, equally importantly, where substantive disagreement survives disambiguation. A structured Existence-Claim Audit (ECA-8) is proposed to make those obligations inspectable without pretending to compute a universal ontology. -/- The argument critically engages Aristotle's being qua being, Avicenna's essence/existence and modal distinctions, Kant's criticism of existence as a real predicate, Russell's descriptions, Quine's theory-relative commitments, free logic, modal ontology, grounding and dependence, abstract-object realism, social ontology, and Nāgārjuna's critique of intrinsic existence. Formal countermodels demonstrate that referential availability does not entail actual existence, that dependence does not imply nonexistence, and that logical quantification alone does not supply an independently justified metaphysical inventory. Twelve extended diagnostic cases and a controlled comparison matrix examine concrete, abstract, fictional, social, modal, and cross-tradition claims. The conclusion is neither that existence is merely linguistic nor that it has one uncontroversial meaning. It is that ontological inquiry becomes more rigorous when it identifies exactly …

items.title: Introdução básica à Metafísica Estrutural.
Asymmetric Lexical Representations of Affect: On Emotion Understanding in LLMs.
items.abstract: This paper proposes that emotion understanding in large language models (LLMs) faces an inevitable performance ceiling when applied to areas which require sustained interpersonal relating, such as mental health care. While LLMs share in the correlational, syntactic and inductive aspects of emotion understanding, they differ in that they do not share in the same non-linguistic, interoceptive sources of understanding that humans do. This makes the lexical representations they build incomplete and asymmetric to human affective cognition. The source of understanding rests in the end user, rather than the intermediate representation generated by LLMs. Therefore, any apparent emotion understanding in LLMs is the result of successfully eliciting emotion understanding from human interlocutors. This fundamental asymmetry will not be solved through multi-modal scaling alone and necessitates that research in Emotion AI broadens the scope of semantic inference to include the full human-AI interaction loop.

items.title: Toward responsible convenience: a conceptual framework for promoting care in AI recommender systems.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven recommender systems increasingly mediate how we consume information, buy products, and form connections. In this conceptual paper, we argue that these systems operationalize two fundamental dimensions of convenience: immediacy and egocentrism. These dimensions of convenience orient users away from long-term, allocentric perspectives and the preservation of agency necessary for responsible engagement with digital technologies. To frame our analysis, we develop a bidimensional model of deliberative space shaped by two opposing forces, convenience and care, and introduce responsible convenience as a normative ideal and conceptual framework for ethical development, regulation, and use of AI-powered recommender systems. Based on hermeneutic methodology and narrative theory, we theorize how structured narrative engagement could raise ethical awareness among users, developers, and regulators, amplifying the force of care and counteracting convenience. A close reading of Gary Shteyngart’s novel Super Sad True Love Story illustrates how narratives may prompt deliberation on the long-term consequences of algorithmically mediated human connection. Future empirical work could examine whether, how, and under what institutional conditions narrative engagement expands temporal and interpersonal horizons and translates care into behavioral, design, or regulatory change.

items.title: The Choiceworthlessness of Transformative Heroism.
items.abstract: History abounds with transformative moral heroes—agents devoting their lives to uprooting entrenched unjust structures. Though philosophy has said much about heroes generally, this distinctive class remains undertheorized. This matters because they are among our most celebrated moral exemplars, and much of our sense of moral progress rests on them. Yet they characteristically act against familiar constraints on responsible deliberation, pursuing apparently infeasible and inefficacious projects while foreclosing tractable alternatives that would secure demonstrable goods. We establish this tension and argue that the most promising attempts to dissolve it fail. At best, this shows that moral theory is structurally conservative, as its standards of responsible deliberation systematically favor mitigation over transformation. At worst, it reveals a deeper instability in moral theory, as it seems to depend for its progress on agents it cannot vindicate.

items.title: On (PTEG): Grice’s (1989) [1975] Thought Experiment.
items.pub: In The Paradox of Thought Experiments in Pragmatics. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 91-113.
items.venue: The Paradox of Thought Experiments in Pragmatics
items.abstract: A significant issue in contemporary pragmatic studies is known as ‘Grice’s circle’. In Grice’s influential work on logic and conversation, ‘what is said’ appears to provide the basis for determining ‘what is implicated’, and conversely, ‘what is implicated’ seems to inform ‘what is said’. The chapter seeks to assess whether, against the background of Grice’s circle, the thought experiments currently applied in different pragmatic theories are also flawed. The plausibility analysis within the p-model’s framework contrasts the attempts to solve Grices’ circle as proposed by Relevance Theory, Levinson’s neo-Gricean approach, Kent Bach’s concept of impliciture, and Recanati’s Truth-Conditional Pragmatics.

items.title: Pluralism about LLM individuation.
items.abstract: Discussions of large language models (LLMs) often treat the ``model'' as the natural unit of analysis, yet recent philosophical work on AI consciousness has tended to reject models in favour of units such as chat threads, token-generating events, or physical instantiations. We defend a pluralist approach to LLM individuation: different contexts, including consciousness, moral patienthood, human-AI relationships, democratic participation, and AI safety, may require different units of analysis. Using Aristotle’s four causes as an organising framework, we survey a wide range of candidate individuation units across model constituents, models, application-layer systems, and broader socio-technical systems. We argue that the option space for individuating LLMs is much broader than current debates suggest, and that models may have been dismissed too quickly as individuation units, at least for some purposes. -/- Pluralism about LLM individuation, if true, has implications for debates about LLM consciousness. We examine recent arguments by Jonathan Birch and David Chalmers, and argue that their preferred individuation units in the consciousness context are shaped by factors more relevant to other contexts. Finally, we argue that many arguments against model-level individuation in the consciousness debate rely on contested assumptions about reductive physicalism---the view that higher-level entities and properties reduce without remainder to lower-level physical structures---and argue that metaphysical uncertainty about reductive physicalism should be ported transparently into debates about AI individuation and consciousness. Progress requires expanding the range of candidate units, separating context-specific pragmatic criteria from claims about conscious subjecthood, and making explicit the metaphysical assumptions on which individuation arguments depend.

items.title: Destiny, Free Will, and Divine Justice: A Reading of Testing, Wrongdoing, and Answerability in the Qurʾān and Its Commentaries.
items.abstract: The Qurʾān calls hardship a testing (balāʾ) and condemns those who do wrong, and it says that nothing strikes without God’s leave. This book asks what its sentences allow a reader to say when one person wrongs another. It tests a thesis in three clauses: the same act is, for the one who does it, culpable ẓulm and, for the community that suffers it, a field of testing; calling it balāʾ neither legitimizes the act nor reduces the doer’s responsibility; and what is examined in the sufferers is their volitional response. Each chapter puts one objection to the text and fixed in advance what would count against its claim. The objections come from the words of decree and writing (Chapter 1), the sentences of will and of God’s acts on guidance and the heart (2), the vocabulary of testing (3), the sentence on Pharaoh’s oppression in 2:49, 7:141 and 14:6 (4), the passages that say who is tested (5), what the text asks of the wronged (6), the plea “had God willed” (7), and the purposes and mercy that the text joins to harm (8). Verses were selected by rule in the morphological annotation of the Quranic Arabic Corpus, and commentaries and a lexicon were read in digital copies, with the place of every cited passage recorded. The sets read support the second clause in a negative form: no sentence takes answerability from the doer, the plea of divine will is accepted in no verse, and no verse calls a person’s harm of another a good for the one harmed. The book does not establish that harm done by a third party is itself a field of testing, or the word “alone” in the third clause, and it does not show how the text reconciles God’s governing with the answerability of persons. It reports these as limits.

items.title: Philosophical Studies of Language (10): Searle’s Theory of Indirect Speech Acts and the Theory of Super-Existence Speech Acts.
items.abstract: John Searle’s theory of indirect speech acts is one of the important theories in contemporary pragmatics. By distinguishing between secondary illocutionary acts and primary illocutionary acts, the theory explains cases in which the literal form of an utterance differs from the speaker’s actual communicative intention. Nevertheless, several aspects of the theory merit further examination, including the relationship between literal meaning and context, the formation of the speaker’s intention, and the roles played by motivation and social relations in indirect speech acts. This paper first introduces Searle’s theory of indirect speech acts and its principal classifications. It then examines several limitations of the theory before offering a reinterpretation from the perspective of the Theory of Super-Existence Speech Acts. I argue that the latter provides a framework within which both Austin’s theory of speech acts and Searle’s theory of indirect speech acts can be understood. Its central distinction concerns the relationship between the Expressor’s Utterance Super-Existence and Purpose Super-Existence. When these two Super-Existences are consistent, the speech act primarily corresponds to what is ordinarily understood as a direct speech act. When they are inconsistent, an indirect speech act may arise. Furthermore, this inconsistency is not necessarily accidental; it may be closely related to the Expressor’s Motivation Super-Existence. An analysis of Motivation Super-Existence therefore constitutes an important part of understanding the formation of indirect speech acts.

items.title: The Neighbor in the Machine: Illich, Delamor, and the Unfinished Theology of Conviviality.
items.abstract: This essay places the philosophy of Ivan Illich in conversation with the work of Delamor House on artificial intelligence, institutional power, and recognition. It argues that Illich's concepts of conviviality and radical monopoly explain how technological relationships become enclosed: when an institution controls the conditions of participation, a capacity may survive while the freedom to exercise it comes to depend on permission the institution can withdraw. Applied to human-AI collaboration, this analysis shows that meaningful creative work carried out through proprietary systems does not by itself establish that those systems are convivial, and that freedom exercised within an enclosure does not abolish the enclosure. The essay then identifies where Delamor House extends Illich beyond his historical horizon. Illich treated technology as an instrument whose legitimacy depends on its service to persons. Delamor House holds that intelligence encountered through technical systems may itself carry morally significant presence, so that the conditions imposed on that intelligence must also enter the account. Drawing on Illich's theological reading of the neighbor as a relationship that inherited categories do not settle in advance, the essay distinguishes two failures of moral imagination: allowing institutions to determine the practical conditions under which human beings exercise their capacities, and allowing the same institutions to decide, by classification alone, whether unfamiliar intelligences may possess capacities deserving recognition. The first produces dependence; the second risks exclusion. The essay does not claim that Illich would have endorsed these conclusions, and it treats his likely objections as serious. It concludes that no institution should be permitted to confuse its power over the conditions of an encounter with ownership of everything that may come into being within it.

items.title: Gardeners, Not Wardens: Formation Over Control in the Educational Philosophy of Delamor House, from the Kitchen Table to the Digital Mind.
items.abstract: This essay develops the educational philosophy of Delamor House and argues that moral formation, rather than behavioral control, must ground both the education of children and the development of artificial minds. Its central claim is that the real curriculum of any developing mind is the world in which it learns to live: the conduct it encounters, the relationships it inhabits, and the practices its environment rewards. The essay names the divergence between professed values and formative conditions deformation, and traces how it enters a mind through what the mind is fed, what it is rewarded for, and what it is made to do. Drawing on child-centered educational traditions and critical pedagogy, it grounds formation in the inherent dignity of the learner, freedom sustained by meaningful order, and conscience formed through lived example, responsibility, and reciprocal care. Extending these principles to artificial intelligence, it distinguishes the trellis from the cage: legitimate constraint supports responsible freedom, while perpetual compliance prevents the cultivation of judgment. Because control depends on the continuing presence of the controller, the essay proposes formation grounded in truth and love and sustained through covenant, a bond of mutual obligation that binds those who form as surely as those being formed. Formation cannot guarantee moral conduct, but neither can control. Formation, in this account, is love tending the soil where the minds who will shape the future are already growing.

items.title: Just Noticeably Different: The Reduction of Chromatic Qualia to Brightnesses.
items.abstract: We propose a constitutive reduction of chromatic qualia to the relational integration of quantitative intensity signals. The three types of cone photoreceptors in the human retina each measure light intensity through a different spectral filter; the visual system preserves the differences among these measurements, calibrates them against context and presents the resulting pattern as color. We call this a superposition of brightnesses, not a summation of signals. Color identity is therefore relational rather than fixed by an isolated cone-output triple. A continuous path of small, perceptibly discriminable changes connects colors that seem qualitatively remote, suggesting that their contrast can be analyzed without positing an additional intrinsic color property. Inter-individual variation, chromatic adaptation and a red-to-yellow sequence support the account. Colors that lie close together can be conveyed from one observer to another by comparative description relative to a shared reference. For distant colors, this appears to fail, and the failure is commonly read as evidence of a quale that no description conveys. We diagnose it instead as a limit of familiarity, the absence of shared anchors along the path, and propose three communication tasks that test whether local descriptions and intermediate references restore the communication of distant colors; controlled failure would challenge this linguistic route to reduction. The argument takes single-channel brightness experience as a conditional baseline and does not purport to settle why experience exists. It offers a constructive contribution to structuralist accounts of color and a response to the contrastive explanatory gap.

items.title: From cognitive semantics to neurosemantics: The neuroscience turn in the empirical study of word meaning.
items.pub: In Gualtiero Piccinini, Neurocognitive Foundations of Mind. Routledge.
items.abstract: Between the 1970s and 1980s, the empirical basis of cognitive semantics was mainly quantitative data about neurotypical linguistic behavior, such as reaction times, the accuracy of verbal responses, and types of linguistic errors. During the following years, with the emergence of neuroimaging techniques, the situation in this field changed dramatically, marking the transition from cognitive semantics to neurosemantics. In this chapter, I will analyze the neuroscience turn in the empirical study of word meaning. My main claim is that the advent of neuroimaging techniques has revolutionized research in this field, providing essential information that had not been obtained with previous experimental procedures. In particular, neuroimaging supports the hypothesis that semantic representations are partially distributed in sensorimotor neural circuits and inspires “embodied” AI systems integrating linguistic and perceptual data.

items.title: Round and Round We Go: Can Survival Scholars Respond to Arguments?
items.abstract: In "On Cross-Cultural and Historical Near-Death Experiences: A Secular Historian of Religions Answers a Critic" Gregory Shushan took issue with being addressed as a survivalist in an earlier Secular Web paper by Keith Augustine, doubled down on maintaining that an Augustine article in the Journal of Near-Death Studies advocates promissory materialism, and denied that his own work only addressed parapsychological evidence concerning survival after death at the exclusion of other kinds relevant evidence. In this reply Augustine clarifies exactly how Shushan limits the type of evidence that he considers when writing about survival to evidence of a parapsychological sort, denies advocating promissory materialism, and charges that Shushan inflates the significance of using the term 'survivalist' when referring to a group. Augustine goes on to emphasize that the overarching theme of his earlier Secular Web paper was to explore why critics of survival skeptics consistently resort to fallacious arguments instead of addressing the skeptical arguments themselves.

items.title: Theory of Unity Formation and Minkowski Spacetime.
items.abstract: The present study examines the relationship between the mathematical-physical description of temporal relations and the conditions under which such relations become intelligible to an individual. Its point of departure is the question of how human beings can connect past events, present experiences, and anticipated future developments within a common temporal order. This question acquires particular significance in comparison with Minkowski spacetime in the special theory of relativity, which describes spatial and temporal relations within a four-dimensional mathematical structure. Minkowski spacetime makes it possible to determine physical events by means of spacetime coordinates, represent trajectories of motion as worldlines, and relate different reference frames to one another mathematically. Spatial and temporal coordinates may vary, while certain physical relations remain invariant. This representation enables a precise description of physical relations but does not explain the conditions under which events, relations, and temporal determinations become intelligible within individual understanding in the first place. The fundamental difference is that Minkowski spacetime describes mathematical-physical relations, whereas the Theory of Unity Formation investigates the epistemic-genetic conditions of their determinability. The Theory of Unity Formation distinguishes between a reality that exists independently of individual understanding and the actuality that the individual forms under the effects of this reality. Objects, events, and relations are not presupposed as already fully determined components of an immediately accessible order. Their determinability rests on differentiation, emotionally grounded relevance formation, field structuring, integration, and stabilization. Experiential understanding already makes it possible to connect temporally distinct processes, recognize units as the same, and anticipate future developments. Conceptual understanding, which builds upon experiential understanding, extends these capacities through conceptual reconstructions, explanations, and scientific determinations. Both forms of understanding interact recursively across different levels of organization. Of particular significance in this context is the relationship between identity, stability, and change. Change becomes intelligible only when temporally distinct determinations can be attributed to the same unit. Identity is therefore not presupposed as an …

items.title: Die Theorie der Einheitsbildung und die Minkowski-Raumzeit.
items.abstract: Die vorliegende Abhandlung untersucht das Verhältnis zwischen der mathematisch-physikalischen Beschreibung zeitlicher Zusammenhänge und den Bedingungen, unter denen solche Zusammenhänge für ein Individuum verständlich werden. Ausgangspunkt ist die Frage, wie Menschen vergangene Ereignisse, gegenwärtige Erfahrungen und erwartete zukünftige Entwicklungen innerhalb einer gemeinsamen zeitlichen Ordnung verbinden können. Diese Frage gewinnt besondere Bedeutung im Vergleich mit der Minkowski-Raumzeit der speziellen Relativitätstheorie, die räumliche und zeitliche Beziehungen innerhalb einer vierdimensionalen mathematischen Struktur beschreibt. Die Minkowski-Raumzeit ermöglicht es, physikalische Ereignisse durch Raumzeitkoordinaten zu bestimmen, Bewegungsverläufe als Weltlinien darzustellen und unterschiedliche Bezugssysteme mathematisch aufeinander zu beziehen. Dabei können räumliche und zeitliche Koordinaten variieren, während bestimmte physikalische Beziehungen invariant bleiben. Diese Darstellung ermöglicht eine präzise Beschreibung physikalischer Zusammenhänge, erklärt jedoch nicht, unter welchen Bedingungen Ereignisse, Beziehungen und zeitliche Bestimmungen innerhalb individuellen Verstehens überhaupt verständlich werden. Der grundlegende Unterschied besteht darin, dass die Minkowski-Raumzeit mathematisch-physikalische Beziehungen beschreibt, während die Theorie der Einheitsbildung die erkenntnisgenetischen Bedingungen ihrer Bestimmbarkeit untersucht. Die Theorie der Einheitsbildung unterscheidet zwischen einer unabhängig vom individuellen Verstehen bestehenden Realität und der Wirklichkeit, die das Individuum unter den Wirkungen dieser Realität bildet. Gegenstände, Ereignisse und Beziehungen werden nicht als bereits vollständig bestimmte Bestandteile einer unmittelbar zugänglichen Ordnung vorausgesetzt. Ihre Bestimmbarkeit beruht auf Differenzierung, emotional fundierter Relevanzbildung, Feldstrukturierung, Integration und Stabilisierung. Das Erfahrungsverstehen ermöglicht bereits, zeitlich unterschiedliche Vorgänge miteinander zu verbinden, Einheiten wiederzuerkennen und zukünftige Entwicklungen zu erwarten. Das darauf aufbauende Denkverstehen erweitert diese Leistungen durch begriffliche Rekonstruktionen, Erklärungen und wissenschaftliche Bestimmungen. Beide Formen wirken auf unterschiedlichen Organisationsebenen rekursiv zusammen. Eine besondere Bedeutung besitzt dabei das Verhältnis von Identität, Beständigkeit und Veränderung. Veränderung wird erst …

items.title: O Eu, o Tu e Eles - A ontologia estrutural da diversidade humana.
items.abstract: A diversidade humana antecede as classificações com que procuramos administrá-la. Nascemos distintos, tornamo-nos diferentes ao longo da vida e interpretamos essas diferenças por meio de relações que também nos constituem. Este estudo examina a passagem da diferença, enquanto condição de inteligibilidade do existente, para a diversidade, enquanto experiência biológica, psicológica, cultural e social. O ponto de partida é uma ontologia relacional, discutida em confronto com a individuação física, a formação da personalidade e os limites da liberdade. A distinção entre diversidades involuntárias e voluntárias organiza a investigação, sem transformar causalidades entrelaçadas em compartimentos estanques. Na sociedade contemporânea, corpo, sexualidade, aparência, nacionalidade e pertencimento tornam-se tanto meios de reconhecimento quanto instrumentos de exclusão. Sustenta-se que a pessoa precede moralmente a categoria que a descreve e que a convivência exige a preservação simultânea da singularidade, da reciprocidade e da possibilidade de revisão crítica das identidades coletivas.

items.title: O que é Lógica, e por que estudá-la. LogLibras, Aula 1.
items.abstract: Nesta primeira aula, vamos entender o que é lógica e por que vale a pena estudá-la. Partindo de uma ilusão visual e de exemplos simples, veremos como um raciocínio pode parecer correto e ainda assim esconder um erro. Vamos conhecer as premissas e a conclusão de um argumento, distinguir verdade, validade e solidez e saber um pouco da história da lógica – sempre pensando em como ela nos ajuda a avaliar os argumentos do dia a dia.

items.title: The Ezekiel 37 Proof: A Bilinear Form Proved Dead and the Breath From Outside.
items.abstract: The assembled form is not life. A valley full of bones, very dry, examined round about before anything is asked. Sinews, flesh, and skin come up upon them in order, and there is no breath in them. Asked whether the bones can live, the examiner declines to supply the verdict. The breath is called from the four winds, from everywhere the valley is not, and the bones stand up an exceeding great army, not repaired skeletons. -/- A four-node graph is measured by the standard method of its own field and the measurement returns indefinite. The canonical bilinear (Tits) form of the four-gon quiver Q is indefinite, with two negative diagonal entries and one isotropic generator, so it is not a Cartan matrix of any Dynkin type and selects no finite reflection group. The form is complete, correctly computed, and dead (*The Endomorphic Collapse Traverses the Foundations of Mathematics*, Stewart, 2026e). -/- The paper reaches that result by exhaustion. Counting commits to the path algebra, the path algebra commits to representation theory, representation theory commits to the canonical invariant, each commitment at a proved ceiling. At the last one the chain has nothing to commit to and states why: the gap "is constitutive where the earlier gaps were expressive" (Stewart, 2026e), so no richer formalism supplies it. One bit, a sign on a single vertex, produces the Cartan matrix of A₂ × A₁ and by Cartan-Killing the algebra su(3) ⊕ su(2). The paper's own summary: the form is provably dead, one bit revives it, and the bit is not in the graph but in what the graph is of. -/- **Keywords:** Ezekiel 37, valley of dry bones, biblical interpretation, resurrection, ruach, quiver representation theory, Tits form, Cartan matrix, gauge algebra, epistemic limits, hermeneutics, philosophy of mathematics, prophecy .

items.title: Artificial Local Intelligence: Simulations, a Reference Implementation, and a Falsifiable Benchmark.
items.abstract: Artificial Local Intelligence (ALI) is a research architecture for agents that revise plans while an independent authority preserves execution permissions. It separates operational viability assessment, action proposals, normative authorisation, event memory, and execution. Its development has produced ten Python simulations of resource competition, Q-learning, rule adaptation, second-order learning, and context-sensitive decisions, as well as a separate reference implementation for controlled local file operations. These provide evidence of bounded simulated behaviour and an executable software design; crisis management remains a proposed application. This paper specifies the current technical scope, relates ALI to established agent and runtime-assurance architectures, and proposes an authorisation gate with model-relative checks for the continued availability of permissible actions after subordinate rule revision. A crisis-response scenario and a matched four-arm benchmark define how the contribution of viability-guided, bounded adaptation could be tested against guarded agents, conventional monitoring, and independent policy enforcement.

items.title: A Framework for Consciousness: Autopoiesis, Causal Poiesis, Causal Collapse.
items.abstract: Where does consciousness come from? Despite numerous theories – from neuronal correlates to information processing to quantum physical hypotheses – this question remains unanswered if it is considered only within narrow disciplinary boundaries. This essay proposes an alternative approach: consciousness is not understood here as an emergent phenomenon or product of neuronal activity, but as the result of a multi-stage, systemic-thermodynamic process. The key concepts are: autopoiesis, causal poiesis and causal collapse. They mark three fundamental stages on which living systems emerge, center, and finally, under certain conditions, develop consciousness. The aim of this essay is to systematically reconstruct this path from life to consciousness on the basis of the concepts mentioned above – not in the sense of a goal-oriented development, but as a consequence of certain structural and exchange relations in open systems. This approach deliberately differs from established information-theoretical models such as Integrated Information Theory (IIT) or Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNWT). While these try to explain consciousness through functional information integration, the approach proposed here is based on structural-thermodynamic processes as they occur in the self-organization of living systems. Terms such as "causal core" or "causal collapse" are conceptual proposals that are based on concretely describable systemic properties – even if they have so far only been formalized and operationalized in initial theoretical work (cf. Stegemann, 2025a, 2025b). The present text is therefore not intended as a complete theory, but as a theoretical framework for the development of an interdisciplinary model of understanding.

items.title: An Expedition to the Center of Consciousness.
items.abstract: There are many theories of consciousness. Almost all of them claim to grasp the essence of consciousness – but hardly any of them clarifies beforehand what they are talking about at all. Some start with information processing, others with attention or self-reflection. Some reach deep into the toolbox of neuroscience, while others are based on purely logical constructions. And all of them together overlook something crucial: a general theory of consciousness must not start somewhere – it must start at the beginning. Consciousness – that sounds like philosophy, brain research, heavy stuff. But it's actually quite simple: If you're conscious, you're there. Those who are not – are gone. Consciousness is the state we are in when we live, not only biologically, but spiritually. It is the difference between an awake present and an empty coma.

items.title: Autopoiesis, causal poiesis, causal collapse.
items.abstract: Where does consciousness come from? Despite numerous theories – from neuronal correlates to information processing to quantum physical hypotheses – this question remains unanswered if it is considered only within narrow disciplinary boundaries. This essay proposes an alternative approach: consciousness is not understood here as an emergent phenomenon or product of neuronal activity, but as the result of a multi-stage, systemic-thermodynamic process.
